div.p: " THE PASSING OP ARTHITE" (DEAN STANLEY). As bird of calm poised high on outstretched wing 'Upon the ether thick with angry spray And blank with storm, he faced the dawning day Presaging sunrise; nor did he cease to sing, Amid the pulses of the hurricane, Of righteousness and peace the eternal reign; • 'Till ever andluon the jubilant ring Of that heraldic voice tilled half the world. Re from high vantage hailed the unrisen sun Beheld " the raven wings of darkness" furled; Nor could he hush his joy for victory won. Right on and through the storm, our bird of Jove. With olive-leaf in mouth, has passed to brood In summer seas, and live on heavenly food Amid the throng of those who greatly love. F—Erange2ical Magazine.

- FOR JESUS' SAXE. Out of blank nought, the world's without a shape, Wherefore, Creative Power, didst thou uproar. And bid the unive-stal light escape From tombs of darkness, dread, eternal drear? With plastic skill why mould each railing siatiefe From mass chaotic, till that over all God-crowned perfection reigned without a peer. From vast immensity to infinitely small? "For Jesus' sake,"'cornes answer from Jehovah's hall. 'Eisen wherefore, proud, presurnpkteudonfosrmtileertaalidcaln, Heaven's spangled banner der The sun opes Orient gates with golden, gleam The Queen of Night smiles from her ebone throne; Shall myriad monstre suns pierce space unkn To twinkle but as tiny stars for thee? Have earth's strauge derdzens now hhapel in stone Through ages wrathful fouaht, gambolled in glee? And has for thee supreme laboured eternity? When man, ungrateful. spurned the claims of heaven, Reproached and mocked his .I.fairer to his face. Leagued with the traitor from his pre.enee driven, Doomed to dark chains uncheered by h )pe of grace; Ye thunderbolts, why sped ye not apace, -Nor daslidsnan to some dread domain below Wherefore dtd mercy spare the rebel race, .Granting them honour who deserved but Woe? "For Jesus' sake" he made them sons wha called him foe.

Alas, poor man! h )sv needy lathy lot Nought but thy threadbare self thfai bring'st with thee: And, pauper, more from earth thou takest not, Whilst all thou needest is God's property; Then how sustain thy poor frail entity? 'Thrice happy man, thy God, richer in nought Than in his bounty, gracious yields the key, " for Jesus' sake," of all his treasures. fraught With vasty stores of good; then laud him as ye ought. Wherefore, ye martyrs, brave the scorching the, Rejoicing even at the glowing stake; In spite of tyranny's: fell power aspire, The bands of superstition and of sin to break? Ye answer from your tombs " For Jesus' sake." Hence did ye count your every gain but loss; Ye feared not of His sufferings to partake, But dared the rack, the prison, and the cross ; Judging, compared with Him, all earthly things but dross "For Jesus' sake "—be this—not human deeds— Ye saints—your hope of joys on highs! And ye! who strive from sin and man-made creeds To rescue souls; be this your battle cry! Ye sons of God, be tills the sacred tie That binds you to each other, strangling strife! Be this the golden rule by which to try The worth of actions—for ambition's rife ! Re this the motto, and the motive of your "For Jesus' sake."
Jos. C. VERCO.

div.head: Variftio.
div.p: Variftio.

At the door of a ready-made clothing store in one of the -poorer quarters of Paris is the sign:—" Don't go somewhere else to be robbed; walk in here." An advutisement reads:—" Wanted, a young man to be partly oat-door and partly behind the counter.' Hereupon the Cleveland Leader asks, "What will be the result when. ,the door slams ?" "When I was a young man," says Josh Billings, "I was always in a hurry to hold the big end of a log, and do all the lifting; now I am older, I seize hold of the small end, and do all the grunting." "Do you know, Mr. Smith," asked Mrs. S., in a reproving way, "that that pipe is hurtful to you; and it is your enemy?" "Yes," replied Smith, calmly ejecting a fleecy' cloud; "yes, I know it, and I'm trying to smoke the rascal out." Conversation is a serious thing with some people. One .of this kind on board a train was asked a very simple ques- tion by a fellow-passenger. She made a deprecating gesture and replied, "Excuse me, sir, bat I am only going to the next station, and it's not worth while to begin a conversa- tion." Captain Bogardue's feat of breaking 500 glass balls in twenty-five minutes and fifteen seconds, says the Philadel- phia News, has been excelled by a Philadelphia man, wird was c arying a basket of glass ball to a shooting range and stepped on a banana peel. A witness being interrogated as to whether the in the case was drunk, replied, "Well, I Can't say that ex- actly; but! saw him sitting in the middle of the floor, mak- ing grabs in the air, and saying he'd be whipped if he didn't catch the bed the next time it ran round him." A man went through bankruptcy. He had owned a fine horse and gig, and they both disappeared for a time, but by and by the horse and gig were both doing service for the same owner again. On being asked what this meant, the man's reply was, "I went through the bankruptcy court, but the horse and gig went round." A boy on Jones-street was the other evening eating away at a big cocoanut that had been cracked open-with a brick- bat, when a pedestrian felt it his duty to halt and remark, "Boy, don't you know that too much of that stuff may give you the colic ?" " I guess so," was the reply. "Then, why .do you eat it?" "Well, if my chum, who lives next door, can stand the smallpox for six weeks, I guess I can put up with the colic for three or foal- hours!" was the reply, as he bit off another big hunk. Alas that there should be so many poor souls who in this world and that which is to come look forward to nothing that is substantially comfortable and satisfying! Here, for instance, is a veritable descendant of. Saint Martha, who came into a neighbour's house in Buffalo, downmst, weary- ing with many cares and cumbered with much serving. "so much to do! cleaning, working, cooking, washing, sew- ing, and everything else! No rest ! never was, never will be for me!" "Oh yes," said the good woman she addressed, "there will be a rest one day for us all—a tang rest." "Not for me! not for me!" was the reply," Whenever Ido die, there will be certain to be resurrection the very next day! It would be just my luck!" THE COMET'S TA.IL.—On the (lay before the shooting of President Garfield, a strange negro appeared among the coloured folks of Richmond, Virginia, and said, in warning tones, "Do comet's tail am up ! he affrighted negroes took up the cry, and looking solemnly into each other's faces, groaned, "Do comet's tail am up!" Just before sunset the sky was illumined by a strange light, which changed and flashed like- the aurora borealis, and the cry of the darkies was, "The comet has done bust I" Leaders among the cal:eared people predicted that within a few hours a blazing mantle from the shattered tail of the comet would inwrap the earth, and that all living things would be roasted under its fiery folds; and the impenitent were warned to seek re- ligion at once. The Rev. John Jasper, who stood out against the world in holding that the sun" do move," had been taken ill; then the President was shot ; and shortly afterwards a popular man among the coloured people, Park Moody, came to a violent death. Evils without termination seemed to have begun, and the cornet was regarded as the bringer of all that had come and all that were to come. The rush to get religion and be prepared for the worst was for .several days so great that the business of the large tobacco factories was seriously obstructed by the absence, either of body or of mind, of the coloured workmen.—American Paper. Tug Usgs OF BEETLFs.—Beetleimayibe said to perform -the function in nature of universal scavengers, chiefly with regard to the smaller quantities of animal and vegetable Matter neglected by the larger animals, but not 'always, their small size and very varied forms and insacirtfiebling them to attack, by methods impossible to other animals, and to clear from earth's surface, the carcases even of large quadrupeds and the dead trunks of the lafgest forest trees. Different groups are organised respectively for terrestrial and aquatic life and for every shade of variety' in each; for living in or 'feeding on vegetable substances, from the smallest cryptogams, to the root, bark, wood, fruit, and seed of the highest forms of vegetation; and for disposing of excrementitiods as well as dead animal substencee. All forms of locomotion are displayed; many are specially adapted for burrowing, and for such curious operations as sawinz branches or drilling holes in solid wood. There are predaceous groups—terreetrial, arboreal, and aquatic—and groups parastic of the living bodies 'of other insects; there are separate sets of alpine, forest, field, and desert forms, in almost every climate, and there is a special beetle fauna in i - iezbei,tbsino s pr gtiethereeaut allmtotest to recesses of limestone caverns. In thirtieth - • gradiations, from a length of one of inch - to a halt a foot. BATHING AND THE ORGA.N OF REARING.—AS the present is the seaside season, M. Henri de Emilie, in his scientifie euilletan in the Debuts this week, opportunely reminds his readers of the injuries to the organ of hearing which may result from sea bathing. Dr. Sexton, of the New York Ear Dispensary, has lately stated that of 800 cases which he , treated between May and September last year, 05 were di- rectly traceable to sea-bathing. Dr. Luis Sand y Molist, of Barcelona, a 1.30 reports ten cases of deafness resulting from the same cause which have come lunder his treatment this year. The shock of a wave will sometimes injure the deli- cate membrane of the tympan'am. In bathing, water often penetrates to the Eustachian tube, and salt water has irritat- ing qualities which sometimes sets up acute inflammation. Dr. Sexton goes so far as to advise people who wish to pre- serve their sense of hearing intact never to plange, but, as H. de Parville observes, close plugs of cotton wool in the ear would probably prove a sufficient safeguard. Tire RAISING or SUNKEN VESSELS.—The necessity of devising some more economic and effective methed of rais- ing sunken ships has forced itself upon engineers and men of science. The processes at present in operation have been found to be crude, elementary, and in many notable in- stances, like the attempts to raise the ironclads Vanguard and Grosser Karl urst, absolutely abortive. The apparatus known as the self-adjasting gripping-camel is the latest effort made to overcome the special difficulties we have men- tioned. In principle the gripping-camel is a pair of huge jaws provided with strong india-rubber bags. The camel is lowered from a derrick upon the wreck, gripping the hull. Air is then pumped into the bags, which becoming inflated, constitute a vigorous and buoyant support to the ship. The pressure thus obtained is of the most powerful kind, the ship being fixed as if in a vice, and forming, as it were, a part of the whole apparatus. Affixed to the back of tl-e vice is a large bell-like dome, which also receives a volume of air, and thus effectually aide the buoyancy requisite to raise the ship. The gripping-camel is invented in obedience to the simple proposition that a ship has become submerged abecause the air which gave her buoyancy has been dis- placed and driven out by the invasion of water. The pencil is constructed to supply collateral buoyancy to the ship, it is easily regulated, and may be raised and lowered from the derrick at will. It may be adjusted to the ship by the aid of a single diver, and when once in position the rest is easy. The whole operation was effectively demonstrated a few days ago at the works of the inventors Messrs. Clark and Stanstield, of the Crown Engineering Works, Lambeth, in presence of a number of critical judges. The contrivance is a distinct advance upon the methods now in operation for raising and floating wiecks. Its principle secures almost everything aimed at—adequate power to lift the largest ships, with their cargoes or equipment; appliances for pre- cluding the possibility of injury being done to the hull; and freedom from the costly risk of breaking chains and ulti- mate failure. Two, even three, gripping-camels may, if necessary, be employed upon the ship; and it is, perhaps, Worthy of notice here that the engineer who attempted to ' raise the Vanguard, and subsequently the Grosser Kart urst, has expressed his opinion emphatically that if he conld have I had recourse to the apparatus now before the public, he I would have succeeded in raising those ships. EDUCATION OF FAUN LABOURERS' CHILDREN.—At the present day we hear a great deal about elementary, scientific, and techeical training for the young who intend to practice farming, but who will give us good technical training schools for the children of farm labourers? The ~ld class of labourers could thatch tolerably well, bat the generality of labourers to be met with at the present day know nothing about it, nor do they care to learn. Going through most rural districts just at the present time, and noticing whet a large number of uncovered hay stacks are in view, forces this subject prominently • on attention, and what is yet worse, the corn stacks will, in too many cases, have simi- larly to wait a long time exposed to all risks and dangers of sudden storms and bad-weather, because there are so few labourers in the country who can undertake to thatch ricks. Every succeeding year more and more cern etachs get damaged by remaining uncovered so long, and farmers have the charges of slovenliness and unthriftiness brought against them in consequence, when really in nine cases out of ten the true reason of the delay is the impossibility of getting the work performed owing to the scarcity of thatchers. By right every farm labourer in the kingdom otrgt- a...1...b1. ia, sbancli a dux. eveneteelaeaeree-to-seaaa the rising generation of labourers the art requires a school of training of some kind, and if once the thing could be satisfactorily designed it would be a great boon to the farming community. Could not something be done by way of having technical instruction of this nature in board schools when situated in purely rural districts? Classes for impertiog technical instruction might be arranged not only for this necessary skilled work but for many others. Agri- cultural labourers at the present day ought to have a great deal of knowledge on, and a practical familiarity with, a great many things of which the greater portion of them are utterly deficient. A great deal of valuable machinery is often spoiled because those who have to use it are un- acquainted with practical mechanics, and take no care of it. As machinery is now so largely employed in farming, if any school or class system could be devised so as to make the rising generation of labourers greater adepts in its em- ployment, it would be a very good thing. 111 it were found practical to carry on technical teaching of this nature in rural schools, surely the elementary principles of animal physiology, as well as the anatomy of the animal frame, I might be taught. We often hear of serious losses nf cattle, sheep, and horses being sustained ~rom the negligence or silly bad management of the labourers who have them in charge; and when affairs of this kind are investigated, the true Cause is generally found to be sheer ignorance or stupidity, instead of wanton intent to do harm. What a good thing it would be if young labourers knew that the stomach of the horse is a small oneou cousequence of which it requires to have a little food and often, rather than a great deal at one time. In a lecture which Professor Pritchard delivered some time since, he pointed out how much better it was for working horses always to have a drink of chilled water when coining in from work before having their manger food, and stated as a fact that since the Loudon Omnibus Company had adopted this system they had reduced their rates of mortality and veterinary bills hi a most astonishing degree. Of what incalculable benefit would it be if the children of labourers could get in- struction on facts of this nature, so that they would not only get familiar with improved systems of treating and manag- ing stock, but know the true reasons on which their utility depends. -Only a few days since we heard a shorthorn breeder mourning over the fact of a valuable animal, worth several hundreds of pounds, having taken a violent fever, and been reduced to death's door through the injudicious want of care of the man in charge, who had turned her out of a comfortable stall, because she seemed in a state of per- spiration, into an atmosphere which brought on a violent cold. Scores of similar instances could be related, and in- stead of waxing wroth on the deteriorated character of farm labourers, would it not be better to consider the possibility of making them better ?—Farniers' Chronicle.

DESERTED TURNPIKES AND DESERTED CHLTRCRES.-Mr. Charles Dickens has given a vivid description of the City churches in the " Uncommercial Traveller." We quote from another paper of that series the following, which might be a parable on the same subject :—" How goes turnpike busi- ness, master?' said I to him, as he sat in his little porch, repairing a shoe. It don't go at all master,' said he to me; 'it's stopped.' That's bad,' said I. ' Bad rhe repeated. And he pointed to one of his sun-burnt, dusty children, who was climbing the turnpike gate, and said, extending his open right hand in remonstrance with Universal Nature: 6 Five on 'em!' 'But how to improve turnpike business?' said I. 'There's a way, master,' said he, with the air of one who had thought deeply on the subject. I should like to know it.' Lay a toll on everything as comes through; lay a toll on walkers. Lay anothen on everything as don't come through; lay a toll on them as stops at home. 'Would the last remedy be fair ?"Fair ? Them as stops at home could I come through if they liked; couldn't they?' Say they , could.' 'Toll 'em. If they don't come through, it's their look out. Anyways,—Toll 'ern !' " "Toll 'ern Pi That's exactly what is virtually done with the parishioners of the City parishes who don't attend the City churches.—Liberator. HALF IMPRISONED.-A thief was lately tried in Cali- fornia for entering a miner's tent and stealing a bag of gold dust. The testimony showed that he had been once em- ployed there, and knew exactly where the owner kept his dust; that on the night specified he cut a slit in the tent, reached in, took the bag, and then ran off. The principal witness testified that he saw the hole cut, saw the man reach in, and heard him run away. "I rushed after him at once," continued the witness, "but when I cotched him I didn't find Bill's bag, but it was found afterward where he had throwed it." "How far did he get when he took the dust ?" inquired the counsel. "Well, he was stoopin' over half-way in, I should say," replied the witness. ' May it please your Honour," interposed the counsel, "the indict- ment isn't sustained and I shall demand an acquittal on direction of the Court. The prisoner is on trial for entering a dwelling in the night time with intent to steal. The tea- timony is clear that he made an opening through which he protruded himself about half-way, and stretched out his arms and committed the theft. But the indictment charges that he actually entered the tent, or dwelling. Now, your Honour, can a man enter a house when only one half of his body is in, and the other half out ?" "I shall leave the whole matter to the jury. They must judge of the law and the fact as proved,' replied the judge. The jury brought in a verdict of "Guilty as to one half of his body, and not guilty ,as to the other half." The judge sentenced the guilty part to two years' imprisonment leaving it to the prisoner option to have the innocent part cut off, or take it along with him.

"Now," said Robert Bruce, " a woman's speed against a king's appetite," and as he raised the spoon to his mouth she took her departure. The track round the foot of the hill was rough and stony, but she heeded it not, and on and on she ran till she neared her own home again. There, lift- ing a rude wooden shutter in the gable end of the cottage, she saw the king and the knight, with helmets off and swords at their feet, talking together, and taking alternate spoonfuls of the brose. "Fair play, my liege, fair play," I cried the dime, and resumed her race. "So easy and familiar were the manners of the great, fabled to be so stiff and decorous," says the author of "Traditions of Edinburgh," who must vouch for the story, "that Miss Eglantine afteriverds Lady Wallace, used' to be sent across the street the Fountain Well Mr water to make tea. Lady Maxwell's daughters were the wildest romps imaginable. An old gentleman who was their relation told me that the first time he saw these beautiful girls was in the High- street, where Miss Jane, afterwards Duchess of Gordon, was riding upon a sow, which Miss Eglantine thumped lustily behind with a stick. It must be understood that in the middle of the eighteenth century vagrant swine went as commonly about the streets of Edinburgh as dogs de in our day, and were more generally followed as pets by the child- ren of the last generation. It may, however, be remarked, that the sows upon which the Duchess of Gordon and her witty sister rode when children were not the common vagrants of tbe High-street, but belonged to Peter Ramsay, of the inn in St. Mary's Wynd, and were among the last that were permitted to roam abroad. The romps used to watch the animals as they were let loose in the forenoon in the stable yard (where they lived among the horse litter), and got upon their backs the moment they issued from the close.' —From Cassell's "Old and Nesl) Edinkrgh" for August. .

AFGHANISTAN. • The following telegram has been received from the Vice- roy) dated Aug. Bthi—F.ollowing from St. John: Messages from Candahar report all quiet there. The bulk of the Arneer's infantry had eventually joined Ayoub after the battle, and accomp'anied him to Candahar two days later. A complete regiment deserted and went off to Khelat. Kabuli troops were afterwards kept in the city. Merchants who • rived at Chaman on the 6th report that Ayoub had dig- Portedu regiments among kis own infantry, also re- that 400 Kabuli soldiers had been disarmed and dismissed. Ayoub sent a Durani chief with Sowars to take Possession of Khelat Ghilzai. The chief returned, having met Kabuli o horses foraging. Suhib Khan and Alizar, chief itiaipmindawar, are at Khelat Ghilzii with Gholam v- ea Khan, who has one regiment of infantry, three Of haverYb, and six guns. The principal Maliks of Kadanai summoned to Candahar. All quiet at Chaman and towards Candahar and in the Hurnai Mani and Kakar country.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Mommy.

Tire Int= LAND BILL. —The House received the report of amendments on the Irish Land Bill, and after some dis- cussion the mbasure was ready for the third reading.—The Earl of CAUNARTON then delivered a speech in steong oppo- sition to the bill, and predicting that if it failed to con- ciliate Ireland we should be compelled either to govern that country as a Crown colony or grant the demand for total independence.—Earl GRANVILIM gravely rallied the ex- Colonial Secretary on the exaggerated fears he had ex- pressed.—After some further discussion the bill was read a third time and passed. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. PROPOSED VOTE OF THINKS TO SIR EVELYN' WOOD.— Mr. linoknutinsT asked the Prime Minister whether the Government would propose a vote of thanks to Sir E. Wood for the services he had rendered by peaceful means in South Africa. ors the ground that such a compliment should not be confined to generals who could boast "triumphs of war." —The PRIME MINISTER pointed out that the transactions in Which Sir E. Wood had engaged, were not yet altogether concluded, and declined to anticipate the Government's decision on the matter; but expressed, on behalf of the Ministry, the highest sense of the zeal, ability, and judg- ment which Sir Evelyn Wood bad shown. Ma. BRADLAUGH. Replying to Mr. Labouchere, Mr. GLADSTONE intimated that if Mr. Bradlaugh should present himself at the beginning of next Session, mid claim to take the oath, and opposition should thereupon arise, the Govern- ment would undoubtedly hold It to be their duty to consider the question with a view to the termination of the con- troversy. The SPEAKER was understood to state that both the resolutions prohibiting Mr. Bradlaugh from entering the House and that which prevents him from taking the oath lapse at the end of this Session, as they were not made standing orders of the House. Tea RELEASE OF Mn. DILLON.—Being questioned as to the circumstances under which Mr. Dillon had been released from Kilmainham, Mr. FOUSTEU read the letter which had been forwarded to the Governor of the gaol. It stated that it had been represented to the Lord Lieutenant that Mr. Dil- lon's life would be endangered by farther confinement. The Chief Secretary added that he had been surprised on receipt of that intelligence, inasmuch as the Inspector General had reported that he had seen Mr. Dillon on the Bth of last month, and that the hon. gentleman had then said that he did not think his health had suffered since he entered the prison. Two independent medical gentlemen had been sent to Kilmainham to see the patient, but Mr. Dillon had refused to allow himself to be examined by them. They had then consulted with the doctors who had attended him, and the' result was that they agreed to confirm the statement that his life would be endangered by further incarceration. THE EDUCATION ESTIMATES.—Mt. MIINDELLA, in mov- ing the education estimates, made an important statement as to the work of the department during the past year. He stated, in submitting the total figures, that in the expendi- ture for the year 1880-1, the sum granted was £2,536,007, and the sum expended was £2,525,767, the result being a saving of £10,240 upon the estimate. The charge of annual grants was estimated at £2,217,348, and the slim reached was £2,230,173, being an increase of £120,231 on the previous year. The estimate of average attendance was 12,842,000, and the real attendance was 2,814,000'— the estimated grant per head was 15s. 81., I and the sum actually granted was 159. 80.— Mr. MUNDELL& afterwards explained the leading features of the new schedule which the Education, Department has framed. The grants for music are so arranged as to give a full grant for teaching from notes wad half a grant for teach- ing by ear. The department find that they must urgently insist upon improved infant school teaching, and to obtain this end, for every sixty scholars a certificated teacher will be required. A further proposal is that the grant shall henceforth be calculated on the result of the examination of scholars passed in proportion- to the passes actually made. The object of this proposal is to take away the temptation to put forward particular children at the expense of others. For the future "the- common-place and miserable stuff which is found in many school books" is to be set on one side as far as possible. It is just as well, Mr. Mundella argues, that children should learn a hundred lines from Milton as of some fourth or fifth rate poet; and some know- ledge both of Milton and Shakspeare will be required in the fifth, sixth, and seventh standards. Special efforts are to be made to encourage night schools which show a falling off in the attendance, and ministers Of religion are no longer excluded from acting as assistant teachers in these institu- tions. The right hon. gentleman also referred to a scheme which he had devised to enable teachers to rise to the rank of inspectors.—Mr. JESSE Comzeras moved that in the opinion of the House grants in aid of eo na et Emadeninnd idbmnnredgauht twor and al Dmuseums ot ourl d on o obneg diconfineddiscussion, otoi nL, o nthd rejected by 85 to 48.

div.p: HOUSE OF LORDS.-TITESDAY.

THE Ray. S. GREEN'S IMPRISONMENT.—EarI BEAUCHAMP moved the second reading of the Ecclesiastical Courts Re- gulation Bill, the immediate object of the measure being to obtain the release of the Rev. Sidney Green, by limiting the term of imprisonment in such cases as his to six months.—The Archbishop of CANTERBURY, who said he was as anxious as Earl Beauchamp could be that Mr. Green should be released from imprisonment, said he hoped that the bill would receive a second reading, but when it got into committee it would be necessary to consider by what means a gentleman with these conscientious convictions was to be kept out of prison after he had been released —The Lord CHANCELLOR said he believed that Mr. Green's release would give general satisfaction if that could be done without im- pairing the majesty of the law and the sense of duty of the clergy as well as the laymen to obey the law. To the Established Church it was fundamentally ne:iessary that those who enjoyed temporal emoluments and temporal rights in it should comply with the conditions on which those emoluments and rights were possessed, and no man had a right to be governed by his own view as to which of the conditions he should observe. The bill was eventually read a second tifne, and the Royal University of Ireland Bill was read a third time and passed.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY.

TliE TREATMENT OF EMIGRANTS.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, in reply to Mr. J. Talbot. stated that he had already ex- pressed his opinion in the Board of Trade minute that so far as Miss O'Brien's accusation embodied any general charge against the shipowners trading between Liverpool and America they had been entirely disproved. He had already sent a copy of the report and the minute to all the principle shipowners, and he had no doubt they would adopt all the precautions calculated to secure the object in view. MRS. BESANT'S SPEECII.—Mr. RITCIIIE quoted from a speech delivered in the Hall of Science, on Sunday, referring to the case of Mr. Bradlaugh, and inquired whether the Go- vernment intended to take any precautions against that gentleman entering the House by force.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that he had nothing to add to what had been stated by the Home Secretary as to the measures taken to maintain law and order in the vicinity of the House, and he had no reason to suppose that they would not be effectual. THE IRISH LAND BILL: THE LORDS' AMENDMENTS.— The House then entered on consideration of the Lords' amendments to the Land Bill, and upon clause 1, at the instance of Mr. GLADSTONE, the words barring compensa- tion to the tenant in any case where permanent improve- ments had been made by the landlord had been altered to the effect that this arrangement should only hold good in cases where the permanent improvements had been not only so made but also maintained by the landlord.—Mr. PARNELL wished to add, as an amendment, that the landlord should not have compensation for such improvements "by increased rents or otherwise." The Government could not accept this modification of the clause.—The amendment was nega- tived, and, on a division, the clause, as amended, was carried by 258 votes against 100.—Upon the next amendment the Government took up a much firmer tone. The Lords intro- duced words enabling the landlord who had purchased the tenant-right to recover the amount out of a sum obtained at the next •sale of tenant-right. The PRIME MINISTER pointed out that even supposing the landlord was entitled to compensation the effect of the amendment would be to make the wrong man suffer, and tenant B would have to pay for a purchase made from tenant A. Even Mr. Brand described the amend- ment as "a monstrous injustice," and although the opposi- tion attempted to vindicate its propriety, it was rejected by 127 votes. In one or two other divisions, in which conces- sions were made to the Lords, the Irish members were sup- ported on a division by a considerable number of English • Liberals. An amendment by the Lords, prohibiting a tenant might stop. from erecting a new dwelling-house or building, was Partwly resisted by 111 Gladstone, who pointed out that it I dwel- ling-house for a 1,,• farmer from substituting a comfortable amendment as ame d n ed was carried on a division. div.p: THE EXkSIINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 13, 1881.

I by the landlords are excluded from the operationes;rati; ie b An amendment proposed by the Attorney-utoi,l la. new sub-section, limiting' the conditions under which ti.." rent of a tenancy could be reduced, was warmly resisted by the Irish members.—The ArrOmaEx-GENERAL proposed that no reduction should be allowed on account of any expenditure made by the tenant of his pre- decessor in title in respect to which be would be entitled to compensation under the Act of 1870.— Mr. HEALY remarked that the Irish members had been told that they lived by agitation ; and if this were so, the Government were now supplying them with the breath of their nostrils.—Mr. MITCHELL-HENRY, Mr. C. RUSSELL, Mr. SRAW, and other members oppose! the amendment, ard the ATTORNEY-GENERAL ultimately consented to withdraw it.— Sir R. Caoss, however, insisted upon a division; and the amendment was rejected by a majority of 134 votes.—Other amendments were thrown out in an equally decisive way. The debate was then adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Taiiiisram ROYAL AssEirr.—The Royal assent was given by Commis- sion to 63 public and private bills. THE Trimasysta..—Lord KIIIIIMILEY, replying to Lord Brabourne, gave the main definitions of the boundaries of the new Transvaal State, and said that after full considera- tion it was decided not to sever from the Transvaal any part of the territory which had previously been considered to belong to the State. THE ECCLESIASTICAL COURTS REGULATION BILL passed through Committee. A new clause-was added, declaring that the proposed Act might be cited as the Discharge of Contumacious Prisoners Act, 1881, and their Lordships adjourned during pleasure. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--TaunsDAY. . DISESTABLISHMENT.—Mr. DICK PEORIA gave notice that early next session he will call attention to the position of the Established Church of Scotland, and move that the House is of opinion that the maintenance of the Established Church of Scotland is indefensible on public grounds, and with respect to the ecclesiastical circumstances of the country, is eminently unjust, and that a measure for the disestablishment and disendowninent of the Church of Scot- land should be passed without delay. THE LAND BILL.—ANOTHER ALL NIGHT, • SITTING. When the consideration of the Lords' amendments to the Land Bill was resumed Mr. GLADSTONE moved to disagree with the amendment as to leases and saving existing leases. —The discussion was important.—Mr. GOSCHEN took part in it, and said the question at issue involved the fate of the bill. He advised the House to accept the proposal of the Government.—Mr. BRAND also supported the Government. —On a division Mr. Gladstone's proposal was carried by 254 votes against 125, a majority of 129.—Another impor- tant debate followed on a proposal of the Government with regard to the resumption of holdings by landlords.—Sir S. NORTECOTE and Lord It. Cutritenim complained that the House was being misled, and Mr. GLADSTONE defended the proposed alterations, and said that the Government were desirous of making the bill as perfect as possible.—Mr. HEALY and Mr. A. M. StruavAN engaged in a somewhat ,heated conversation, in which the latter strongly repudiated any sympathy with suggestions as to the shooting of landlords and bailiffs which had been quoted by the former.— On the Lords' amendment striking out the provision that the court may stay' prozeedings pending against a tenant until the judicial rent is fixed, the ATTORNBT-GENER.AL for IRELAND having asked the House to reject the proposed modification providing the court shouldobe satiqfied such rent should be fixed within three months, Mr. DALY suggested the insertion of ‘• six " months instead of "three." —Mr. GLADSTONE refused to accept the alteration, which was rejected on a division, and Mr. Law's amendment was carried.—Mr. PARa4irLL then proffered the Government another chance of proving their bond-fides by empowering the court to extend the time if satisfied that Inability to get the rent were not the tenants' fault.—Upon this point the war waged fiercely. Mr. Law and Mr. FORSTER declared that Mr. Parnell's proposition could not be accepted; and Mr. O'DoNNELL moved into the fray, and was mildly remonstrated with by the SPEAKER for re- peating the same arguments over and over again.- -Mr. D. Sum.rveri, noticing Mr. Gladstone's absence, ex- pressed his conviction that he would have accepted Mr. Parnell's amendment, and moved the adjournment of the debate, to give him the opportunity of hearing it. There- upon Mr. FORSTER declared that if not passed that night the bill would be in danger of beingiost—This threat did not ' alarm the Irishmen, who continued the discussion with vigour. Ultimately, the House divided on the motion for adjournment at a quarter-past three, and the motion was rejected by 168 votes against 24. Mr. HEALY thought the protest made by the Irish members sufficient, and said they should allow the bill to go back again to the Lords. It was a melancholy sight to see that glorious chamber in full glow with nothing in it.-Ir. McCaterur said the tenant would have the protection of the Act, and then he had the three courses open to him which Mr. Healy had spoken of earlier—to shoot the landlord, the agent, or the bailiff. That ought to suffice a reasonable man.—Mr. T. P. O'Comion complained that he had been forbidden by his leader to move a further amendment, ' which he deeply regretted, as he wanted to improve his morale. This candid confession caused a roar of laughter, on which the orator congratulated himself on being able to amuse the House at half-past three; but when he went on to describe the bill as Dead Sea fruit, and to indulge in other flowers of speech, his eloquence was curtailed by the Speaker, and he satisfied himself by declaring that the bill, without Mr. Parnell's amendment, would be a message of war.—Mr. O'Dolucar.r.' on again rising, was told he had already spoken, and finally the House divided on* Mr. Parnell's amendment, rejecting It by 143 votes against 38.—The Lords' amendment, as amended, was then agreed to.—Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Forster, Mr:Shaw-Lefevre, the Attorney- General for Ireland, the Solicitor-General for England, and Mr. Dodson, were appointed a committee to draw up reasons for disagreeing witn the Lords' amendments.—Mr. T. P. O'Comros proposed the addition of the name of Mr. Parnell, but the SPEAKER ruled it out of order, as the names had been passed, whereupon Mr. PARNELL, amid some laughter, declared that in any case he should have de- clined to serve. - •

MEETING OF THE LORDS AT 4 A.m. The bill was then returned to the Lords amid loud cheers from the Ministerial benches and derisive echoes from the Home Rulers. In point of fact, the Lords had suspended their sitting "during pleasure," anticipating that the bill would be shortly sent up. The four Peers necessary to make a quorum passed the weary hours in the gallery of the Commons, watching the slow progress of the bill. The four Peers who had been waiting patiently for the climax now hastily retreated, beaded by Lord Monson, to reassemble with due solemnity in their own chamber. In the absence of the Lord Chancellor, Lord Thurlow took his seat on the wool- sack, and the Land Law (Ireland) Bill, as further amended by the Commons was brought up, sad the Commons amend- ments to the Lords' amendments were ordered to be con- sidered on Friday, at five o'clock. Meanwhile the Com- mons had disposed of the remairiing orders of the day, and both houses adjourned a little after four a.m., leaving the Land Bill a step nearer completion. •

MR. GLADSTONF.'S SITORTRST SPEECIL—TherC was a speech made by the Prime Minister on Thursday night in the course of the Lords' amendments which does not appear in the Parliamentary reports. The right hon. gentleman went out to dinner shortly before nine, and returned at twenty minutes past ten. At this moment Mr. Healy was addressing the House on the question of the resumption of leases, which had been started nearly three hours earlier. As the Premier entered and sat down, with a weary air, be- tween Mr. Forster and the Irish Attorney-General, he ex- claimed, in a voice sufficiently loud to be heard all over the House," Here we are still, are we ?"

A CENTENARIAN.—A pauper woman named Hiscocks, I who, there is reason to believe, was 105 years of age, died on Wednesday, at Plymouth. Her husband, then an old ' man, died 55 years ago. In the Queen's Bench in Dublin, on Wednesday, Mr. Colelough, late stamp distributor in that division was con- victed of having forged stamps to the amount of several thousand pounds. Sentence was deferred. An extraordinary outrage is reported from llyde. As one , of the head workmen at Ashton's Mill was entering the clothroom he was seized from behind by two masked men, and Lags containing £l2B stolen from him. The men escaped. A SLEEPY MEMBER OF TEE GOVERNMENT.—In the divi- sion taken at one o'clock on Wednesday morning on Sir Stafford Northcote's amendment to the 7th clause a member of the Government was discovered fast asleep in the Oppo- sition lobby. Great pains were taken not to disturb him till the doors were locked, after which he was obliged to give his vote against his colleagues and party. He was loudly cheered on emerging from the lobby.—Daily News. The President of the Board of Trade states, in a letter to Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., the Secretary of the Trade Unions Congress, that he hopes to be able next session to make pro- posals with regard to the Patent Laws. He considers that the chief feature of any change must be such a reduction of the initial fee as may remove any obstacle from that cause placed in the way of inventors of small- means. Mr. Chamberlain also says that if the Bankruptcy Bill had been proceeded with he should have proposed clauses for giving to poor debtors the same facilities as are now offered in the case of the larger insolvencies—in other words, of taking a long step in the direction of the abolition of imprisonment for debt. THE STATISTICS OF CHURCH SUNDAY' SCHeOLS.—The last report issued by the Committee of the Church of Eng- land Sunday School Institute contains an interesting state- ment of the position and extent of Sunday schools in the Church of England. The parishes in the dioceses of Eng- land and Wales which made returns were in number 8,405. The number which did not make returns were 6,064. The total number of scholars on the books of the schools in the 8,405 parishes making returns is 1,289,273, giving an aver- age of 78 for each school. Allowing the same average for the 6,064 parishes not making returns, the total number of scholars in the Chutch of England schools is 2.222,891. The total number of teachers on the books of the schools in the 8,405 parishes making returns is 113,412, giving an averar:e of 6-87 for each school. The nuniVer 10, teachers who were formerly scholars is 30,764. Separate services for children are hela in connection with 2,705 of the schools making returns.
TRADE NOTES.
The great strike in the Worcestershire and Staffordshire trade has come to an end, the men having determined to accept i!.,e 20 per cent, advance offered instead of the 30 per cent. demanded. • _
In conseqneace of the dispute between the platers and helpers in the Wear shipbuilding trade, the masters have in contemplation the advisability of closing the yards, all work being at a standstill.

At the meeting of Welsh anthracite colliers at Brynmawr, on Wednesday, it was determined that the men at all the collieries where a promises of an advance of wages had not been given in South Wales and Monmouthshire should give immediate notice to terminate their contracts. •

A company of about 500 seamen from the various metro- politan docks, headed by a brass band in a waggon display- ing flags and large placards about "Seamen's rights," de- manding "A fair day's pay for a fair day's work," and declaring "No surrender." on Monday morning paraded the principal streets of London. , Notices have been posted at the Malleable Iron Works, Coatbridge, Holytown, and Motherwell, Glasgow, that a re- duction of 24 per cent on the wages of millraen and others in the finishing departments, and 31. per ton on puddlers', will be made on the first pay day. _

At a meeting of sailars held on Wednesday, "to consider the wages question," a strong opinion in favour of demand- ing an advance was expressed, and a deputation was ap- pointed to wait upon the Shipowners' Association. The sailors in the East-end of London on Wednesday, were in a very excited state upon the subject of the abolition of advance notes. They insist that the minimum pay shall be £3 ss. per month for sailing vessels and £3 15s. for steamers.

On Monday, an open air meeting of the nailers now on strike for an advance of wages was held at Hales Owen. Mr. John Price stated that the people in the various districts were still firmly adhering to the original demand. He could not advise any of the operatives to return to work on the offer of a few of the masters, but they must wait the result of a masters' meeting, when it was hoped the wages question would be placed on a permanent and satisfactory basis. It was unanimously resolved to play on until all the employers concede the 1879 list.

He was confident the engine was reversed on entering the station. In the course of the inquiry Mr. Oaten, agent to tho Westingimuse Brake Company, stated that the brake might be put on in a second or two, and taken off in six or sevei Seconds. Col. Yolland said he did not yet know whether the brakes on the express were applied or not. The inquiry was adjourned until this morning. A second message has been received from the Queen, inquiring into the condition of the suf- ferers.

Thomas Butterworth, engine driver, who was severely scalded in the collision which occurred on the railway at Shaw, near Oldham, on 'Monday night, has died. The damage done by the collision is found to amount to £5,000.

div.head: SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT BLACKBURN.
div.p: SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT BLACKBURN.

FIVE PERSONS KILLED AND FORTY INJURED. A fearful collision between two Scotch express trains took Place in the centre of Blackburn station at 3-15 on Monday afternoon. The 2-25 from Manchester to the North, via Hellifield, Lancashireand Yorkshire, with Midland carriages attached, in addition to Lancashire and Yorkshire carriages, dashed into the station about a minute behind time with ap- parently little or no brake power applied. It is said thatthe train was going at a speed of about 40 miles an hour, and with terrific force telescoped itself on to a Liverpool and Yorkshire express which was stationary. There was an engine behind the Liverpool taking off a Glasgow " through " carriage to be attached to the train from Manchester, and this received the force of the shock. Both engines, however, being power- fuls, they retained their positions on the rails, but the three nearest carriages to each engine were reduced to splinters. The guard of the Manchester train whose van was next but one to the engine, had a wonderful escape, as he emerged from the debris with a slightly fractured leg and a few bruises. The driver had his arm fractured, and the driver of the stationary engine was conveyed to the infirmary with a broken leg. The fireman of the Manchester train was also badly injured. Over 20 were got out with severe injuries, 17 being sent to the infirmary, and the others to private homes. One of them, an' old lady from Carlisle, name un- known, died on arriving there, andseveral others are expected to succumb before morning. A well-known Blackburn gentleman, Charles Lomax Tiplady, accountant, died at the station, and also Mrs. Hargreaves, of the Commercial Inn, Over Darwen, their deaths being almost instantaneous. The cause of the accident cannot be definitely stated. The brake —as onall such trains—was a patent Westinghouse vacuum I one, and applied by the driver of the engine. Before arriving at Bolton there was some cause for a sudden stoppage, and the train was pulled up without any difficulty, but on going into Blackburn station one of the passengers, who was in the next carriage to the engine, noticed that the trein was going at express speed, although the wheels were skid- ding." He thought that the train was going through the station, and resumed his reading, when he immediately afterwards found himself pilched against the opposite side of the carriage, a third-class one, but cushioned.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPES.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY ESCAPES.

The inquest on the bodies of Victorien G. de Yeasi, wine merchant, 39, Bloomsbury Villas, Kilburn; C. L. Tiplady, accountant, Blackburn; Mrs. Hargreaves, Commercial Hotel, Darwen ; and Mrs. Swift, Otley-road. Bradford, who were killed in the railway collision at Blackburn Station, on Monday afternoon, was opened on Tuesday, before Mr. Robinson, and, after evidence of identification had been given, was adj aimed until next Tuesday. Beyond those already reported no further deaths have occurred, but several are not expected to recover. There were several very narrow escapes. Mr. Evans, proprietor of the Manchester Evening News, narrowly escaping from the Manchester express with his daughter, who jumped out juet as the collision happened. The young lady had been previously looking out of the window, and exclaimed, "There's going to be a collision." The driver of the Manchester express, Standdeld, states that all the signals were off as he approached Blackburn Station, and he did not expect that a train was standing on the platform. - •

An Accrington correspondent save: The unfortunate acci- dent is the subject of as much criticism as surprise, and the railway management in respect to these two express trains is very severely commented upon. Of course, if the Liver- pool express is in the station punctually to the minute, and if the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway officials are suffi- eiently expeditious in despatching the Liverpool train, a clear line is left by the Scotch express; but the Liverpool express being a few minutes late, the line is frequently blocked, and the Scotch express driver has to pull up close to the buffers of a stationary engine. On the occasion in question the Yorkshire train was not got off with as much celerity as it might have been, although it was several minutes behind its time, and as a consequence the passen- gers in it have been the chief sufferers. Passengers by the Yorkshire express have been accustomed to see the Scotch- man come in at such a high speed and pull up short that they felt no alarm. It is expected that the inquiry before the Coroner as well as the Government investigation will be of a very critical nature.—Mr. Edwaod Yates, yarn agent, of Sudell-road, Darwen, had a narrow escipe. He was in a second compartment of the train which was standing, when he happened to look out at the window, and seeing the com- motion on the platform he took a flying leap from the car- riage and landed on the platform. The next instant the carriage was dashed to pieces. A Bolton correspondent writes : Several persons entered the train at Bolton, but with the exception of one gentle- man, all escaped injury. This was Mr. James Win. France, aged 20, of IP, Yarrow-place, Brownlow Fold, who says : "We went on all right until about 400 yards from Black- burn station, when, on passing the engine shed the driver apparently applied extra speed, the train travelling at a greater pace than had been the case since leaving Bolton. It was so fast that some of the men in the engine shed ap- peared to look out and watch the train as it dashed into the station. A few yards before entering the station the driver commenced whistling vehemently several thoes as though at the approach of danger. I looked out of the window and saw some one, probably the driver (Redforth) jump off the engine standing in the station, and fearing there was going to be a collision I sat down on the floor of the, carriage, and firmly set myself between the two seats with one arm on each. The next moment there was a terrific crash, and the guard's van, which was next to the carriage I was in, seemed to be hurled on to the top of my carriage. I was covered with, a large pile of broken timbers, and my head was forced down between my kners until my forehead actually touched my feet. The work of extrication was a long and rough one, the woodwork having to be torn in pieces from around and above me. A man with an iron rod broke through the windows of the carriage and struck me once or twice on the head, the swelling from the blows being till perceptible. I could hear the voice of some one at the top of the carriage calling out, Lie still, my beady, we'll 8000 have you out.' It was quite a 'quarter of an hour before I was rescued, and then I was dragged bodily out of the car- riage by my shoulders. The force of the collision may be imagined when I say that a man from the next compart- ment was crushed bodily through the woodwork into our compartment." Mr. Charles Lomax Tiplady, the first who perished by tne collision at Blackburn Station, on Monday, was interred in Blackburn Cemetery, on Thursday. The funeral. was of a quiet and unostentatious character, there being. a hearse without plumes and four ordinary mourning coaches to carry mourners, whilst the carriage of Dr. Forrest, deceased's medical attendant, brought up the rear. Still a, large body of gentlemen connected with the Freemasons', Oddfellowe, and Licensed Victuallers' Societies attended to show a last mark of respect for their deceased companion, and walked in the procession in front of the hearse; but in accordance with • the private character of the funeral they abstained from wearing the regalia of their respective orders. The Rays. J. W. Pengelly and J. Place conducted the funeral service.

div.head: HEARTLESS. ROBBERY OF THE DEAD:
div.p: HEARTLESS. ROBBERY OF THE DEAD:

--.....-- ...--..... —. ...... ------ A case of robbery from the body of one of the deceased, whilst laying on the station platform immediately after the collision, was detected on Thursday. James Gibson (14), spinner of Blackburn, has been in custody since Monday, on suspicion of having, stolen a lady's valuable gold keeper ring during the bustle following the collision, and Edward M'Carthy (23), collier, Union-street, Oldham, was appre- hended at the same time for having received the stolen property. On Tuesday, the Blackburn magistrates remanded them for a week tor inquiries to be made, and by diligent inquiries the police, this morning, ascertained that the ring was the property of Mrs. Hargreaves, Commercial Hotel, Darwen, who died after the disastrous collision, and who was temporarily hid on the platform. The Board of Trade inquiry into the collision at Black- burn wa.s opened on Thursday, before Colonel Yolland. div.head: LIBERALS AND THE LAND BILL.
div.p: LIBERALS AND THE LAND BILL.

The Liberal Association of Glasgow, met on Wednesday, to pass resolutions to strengthen the hands of.tbe Govern- ment in regard to the amendments made in the Land Bill by the House of Lords. Resolutions were passed expressing regret that the Housl of Lords had so changed the bill that if it passed as altered by them the value of the measure would be very seriously impaired, and rejoicing that the House of Commons, so far as it had gone in the reconsidera- tion of the bill, hart rejected such of the alterations as were inconsistent with the principle of the bill. It was also resolved to petition the House of Commons to firmly resist all attempts to have the Lords' alterations embodied in the measure, the Association preferring the bill to be dropped rather than that these alterations should be accepted. A petition in terms of the resolution was at once despatched for presentation to the House of Commons. At a meeting of the Plymouth Liberal Association, on Wednesday, resolutions were passed expressing satisfaction that the Government had not given way to the Lords' amendments on the Irish Land Bill, and the conviction that if further concessions were made the measure would cease to be a message of peace to Ireland. At a meeting of tenant farmers at Portadown, the hope was expressed that the Government would abandon the bill rather than accept it in a mutilated condition.

div.head: DYNAMITE CONVENTION AT CHICAGO.
div.p: THE DYNAMITE CONVENTION AT CHICAGO.

Reports from Chicago speak of dissentions and "treachery" in the Fenian Convention now sitting there. It is said that one of the prominent members of the Organi- sation is suspected of being a "British spy," and it is even added that he has been recognised as a former member of the Royal Irish Constabulary. Mr. West, the suspected member, has had a good deal to do with the disbursements of the "skirmishing fund." A Reuter's telegram says that "many wild schemes" have been broached in the Conven- tion. From another source we learn that the Convention represents 6,400 "lodges," that money is abundant, and that when the delegates have decided upon the fate of Mr. West they will proceed to draft "an organisation and complete gtvernment " for Ireland. The Convention is partly com- posed of the friends of Jeremiah O'Donovan (Rossa), who in a recent issue of his paper wrote that a "sentence of death " would be recorded by "the Irish race" against any landlord who exercised the power of eviction in Ireland. On this subject the Irish American itays :—" The stupid brutality of the threat could not be excelled in any particular. That O'Donovan Roses has lent himself to such a policy is his own affair, and we leave him to the judg- ment of his own countrymen and his own conscience. The man who advocates murder does not speak the sentiments of the Irish people, and will be repudiated by them with scorn should he ever attempt to ask their auffrages on the subject."

div.head: WINSFORD:
div.p: WINSFORD:

OVER Hon'muumuu. Swow.—Over and surrounding district had its annual show, on Saturday, in Delamere- street. The day being fine there was a good attendance, and the vegetables, fruits, and flowers were quite up to former years, and in some instances considerably in advance. The show was under the patronage of Lord belamere and many of the surrounding gentry. including the county members. The President was Mr. J. D. Kay, J.P. A special prize for cottigers' butter was offered by Mrs. Turner, and another for wild flowers by Miss A. Turner; and special prizes were also given by Mr. T. Knowles, M.P., for Wigan, Mrs. Banner, the Rev. W. Finch, Miss Turner, (tc., for various things. One great point of interest was the changing of bees from one hive to another—the manner of taking the comb, kc., which was shown by two gentlemen. The athletic sports were ex- ceedingly well attended and efficiently carried ont. The Rifle Corps band played a selection of music during the day. Refreshments were provided by Mr. John Beeton. SILT TRADE, Wngsronn.—The demand for this com- modity has been fairly sustained. Brine is still scarce, and limitation of supply must soon raise prices far above what have been recently quoted. The Baltic trade forms an ex- ception to all past experience, the export having been much curtailed by the real scarcity of ships. Freights for all Baltic ports have risen largely, as will be shown, and are still rising. Very high figures will probably be paid before the season ends. The chtet items of exportation are as fol- lows .I—July, to the United States, less than for years, but it includes none to the South States and especially to New Orleans, reaching only 11,442; to British North America the highest July average for seven years, namely 12,020; West Indies and South America coins below the last two years, though in excess of three or four before. Africa has never been so low since 1875, for this month being only 1,914 while the East Indies are greatly in excess, 50,27,8, of any July of which record is at hand. Australian colonies come up well also, 2,870; and though the Prussian ports take only about one third of last July, yet they take three times as Much xa lu July 1870, while Rtaala has not b-ell higher since 1870. Other Baltic and North Sea ports are below the average so far, for the cause named above. France and the Mediterranean ports might virtually be excluded from the salt export trade of England, being only two for July Home consumption coastwise reaches 5,225; this is inde-. pendent of the canal and rail traffic. Holland is below the average, though Belgium is in excess, reaching 4,934 which has not been surpassed for years. The total amount from the Mersey reaches for this month the grand total of 139,599 tons, which goes much beyond any July for years back.

ANNIVERSARY OE WHITEGATE UNITED METHODIST Flan CHURCH SCHOOL. The annual sermons were preached on Sunday last, by Mr. John Clough, of North- wich, whose well-known public oratory drew many to this rural neighbourhood. The collections were very good and largely supplemented on behalf of school and trust fund on the Monday following, when an excursion took place to Liverpool and New Brigliton. Many began the descent of the rivers Weaver and Mersey at the early hour of five or be- fore, and after many delays and showers, returned about the same hour of Tuesday morning„ having had 24 hour s' tripping.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.

HOPE or EARLESTOWS LODGE OF GOOD TEMPLARS.—The usual weekly session of this lodge was held in the lodge- room, Earlestown, on Monday. After the usual routine business had been gone through, a member was restored and another was initiated. Four members were proposed for next session. Arrangements were made for the visit of the Warrington Temperance Lodge on Monday next. On Tuesday evening two new members were admitted by Bro- ther John Warburton, lodge deputy, and other officers. NEWTON NURSERY V. EARLESTOWN.—A. match between the above clubs took place on Saturday on the Nursery green. The afternoon was fine, and, as will be seen by the annexed score, some close finishes and several quite the opposite were played. Those of Messrs. J. and R. Lythgoe appeared to create most Interest. They belong to a bowling family, and both have dis- tinguished themselves in many a well-contested match. Their opponents on this occasion, Messrs. Mellardy and Wood, are both unknown to the game. yet they each just managed to win, amidst much excitement, by one chalk only. When the match was over an adjournment was made to the White Lion, where an excelicat knife and fork tea, got up in Mrs. Walmsley's usual good and abundant style, was provided, and he which ample justice was done, and a pleasant evening was spent. SHETLAND LASSES AS ROWERS.—A Kirkall correspondent. telegraphs that the great event of the Shetland Islands regatta this season was the pulling race. Last year the Shetland lasses beat a boat manned by a revenue cutter crew, and this year the same three strapping girls came in victorious against all corners. Last year Sheriff Thomas acted as coxswain, but this season all the crews pulled with- out coxswains, the winning crew covering the mile count, in half a minute less than the clasest competitor. They were enthusiastically cheered, as they deserved, foe the ladies used the oars. in a manner that would shame many male crews.

The roof is in course of, construction, the contract of this • piece of work, exclusive of the lead work, carving, and tracery, involving a cost of £1,219 Ss. In taking down some of the old stone work, several interesting pieces of masonry, apparently of very ancient date, were discovered; and to preserve the antiquity of the plate the committee are having these rebuilt in the interior walls of the tower. The whole cost of the restoration is estimated at £7,000, nearly £6,000 having been promised, of which a good portion has been paid to the treasurer. The church when restored will, it is calculated, have accomodation for about COO persons, bring slightly below the holding capacity of the edifice I before the alterations, this being due to the removal of the 1 galleries referred to. To raise the required sum it was I decided to hold a bazaar, and lower show, and the following I gentleman were appointed a committee to carry out the , scheme :-The Rev. H. B. Blogg (chairman), Mr. Charles ! Reynolds, J.P. (treasurer), Revs. A. P. Reynolds, and L. I K. Kinder (hon. secretaries), Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton, I Dr. Robinson, and Messrs. Samuel Ashton, Ralph Bate, Bolderston, Clark, S. Davies, T. W. Dunsford, Gleave, Gorst, Knibb, Lewis, C. E. Linaker, Pollard, Henry Reynolds, J.P., Riley, Bothwell, Speechley. Steward, A. Thomas, J.P., R. E. Walford, Maddock, E. Gorst, Hulse, ,and Watson, The baz tar and flower show arrangements were carried on with considerable spirit, the ladies working energetically to make the affair a success. The grand col- lection of articles to be seen on Tuesday, Wednesday, and , Thursday testified that there had been no lack of energy on I their part. The opening ceremony had been announced to ' be performed by Lady Rocksavage, but from some cause or other the Countess did not appear. The Rev. Henry B. Blogg, the vicar, said he was sorry to any Lady Rocksavage was absent; and in the absence of Lady Brooke, who had kindy consented to take her place, but who was ill, the duty •of openlng the baziar devolved upon him, and he undertook that duty with exceedingly great pleasure. He felt that bazaar would be a blessing to the parish, that it would promote a good feeling and help them to realise their co-union' friendship, and brotherhood. He was glad to see so many ladies and gentlemen of the parish present, for their presence was an expression of good feeling creditable to the parish, and a wonder to everyone. They would not want him to say much upon that occasion, because he fully ex- pected some lady would have taken that place. He was not only expressing his own wishes bat the wishes of all pre- . sent when he hoped that that bazaar would be an eminent success, and that they would have the pleasure of looking back upon the occasion as one in which they strove to do their best in that great and good cause. He folly believed that the blessing of God would be upon it. He then de- clared the bazaar open. Buying and selling then commenced briskly, the sellers being busily engaged, from the fair ladies behind the stalls down to the winsome little creatures of tender years with bouquets of bright flowers, which they endeavoured to dis- pose of in a sweet and gracious manner, yet, with an eager- ness that would have done credit to an experienced business man. The stalls were splendidly arranged and decked with a thousand skilfully worked articles of all sorts and shapes. On entering the bazaar the first stall to be seen was Mrs. Simpson's stall, under the superintendence of that lady and Mrs. Dunsford, Miss Bibby, Miss Malleson, and the Misses Simpson. Among the many articles upon it were to be seen a curious set of china on metal stand, worth £3," Professor Huxley's frogs." made for the bazaar by an invalid boy. These frogs, which were very clever imitations, were made of single pieces of note paper, and painted. They were sold at one shilling each. There was also a beautiftl window flower stand made of leather, sketching chairs, fancy ink- . stands, water-colour paintings. costly perambulator, shawls, and dolls. There was alao a wedding cake made by Miss Bibby, of Frodahain. Adjoining was Miss S. Crosfield's stall, superintended by that lady, and Mrs. Bolderston, Mrs. Bate, Mrs. Rothwell, Miss Latham, and Miss Sharpe. On this stall were Sect of antique china sold, price £1 7s. : a vast variety of woollen articles, pincushions in curious shapes. The shill superintended by Mrs. J. Crosfield, Mrs. Lewis, Miss Ashley, Miss Clough, and Miss Clarke also con- tained a rich collection of articles similar to the other. The next stall was similarly decked, bearing in addition a variety of fan., and " advice to single gentlemen" doled out in packets at the very moderate price of sixpence each. There were also pictures, ship in glass shade and sofa rags. This stall was attended to by Miss Sutton airs. Aston, Mrs. Riley, Mrs. Steward, and Mrs. Gorst. The vicar's stall con- tained a number of prayer hooks, smoking caps, fans, shawls, fancy baskets, dolls marked .22 10s. and .£2, Swiss inkstand, Turkish coffee pot, and slippers, d:c. This stall was under the superintendence of Mrs. Heron, Mrs. Hague, Mrs. Whytehead, and Miss Linaker. There was also a book and a toy stall. An interesting piece of workmanship was a small house of common pine in the old Cheshire style of architecture, comprising eight rooms elaborately furnished in the mest modern fashion, hall and staircase, iic. It attracted considerable attention, being the handiwork of Mr. George Ashton, In close proximity to this object of attrac- tion was the equally attractive one of a colossal shoe, pre- sided over by 101 d Mother Hubbard, that immortal personage being represented by a little girl dressed in the curious cos- tume familiar to all youngsters. The shoe was of course filled with all sorts of purchaseable articles. Going out of the tent in which the bazaar was held, the visitor entered another tent, the first half of which was utilised as a refreshment place, and the other half for the dower show. The fruits, vegetables, and flowers were well worth a visit, the various specimens, especially the fruits and vegetables, being excellent. The following is a list of the prizes :-Six I stove or greenhouse plants: 1, Rev. H. B. Blogg. Six ferns: . 1, Mrs. ilaziehurst, Runcorn; 2, Rev. H. B. Blogg. Four ! variegated plants: 1, Mrs. Hazlehurst. Liliurn : 1, Mrs. 1 Heron, Manley Hall, near `-Frodsham. Fern: 1, C. E. 1 Linaker, Frodsham; 2, Mrs. Hazlehurst; Stove plants: 1, ! Mrs. Hazlehurst. Mrs. Hayes, of Fred- I sham, displayed, for non-competition, some exceedingly fine I stove and greenhouse plants; and Mr. A. E. Wright, Castle I Park, Frodsham ; Mr. R. Hagfish, Aston Hall; and Mr. Dickson, Chester, exhibited some rich foliage plants and cut roses for the same purpose. Messrs. F. and A. Dickson.also of Chester, and Mr. G. Smith, Rock Ferry, sent some splendid cut roses, stove and greenhouse plants, sad ferns. There were several auxiliaries besides those described, which helped to fill the exchequer; Olelieunt Sally, archery, naarrionettes, and the Aegean Sea attracting some attention. Among those who visited the bazaar were Mr. Tonekinson, the late candidate for Parliamentary honours, and Mr. W. 13eamont, of Warrington, several of whose weeks of antiquarian interest were offered for sale on the book etall. On Wednesday afternoon, the bazaar tents' were blowp down by the strong North-West wind which prevailed. A kindly warning was given, but too late to save the stock, rind much damage was done to the fancy good. The bazaar was continued on Thursday and Friday at Belle Mont.

KILIND BY • nBCB OF WOOD AT ST. HBLIOM.__ Daniel Moran (68), Bold-street, Eccleston, died on Saturday from injuries received at Messrs. Pilkington's timber yard Deceased, who had worked in the yard for the last five years was assisting at the circular saws, which are used for cut- ting timber, on Friday, and was cutting a hard piece of timber, when the wood by some means jumped from the saw and struck him in the abdomen. He was taken Lome, and Dr. Gaskell attended him until the following day, when be died.

ATHLETIC FESTIVAL AT ST. HELENS JUNCTION.—As wil be seen from our advertising columns the cricket club in connection with the Sheeting Department of the Lordon and North-Western Railway Company at this place will bold an athletic festival this day (Saturday). Nothing but a favourable conditiOn of the weather will, we are sure, be lacking to make the sports a pleasant and successful boll- day.

lACCIDENT ON CROPPERS HILL, ST.•HELENS.—OR Mon- day, Mr. John Fiddler, Lagsmore House, one of the gnar- ldiens for Eftleston, met with an accident while driving in- to St. Helens with Mr. James Hatton, butcher. On .! descending Croppers Hill the horse fell and broke the ' shafts of the carriage. Mr. Hatton, who was driving. held I the reins and maintained his seat, but Mr. Fiddler was I thrown heavily into the road, close to the Engineer Hall. I He was taken into the hall, and it was found that his right I leg and knee was severely bruised, and one of his wrists and shoulders also injured. Dr. Ackerley attended him, and in a short time he was able to return_ home in a cab. PRESCOT CHURCH OF ENGLAND SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT.—For many years the scholars attending the Church of England Sunday Schools, Houghton-street, have had 1 their annual treat in a field attached to the vicarage, but 1 owing to the indisposition of the vicar and the fact that at previous gatherings a proportion of the rough element found its way, despite the strictest vigilance, on to the ground, it was thought advisable to have the treat in a more secluded place, and Knowsley Park was selected. The permission of Mr. Hale, Lord Derby's agent, having been obtained, the scholars had their annual meeting on Tuesday last, and it was in every respect quite as successtu' as ite predecessors. The 'children to the number of 700-380 boys and 320 girls— assembled at the schools at half-past one o'clock, formed into procession, and, headed by the Prescot Rifle Volunteer band marched to the park, where they dispersed and proceeded to enjoy themselves atthe games customary at such gatherings. At about four o'clock the youngsters were provided with a good tea, to which full justice was done. Puling the after- noon a number of races were run for small prizes, and dancing was indulged in to a large extent. In addition to the scnolars there were about a thousand persons present in- cluding parents and subscribers. Among those who attended were the Rev. L. W. Sampson (the vicar), Rev. F. R. Lee (curate), Rev. B. S. Clarke (curate of Eccleston), Mr. W. L. Evans, J.P., and Mrs. Evans, and a number of ladies of the parish.

MEETING OF MINERS AT Sr. HF.LENS.—On Monday even- ing, a meeting of miners was held on the Fair Ground, Mr. P. McKinley presiding, and about 200 were present. Mr. John Cross, miners' agent, said the meeting was convened in consequence of a change in the zules at Messrs. Bournes and Robinson's, Pilkington Brothers, and Sankey Brook Collieries, and he believed that unless some action was taken the change would not be confined to those three places, but would become general throughout the district. Although a great many had joined the society since the strike, the masters knew very well that a great many, in order tolsave a penny a week, had left It, thus throwing themselves at the mercy of the masters. One of the rules the collieries he had named intended, putting into operation was that the men be required to work on Saturday. As trade was improving the masters wanted to fasten the men down, and get them to work longer, but if they were all lf one mind, and acted accordingly, they would not be told to go about their busi- ness, as would be the case if oue or a few went to the masters and said they would not work under those rules.— Mr. P. McKinley said that new rule was an evidence that the masters knew that trade was improving, and the colliers being required to work half a day a week longer was a fact which showed that the masters were able to sell their coal better. The revival in trade was further attested by the fact that Brirnilows had refused a twelve month's order at the present prices, and in Pilkington's raising the price of their sheet glass ten per cent —lt was decided to appoint deputations to wait upon the masters and tell them their terms and it was also decided to work no more than 5 days a week. On Thursday night another meeting of the miners work- ing under Messrs. Pilkington was held on the fair ground. The meeting was convened for the parpose of considering a statement which had been made by the managers to some of the men that if they did not work on Saturdays the col- lieries would be stopped. Mr. Jdm Cross presided, and there was only a small attendance. A resolution was passed to the-effect that no work be done on Saturdays.

I LORD CHIEF JCSTICR COLERIDGE ON BREA.= OF PRO- MISE OF MARRISGE.—In sumining up in an action for breach of promise of marriage, at the Liverpool assizes, .Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, alluding to SOME remarks as to the expediency a this class of action, said that whatever might be the enligho-ned conclusion of Parliament on the question he did not know. Parliament might think fit to abolish breach of promise as a ground of action, but it ' was mach to be considered ere that con- summation was arrived at, whether in certain ranks of life women would have any protection against the misconduct of men. It was too much forgotten that these actions were often extremely useful in keeping people within the bounds of duty which, if Caere were no such laws, they would avoid. It very often happened that a woman gave up honestly and affectionately the best years of I.er life to a particular man, and put aside all thoughts of marry- , lug anyone else. When that man dishonestly and illegally broke bia connect with her the only compensation she could ' lobtain for the wrong done to her was to seek heavy and substantial damages in a court of law.
