made it clearly understood that be did so to show the Lords he was not prejudiced against their views; and though the advanced Liberals :voted with the Irish members against certain of these concessions—not without service to the common cause in the way of protest—we are convinced that the decision to offer these safe concessions was one of wisdom and skilful tactics. These • small surrenders will, or ought to, pave the way to a peaceful understanding between the two Houses on the whole Bill at the end of these differences, and of this seeming game of cross- purposes; and if they do they will have amply sompassed their purpose. The majority lathe Lords will have to swallow a great deal they don't relish as it is; but they can yield with a good grace on the plea that after all they have had a share, not utterly useless, in moulding the Land Bill, and have here and there left the impress of their fingers upon it. Whereas, had the Commons at the instigation of the Government rejected every amendment of the Lords without exception, no smallest loop-hole would have been left for the escape of the dignity and self- esteem of the opposing Peers; and in the rage at being thus convened and summoned to yield uncon- ditionally without promise of quarter, they might have turned round and fought and died hard like wild animals driven to bay. In that extremity, it is possible the Lords might have mustered just enough resolution to take their last stand upon some point in contention with the Lower House, and refusing -to budge, with desperate disregard of all consequences to their order and its interests and monopolies, might have caused the loss of the whole Bill for this Session. As it is, they have generously provided for them a soothing salvo for their wounded self- conceit. They can boast, if they liko, that they have carried some of , their amendments, and hug the belief that these amendments will prove of use in con- serving the Irish landlords' interests; and on the strength of that, these opposition Lords can rush off to their grouse shooting, and leave the House of Lords after their disappearance to notify its formal acquiescence in the Commons' amendments of the Lords' amendments. That something like this will be the terminating incident of this stiff party contest over the Land Bill is the general expectation. Any other issue would cast the most damaging reflection upon the character of the British Parliamentary system as a workable machine for law-making.

At this sum the lot was withdrawn. The Runcorn Commissioners met on Thursday for the par- I pose of again considering the preposed contract with Mr. Cliff for street cleansing. The Highway Committee had I met in solemn conclave previous to the gathering, and should, in the ordinary course of affairs, have presented a report for the consideration of the Board, but their delibera- tions were brought to a rather sudden termination, when they came to c msider their legal position, by the absence of the I 'Law Clerk (Mr. W. H. Linaker) who sent a telegram saying; that he could not possibly attend. The meeting was con- sequently like the play of Hamlet with Hamlet left out, and there was no small amount of discontented mutterings in- dulged in at the clerk's absence. I hear that the memorial forwarded to the Commissioners is to be carefully examined for the purpose of testing the genuineness of the signatures. The Widnes Local Board monthly meeting, held this week, was one of considerable interest. Mr. Allen, the new clerk, took his seat, which he will no doubt feel still more comfortable now that his salary is raised £lOO per annum. Mr. Allen is a very lucky Man to get such a nice advance lin these times of general depression. The Board had under their consideration two schemes of sewerage for the town. Mr. Kershaw and Mr. Carey both gave their hearty support to attajor Cross's scheme, and bore testimony to its great I superiority to that of Mr. Higginson, the Board's surveyor. Kral shaw said that Mr. Higginson's scheme would cost £19,000 to carry out as against the Chairman's at £12,C,00; and it was agreed that a special meeting of the Board should be held on Tuesday next, so that the members might reserve full explanations respecting both plans. The members of the Widnes Ratepayers' and Property Owners' Association, do not seem to be discouraged by the coldness with which their visits have been received by the board in the past, for on Tuesday, another deptuatton from that body asked for an interview, in order that they might discuss the estimate for the new rate. Mr. Heyes ridiculed the notion of giving the gentlemen an interview, and thus wasting time, considering the fact that the new rate had been passed some two months ago • and said that if they had any objection to raise to its salidity, they should do so by refusing to pay it when demanded.. He was, however, overruled by the Chairman and other members, who agreed to give the deputationists an interview at the close of the ordinary business. This accordingly took place, but the deputation were informed that the board could not consent to hold a discussion with them as to any points in the estimate, though they were quite willing to answer any reasonable questions, notwithstanding the fact that they had not come before them previous to the rate having been sanc- tioned. Mr. Rimener, the chairman of the association, inquired how it was that a sum of £5O had been put down for a new cart, and another of the deputation appeared to think he had made a strong point by saying it must be a very pretty cart to cost such a sum, but the reply of Mr. Kershaw seemed to be satisfactory when he s tid that the cart was not an orelinary one, but for watering pur- poses, awl it must not be necessarily concluded that the ap- proximate sum mentioned in the estimate would be spent. Mr. Carey remarked that such questions as this particular one could very easily have been put by one of the represen- tatives of the Association at present on the Board, of whom there are two, and it seemed very unnecessary that a deputa- tion should attend in order to put it. Another point raised was the interest paid on loans, which strange to say, one of the deputation imagined to be about 7or 711 per cent. He was asked to the upper end of the Board table, and after a minute's consultation with the chairman and the accountant, he acknowledged that his objection was based upon an en- tire misapprehension. Mr. Carey said it would have been far better if the gentlemen in question had waited upon the accountant, and asked him for an explanation which weld' have been furnished most readily. It was ridiculous to sup- pose that the Board paid any such interest as seven per cent. for leans. Then the sum paid to provide milk for the cat kept at the Accident Hospital was raised, but' this proved the proverbial straw which is sail to have broken the camel's back, and the Chairman said he was extremely sorry that the deputation should have taken up their time with such peurile and absurd questions. Then the discussion became rather hot, it being led by Mr. IRichard Webster, one of the deputation, who said it seemed the ratepayers were only good for paying rates ; and he was rather sharply reminded that neither he nor his friends had any legal standing in the Board-room, but was only there on sufferance. Mr. Kershaw clinched the matter by saying that it was perfectly within the power of the Board to hold their meetings without even the presence of representatives of the press ! FLACCUS.

Lancashire seems very likely to gain an uncn. viable notoriety for railway accidents.. Two of these terrible disasters have occurred this week in this county within a few hours of each other. The acci- dent which took place on Monday afternoon, at Blackburn, is one of a very terrible character, and there are circumstances connected with it which, unless satisfactorily cleared up, cannot fail to carry alarm into the public mind. At first sight it seems that there must have been incomprehensible blunder- ingsomewhere. There has been in the past blundering on or lines of railway of a very extraordinary kind, but we question whether it is not something new even in the annals of English railway disasters for an express train to dash through an important station into another train which was shunting on the same line, with the inevitable effect of scattering death and destruction all around. Various theories are advanced to account for this terrible mishap. One report states that the general impression ot the passengers in the Manchester train is that the accident is attributed to the failure of the Westinghouse brake. This, however, is partly accounted for by the statement of the driver of the train tha.t he "did not quite understand its working ." If it be true as alleged, that this was the first time he had driven an express train and "did not quite under- stand" the working of the most powerful brake yet invented, one which from all accounts ought to have made Monday's occurrence an absolute impossibility, the accident admits of a very easy ex- planation. It is, however, better not to arrive at a premature conclusion on the subject. There is bound to be a rigid enquiry into this—one of the most alarming occurrences that have take phut, for a I very long time—and the company will have an oppor- tunity of showing how the Westinghouse brake, so strongly recommended by the Board of Trade as a I protector to passengers, did not act on this occasion, ' and whether its failure was really attributable to the I inexperience of the driver. Anything more calculated to destroy the confidence of the public in our railway system than the latter assertion cannot be easily imagined. The second accident happmed but a few hours after the Blackburn disaster. In this case a passenger train, while rounding a curve near Oldham, ran into an engine which was drawing a number of empty carriages. The passengers, in addition to the I severe shaking they received, had to contend with lan unusual danger. The forepart of the train caught fire, and two first and two third class carriages were consumed, but happily no one was burnt. The fire is said to have been occasioned through the fire box of the engine being damaged. These, accidents plainly intimate that there is yet plenty to be done in the way of soiantific improvement before the timid traveller will Ibe satisfied that he is safe upon the iron road. In one day he has had two very painful proofs that he is I now liable to be mangled and roasted.

RUNCORN FESCUE ORDER OF DRUIDS. The mem- bers and friends had their annual dinner on Monday, at the Anchor Inn, kept by Mrs. Waterworth. Owing to the past twelvemonths having been such as to thoroughly test the stability of the club, there was no balance in hand to report by Mr. R. Roberts, the secretary. It is, however, pleasing to know that the total worth of the lodge is £3 7s. per member, of whom there are 30 now on the books.

CALVINISTIC METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, RITNOORN. Mr. James Richardson, secretary of this school, has car- ried off the first prize for scriptural knowledge in the exam- ination connected with the Lancashire and Cheshire Presby- tery. First class certificates of competency hays also been presented to the Misses Humphreys and Worgam, and Mr. J. E. Longshaw. The following scholars belonging to the school were awarded certificates in the junior examination : —Misses M. A. Hayes, S. A. Dodson, Annie Harrington, Charlotte Edwards, Lizzie Leach; and Masters F. G. Leach, and John Leach.

Mr. Charles Garnett, of Runcorn, who was one of about 100 candidates for the appointment of missionary to the Manchester and Salford Wesleyan Lay Home Mission, bas proved the successful candidate. Mr. Garnett is a very popular young man in Runcorn, and his success has given general satisfaction to his fellow denominationalists.
Exonmsmiz FROM WIDNES.—On Monday, a number of excursionists left the West Bank Dock, Widnes, for Northwich and Vale Royal. The weather was not of a very favourable kind.

BURGLARY AT ASTON HEATlL—During Sunday night the house of Mr. Davies, farmer, Aston Heath, was entered by burglars. Entrance was effected through a window at the rear of the house, and the drawers in the room down stairs were carefully examined, but only three pairs of boots were taken. In one of the drawers was a pocket book, in- side of which was a £lO bank note, but is was overlooked. It is supposed that the burglars were disturbed during their work, for they left a chisel in one of the bedrooms. RECOGNITION OF TUE REV. W. ROBINSON'S SER- VICES IN RUNCORN.—The other evening a deputation, con- sisting of Mr. Buckley (churchwarden of Trinity Church), Mr. Hankinson, sen. (sidesman), and Mr. Yates, waited upon the Rev. Win. Robinson, their late curate, who was in the town on private business, and presented him with a purse of gold. The deputation, in making the preEentation, re- marked that unanimity and willingness had been shown by all who had subscribed. More would have done so had they been waited upon, but the short time before Mr. Robinson's departure would not allow the collectors an opportunity of visiting a large number. It was a matter of regret that cir- cumstances did not permit of a public meeting, as many had wished. The effects of his ministry would long be felt and pleasant memories be treasured by all. No doubt some of the worshippers at Holy Trinity would be sorry that they knew nothing of the presentation, and were therefore not among the contributors; but it was impossible to call upon all, yet the widow's mite and the cordial offering of the workingman had made up the amount. The very best wishes were expressed for Mr. Robinson's future success. In acknowledging the presentation, Mr. Robinson expressed his gratitude to all those who had co-operated in the matter. He briefly reviewed his work among them and rejoiced in the cordial good feeling which had subsisted between him- self and the congregation. We may also add that several other presents were made privately to Mr. Robinson, as tokens of the esteem in which he is held. CONGREGATIONAL Tr.—On Monday last the con- gregation worshipping at St. James's Church, Latchford had their annual trip to New Brighton, the favourite resor of pleasure seekers, and, although the afternoon proved showery, on the whole an enjoyable day was spent. MUSIC IN THE PARE.—St. Paul's Sunday School bans will play the following selections in the Park, on Wednes- day evening next, at seven o'clock :—Quick march, "To arms" (Newton); fantasia, "La val de amour" (Blanche- teau) ;.quadrilles, "Ella Leene " (Blegir) ; trombone solo, King's herald" (Round) • valse, " Water lily "(Wright); selection, "La valle de ha Meuse " (Ryembault); " God save the Queen."—Thomas Armstrong, conductor. THE SOUTHPORT AND WEST LANCA9AIRE BANK.—The directors of the Southport and West Lancashire Banking Company (Limited) announced that arrangements are in course of completion for opening the bank on an early day, of which due notice will be given. It is said that, now that the Master of the Rolls has sanctioned the reconstruction of the bank, shares are being taken up rapidly.

WIDNES BAPTIST SUNDAY SCITOOL.—On Thursdak, the annual treat to the scholars of this school took place. The children, who with their teachers and friends numbered about 80, left Widnes about half-past one for Overton Hills, by way of Ditton and Runcorn. The weather was very un- favourable, a drizzling rain falling throughout the greater part of the afternoon. Despite these disadvantages, how- ever, the children managed to spend a pleasant day. LACEY-STREET, WIDNES, WESLEYAN STNDAY SCHOOL.— The select class and teachers of the above schools held their annual treat on Wednesday, the Overton Hills being the place chosen for the excursion. The scholars and teachers, numbering about 50, proceeded to Frodsharn, going by way of Ditton. In the morning a steady drizzling rain rendered the excursionists' prospects anything but cheerful, but in the afternoon the sky cleared and the weather became fine. Though the somewhat gloomy sky prevented the natural beauties of the hills from appearing to the fullest advantage, the children found no lack of amusement and recreation. The treat was heartily enjoyed, and the excursion through- out proved a complete success.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN METHODIST ExcunsioN.,—The Runcorn, Brunswick, Halton-road, and Camden Wesleyan Methodist Sunday schools had an excursion to Liverpool and New Brighton on Monday, in the steamer "Fairy Queen." The weather was of an unfavourable character.

SENTENCE ON RUNCORN PRISONERS AT THE SESSIONS. --On the sth inst., at the Cheshire Adjourned Sessions, before Mr. Horatio Lloyd and other magistrates, Peter Leather (40), James Johnson (61), Joseph Smith (43), boat- men, were indicted for stealing a sack and 50Ibs. weight of rope, the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, at Runcorn, on the 15th ult. The prisoners, when in a Istate of partial intoxication, stole the rope from one of pro- secutors' boats and sold it to buy more drink. The jury, after considering the case for an hour were still unable to agree, although the guilt of the prisoners was clearly esta- blished. Mr. John Wood, the presiding magistiate, said that if they could not agree he would discharge them and try the men over again. In consequence of obstinacy on the part of a member of the jury, prisoners would not be acquitted. After a few minutes' further consideration the jury returned a verdict of guilty, and Leather and Johnson were sentenced to nine months' imprisonment With hard labour, and Smith to six months.--Thomas Conway (18), labourer, was found guilty of unlawfully wounding Thomas Giblin, at Runcorn, on the 18th ult., and he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour

OAKLAND-STREET„WIDNES, WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL—On Saturday the scholars of the above School had their annual treat. About half-past one in the afternoon, the scholars to the number of 800, assembled at the schools. Thence, headed by the Star of Temperance brass band, they marched in procession to a field in Moor-lane, which had been lent for the occasion by Mr. Kilsall. Trie procession was led by Mr. Hartland, a prominent member of the con- gregation. Then came Mr. William Jackson, the superinten- dent of the Sunday school. After him followed the boys and girls, who, being dressed in their best attire, presented a very pleasing spectacle. The children proceeded through Victoria-road, Simm's Cross-lane and Dock-lane to their destination, where they arrived about a quarter past two. Arrived at the field, the Sunday scholars found that a variety of amusements had been provided for their special delectation. Here games of various kinds were thoroughly enjoyed. About five o'clock tea was ready, and the scholars sat down to an abundant repast—abundant it will be seen from the fact that no less than 80 gallons of tea were pro- vided and between two and three cwt. of provisions. Tea over, the homward journey was commenced. On the way calls were made at Mr. Kelsalls's, where a hymn was sung, and at the Rev. C. Bingant's, the minister of the Oakland- street Chapel. Widnes was reached about nine o'clock. A very pleasant day was spent, as the weather was all thet could be desired, and not a hitch occurred to mar the pi o- ceedi ugs. -

A COMPLIMENT TO LANCASHIRE Jul:ans.—At tho close of the Liverpool Assizes on Monday Lord Chief Justice Coleridge iaid that ended the duties of the jury for those assizes, and added :—ln parting from you, gentlemen, I desire to say With what satisfaction I have had to do with Lancashire juries. If I were unfortunate enough to be a party in a law suit I should desire nothing better than that I should be tried by a Lancashire jury. "FORBIDDING THE BANNS."—" The large and some- what fashionable congregation of St. Mary's, Moss Side, were greatly startled on Sunday morning last, when the rector, the ißev. F. C. Woodhouse, after publishing the banns of marriage, made the usual announcements,a woman at the west end of the church, in a piercing voice, cried out 'I forbid the banns.' Fhe rector thereupon intimated that the woman should see him in the vestry at the conclusion of the service. It was subsequently ascertained that there was no sufficient reason for the objection raised."

TUN hfrufs,oN3LENT or Mu. ClatErx.—A petition praying for the Rev. J. F. Green's release from prison from Miles Platting has been forwarded to General Ponsonby for presentation to the Queen, signed by 911 adults, heads of families, and as the parish of St. John's, Miles Platting, con- tains 1,160 houses (90 of which are unoccupied), the petition may be fairly considered as the almost unanimous request of the whole parish.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.—On Sun- day the anniversary services in connection with this branch were held in the Public Hall, and addresses delivered by Mr. W. P. Roberts and Mr. H. A. Pearson, of Liverpool. Mr. Roberts, who was the winner of the baritone and bass prizes at the Manchester and Salford vocal festival in 1875, sang, with very good effect, several solos from Sankey's selection. On Monday the steamer Kingstown was engaged for a trip to Liverpool. About ten o'clock the excursionists embarked at the Duke's Pier, and proceeded without " let or hindance " down the river. On arriving near Liverpool the passengers were permitted to look over the training ship Indefatigahlo, and the cleanliness and smart appearance of the ship and her youthful crew were remarked upon by all. Re-embark, ing, the party were saluted by a ringing cheer from the boys of the training ship, which was answered by one as hearty, if not quite so loud, from the Kingstown, which now proceeded to her destination. Oa 11..rriviL,g at Liverpool many availed themselves of the pri7:fege of visiting the transatlantic steamer Celtic, of !Lo White Star lino. Con- ducted by Mr. Shawi,the. -party next proceeded to visit the me Home, e iris Engine Station, and the Exchange. The lads of the Mersey Mission drum and fife band (which I had been In attendance on the Kingstown), dressed in their sallms. suits, attracted general attention as they marched in Order through the streets. Several persons were heard to ask what training ship they belonged to, and the merchants' on the Exchange requested them to favour them with a selection, with which request Mr. Shaw complied. Tea was provided at the Excelsior Dining Hall, Castle-street. About 190 persons sat down, and, judging from the spirit of good humour which prevailed, each one seemed thoroughly satis- fied with the repast. After tea a meeting was held, over which Mr. Alderman Shallcross presided. There were also present the Revs. Mr. Patrick and Mr. Edmundson, and two chaplains to the missions, and Mr. H. A. Pearson. Appro- priate speeches were made encouraging the workers to , further diligence in the cause. The weather, which had I during the afternoon been rather " ditty "—to use a nautical expression—now cleared up, and the excursionists had a beautiful and enjoyable sail home, where they arrived at about half-past nine. The fife band played several airs, and a great proportion of the passengers gathered together on the lower deck for the purpose of singing hymns. A number of young men formed a group and commenced sing- ing in opposition. The effect, to anyone on the upper deck, was anything but melodious. First there would come a burst of sacred music; and then, tome on a sudden puff of wind, a snatch or two of a song, the burden of which seemed to be a certain "horse" which came to an untimely end last winter, would greet the ears of the listener. However, everything was conducted within the bounds of decorum, and all appeared perfectly satisfied with the day's ad- ventures.

NEW UNIVERSITY COLLEGE, LIVERPOOL. -A.. copy of the charter of incorporation to tin University College, Liverpool, has been published. The object of the college is to be the promotion of "such instruction in all the ! branches of a liberal education as may enable residents in the city of Liverpool and the neighbourhood to qualify for degrees in art, science, and other subjects at any of the universities granting degrees to non-resident students, and at the same time to give such technical instruction as will be of immediate service in professional and commercial life." Female students are to be admitted, and it is a fundamental condition of the constitution of the college that no one con- nectedSwith;it is to be required to make any declaration of re- ligious belief. Lord Derby is to be the first president of the college, and Mr. Christopher Bushell and Mr. Rathbone the first vice-presidents. The Town Councils of Liverpool, Chester, Birhonhead, Bootle, St. Helens, Southport, War- rington, and Wigan are invested with the right of electing governors. The charter winds up by saying that the col- lege shall not at any time hold real property excaeding the annual value of £lO,OOO.

TOTE REV. HENRY VALENTINE'S FAREWELL SERMON AT RUNCORN.—The Rev. Henry Valentine preached his farewell sermon in St. Paul's Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday evening, previous to his departure for the Salford (Manchester) circuit. The reverend gentleman took for his text Eccles. xii., 13-14 :—"Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God and keep His commandments: for this is the whole duty of man. For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing, whether it be good or whether it be evil." At the close of his discourse, Mr. Valentine spoke as follows: now close my ministry among you, God knows, and you know, that I have not failed to declare among you the Whole counsel of God. And now, what shall we say unto Him who sent us? What report shall we gr,T to the King? Concerning some of you I have reason to rejoice. You love God; you keep His commandments. I congratulate you. Concerning some I cherish fear. It would be simply absurd for me to say you do not love God when you know perfectly well in your own consciousness you do not. Do you wonder, therefore, that I cherish fears; fears lest the very Gosp 1 of reconciliation which it has been my privilege to declare unto you should become to you the Gospel of condemnation, and that I, a minister of Christ, should be summoned to give evidence against you. The thought seems to overpower me." I can think of this magnificent world becoming a wreck, but I cannot bear to think of any of you ever being lost; and yet I have to say, with all the earnestness of which my soul is capable, and with this inspired volume lying before me, if you don't accept Christ, and love God and keep his com- mandments, you will be damned. Listen, therefore, to the voice with which you have been familiar: "Fear God, keep His commandments ; for this is Lk e whole duty of man. For God shall bring every work into judgment, with every secret thing. wnether it be good or whether it be evil." So my ministry closes. It hardly seems possible that three years have passed since I first stood in this pulpit, and yet ; so it is; so rapidly do our weeks and months and years fly by. When I look back upon those three years I look back , upon them with great gratitude to God. He has been very ; good; God has been very good to us at home. He has been , good to us in many respects; good to us in that He has I, given me favour in the sight of the people. Dear brethren, many times when I have come up here I have come with I I peat heaviness, but when I have looked at you, and seen ; your countenances, when I have listened to the singing of I j the congregation, when I have remembered that I have had I an interest in your prayers, I have felt very much strengthened and encouraged. I thank all of you for your , kindness to me. My three years' sojourn here has been a very happy one. I have said elsewhere. and I may repeat it again to-night, that during that time I have not had an un- kind word said to ma. You have been very forbearing, lcng-suffering, tender-hearted. I have had reason to mourn many times because 'of my unfaithfulness. I have been sorry that my work has not been more successful, and yet I I am thankful to know that it has not been altogether in vain. Here and there I have testimonies of the fact that God has made me instrumental in conversions to God. lam thank- ful for that. I feel it to be a great henour and a great joy ebvieh.eidineelp: ectrehmseiotntf dwh sosagliinevntelal generosity bagonluirdifikn:tahnaThomas kindness. • ••••- --nntecl with this circuit; the circuit in , lived, and jgave, and died. lam thantful to God that I have circuit,thank wherek) e yu or °us t, good a:A godly a man lived, and where there are so many 1 dear friends, for all your kindness to me. I shall not forget I Runcorn—never forget Runcorn. I cannot .do that. I have two little graves here. I carry tle memory of them with me; and I shall think of Runcorn rnAnv a time. RE THOMAS BEASLEY.

This bankrupt came up for his adjourned public examina- tion at the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, before ' Mr. Collier. Mr. Segar (instructed by Mr. Hitchen, of Run- corn), appeared for several creditors front Runcorn and the district, and Mr. Gregory, of Liverpool, for other creditors. , Amongst those present were Mr. Thomas Handley and Dr. I McDougall. As soon as the case was called on, Mr. Gregory I said he was not prepared to go as fully into it that day as he should have liked, and he must ask for an adjournment. —Mr. Beasley said these repeated adjournments were a ' most serious affair to him. The matter had now been hang- ing over about five months.—Mr. Segar remarked that be was quite willing to go on with the examination as far as he could, but he was afraid he should be trespassing upon some of the ground to be dealt with by Mr. Gregory.—lt was decided that the examination by Mr. Segar should be pro- ceeded with, and for this purpose the bankrupt and the ' other gentlemen concerned adjourned to another court, where the case was heard before the Registrar. After our representative had taken a full ! note of the proceedings for about an hour, Mr. Segar said he did not think it was customary to publish in , the press examinations so conducted, which were understood to be private. Any creditor could obtain copies of the shorthand-writer's notes of the examination, on making proper application. Our representative was requested to see one of the chief officials of the court on the matter, and he said that on no account must the examination be published. We may remark that the point would probably not have ' arisen had not a request been made to Mr. Segar that a ques- tion affecting a prominent Widnes gentleman, and not really material to the examination, should not be put in The , Examiner. The examination of the bankrupt in open court was adjourned by mutual consent, to the 19th inst.

--- BUDDER DEATH AT AIIIIAT BTATION.—Att awfully sudden death took place at Arpley Station, Warrington. on Wednesday evening. It appears that a woman named Margaret Balfour, about 40 years of age, cook to Mr. Peter Riyands, my., Massey Hall, Thelwall, arrived in town to do some shopping, and having finished her business went to Arpley Station for the purpose of returning to Thelwall by the 6-45 p.m. train. Arriving at the station a few minutes before the time, she sat down en a seat. Shortly afterwards Ellis Holywell, employed by Mr. John Cross, botcher, went to the station with some meat for deteased, and saw her fall from the seat. He sent to her and found her dead. Drs. Sruith an.il Sherratt were sent for, but on arrival they pro- tt-nat,c,..l btu extinct, and the body was removed to the NWoolpack Inn. An inquest was held on Friday, and a ver- d.ct of died from "Natural causes was returned.
WIDNES POLICE COURT.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. H. S. Hall (chairman) and Mr.
Brock.

ALLEGED CRIMINAL ASSAULT.—A dirty looking fellow named John Kirk was brought up on remand, from -Monday, Charged with a criminal assault on a girl named Catherine Price, aged 12, on the previous Saturday.—The evidence on Monday was to the effect that on Sattnclay the prisoner went to a house in Pleasant-street, where Price lived with a woman named Gray, and asked to be allowed to stay there all night. Mrs. Gray consented. Defendant went to bed about eleven o'clock; and, according to the statement of the girl, he called her to his bedroom early on Surday morning and committed the offence.—On the application of the Superintendent of Police, the prisoner was remanded for a week. ... MINOR ASSAULT CASES—Thomas Duffy was summoned for threatening to assault Mary Nolan. Complainant said that on the 7th inst. the defendant took off most of his clothe.: at the front of her door and wanted to fight. One of the windows in the house was open, and he threw the stone Produced, which waS of considerable size, through it. In reply to Mr. Blackwell, deputy magistrates' clerk, complain- ant said she could not swear that defenant threatened to assault her, and the summons was therefore dismissed.— Alice Sandbach was charged by Lydia Harrison with assault- ing her. Complainant said that after an introductory war of words near her house, defendant ran her into the back yard, dragged her into the entry, and beat her shamefully. Several witnesses were called on both sides, and the Chair- man said there appeared to be very little difference between complainant or defendant as to which was the more blame- worthy. The disturbance between them had been of a most disgraceful character, and he was of opinion the best way of settling it would be to bind each of them over in her own recognizances of £lO and one in £5 to keep the peace for six months, or go to gaol for seven days.—Ernest Follon, a boy, was charged with assaulting another lad named William Henry Pawlson. Complainant said that on the 23rd ult, the defendant hit him on the head with a stone which he threw at him. Mr. Husband, who appeared for the defence, said he was willing to write to Follon's school- master, at Simms Cross school, asking him to caution the lad against stone throwing. The Chairman said as this was defendant's first offence, they would only order him to pay the Coats; but it was certainly high time that something was done to put a atop to the great amount of stone throw- ing which took place in the district.—Hannah Jones was charged with assaulting Mary Carmichael, on the 6th inst. Complainant said defendant came to her door at night time and did all she could to tempt her to come eut, by knock- ing loudly. She, however, refused, until her (complainant's) boy came up the street and told defendant his mother wait quite as good as she was. She then ran out, on which de- fendant hit her in the face with her open hand. Defendant was fleed ss. and Bs. 6d. costa, and, in default of .payment, sentenced to seven days' imprisonment. Defendant (ex- citedly) : I will have seven days.—James Collins was charged, on remand from Monday, with unlawfully wound- ing Ellen Hunt,who stated that on Saturday night, about! half-past eleven, she was in her own house, when sorde one knocked at the door. She slaked several times who was there, but received no answer. She then went to the back door, and on opening it the defendant, Who WAS standing there, struck her on the head with the large stone produced, withoet making use of any remare. She had given him no provocation. Several witnesses were called for the defence, who swore stoutly that the defendant was in bed at the time of the assault. The magistrates dismissed the case. DEFYING ANY POLICEMAN IN WIDNES AND THE BE- -SIILT.—A respectably dressed man named James Gray was charged with being drunk and assaulting P.C. McDonald.— The officer said that about eleven o'clock, on Saturday night, he was in Mersey-road, in company with P.C. Timperley, when he saw the defendant, who was drunk, cursing and swearing, and challenging another man to tight. The se- cond mart left, and he then went up to defendant and re- quested him to be qniet, but he said he should not. He next asked him for his name and address, but he would not give them. He told Gray that if he did not do so he should have to take him to the police station, but he replied that , there was not a policeman in Widnes who could do that. Defendant then tried to strike him, and he closed with him. During the struggle Gray kicked at him several times, and also str:lck him with his fist. —P.C. Timperley and P.C. No. 73 gave corroborative evidence. Timperley added that he saw defendant strike McDonald on the helmet and on the head, and he also tried to bite him (witness).—Gray, in de- fence, said he was talking to another man who had had a pipe broken, and a passer-by said "What are you bothering about ?" He asked the man what he had to do with the matter, on which the policemen came up and ordered him to go home. He replied, " No ; I Abell not go home till I like." One of the officers took him by the collar and shook him, Ina with the assistance of another policeman they threw him on the ground and Mused him.—Wm. Lythgoe, Henry Allen, and another witness were called by defendant, and swore positively that he was quite sober. Allen said the officers collared defendant,lmocked him down, and put their knees on him "so that he had not a chance." They also drag- ged him several yards through the streets, and did not give him an opportunity of getting upon his feet.—The Chairman: , We see no reason to disbelieve the three officers, and defen- dant will be fined Ss. and the costs, 7s. 61. in each case ; or in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment —A similar charge was preferred against a man named John Owens by McDonald. The officer said that when he was taking the last defendant in charge, Owens came up and asked him to let him go. He replied that he should not, on which de- fendant took hold of his (witness's) arm. He told him to stand back and not interfere, but instead of doing so, he seized Gray by the collar and tried to take him away.—P.C. Timperley gave evidence in support of McDonald's state- ment.—Mr. Hall said the Bench were obliged to protect the police in the execution of their duty, Defendant would be fined 5s and 7s. 6d. costs, or seven days' imprisonment, and he might think himself fortunate in escaping with such a light punishment, as in very similar cases the magistrates in that court often passed much severer sentences. His advice to such men as defendant was "Don't interfere." Two OF THE GENTLER SEX Flonmen.—Annie Smith and Rachel Hunt were charged by P.C. 1,008, with fighting in Victeria-road, on the night of the 30th ult. The case against Smith was dismissed, and the other defendant was. ordered to enter into her own recognizances of £lO, and one surety of £5 to keep the peace for three months. A WARNING TO LOVERS OF DOGS.—Thomas Tomkins, whose wife appeared for him, was charged with keeping a dog without a license.—P.C. Strickland said that on the afternoon of the 4th, be visited defendant's premises in Deacon-road, and found in the backyard a dog for which they had no license. The Chairman said defendant appeared to belong to a respectable position in society and he must have known that he was breaking the law.—He would be fined double the value of a license-15s.—and the costs, making 275., and, in default of payment, be committed 21 days. A BRUTAL Assautg.—Edward Loines, who:did not put in an appearance, was summoned for assaulting Joseph Ger- rard.—Complainant said that on Saturday night he was walking down Davies-street, when defendant said something to another man about a married woman. Complainant made a remark about the woman's husband which he thought would be accepted in a proper spirit, but defendant struck him in the face and knocked him down, causing him to lbecomains.nsible.—Defendant was ordered to pay A fine of I 20s. and 7s. 61. costs. In default of payment, he was ordered to he committed to gaol one month. • MAKING A BAD START IN LIFE.—A boy named Patrick Quinn was charged with stealing it coat, value 4s. 6d., the 1 property of TI:q111/19 Hill, labourer, Bold. Prosecutor works at a foundry in Ellison-street. and on Saturday, the 6th instant, be left the coat on the boiler. On returning to work on the Bth, Ile found the article had been Stolen. It was worth i Is. 61, and hid been purchased by. John Duffy, marine store ! 1 dealer of Pleasant-street, for threepence.—The prisoner was I sentenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod.

YOI7THFUL COPM STEaratas.—Three girls named Mary A. Calland, Mary A. Stokes, and Mary Walton were sum- moned for stealing a quantity of coal, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Co., from Messrs. Hutchinson's works.—The case was proved by P.C. Ross. 1 who caught the prisoners in the act of stealing the coal from a wagon on Messrs. Hutchinson's premises.—They were each fined 10s., or seven days' imprisonment.

AFFIRMATION AND OATHS.-811 W. HARCOURT, replying to Mr. Labouchere, said be had no power to interfere with judges and magistrates for their refusal to allow persons to give evidence because they wished to affirm instead of taking the oath. Tim NEW RUSSO-PERSIAN FRONTIER.—Sk C. DILXE said no proposals had been made by Russia 'RE regarded the new Russo-Persian frontier. COLLECTION OF POOR RATES IN IRELAND.—Mr. Fora= promised an inquiry if preper materials were forwarded to him, in the case of certain collectors in Ireland receiving ninepence in the pound for collecting poor rates. REPLIES TO QuEorron.-Mr. CHILDERS said Colonels who held that rank before October, 1877, would receive on re- tirement fair actuarial value of their prospective succeeding to honorary colonelcies.—Mr. Grtangrolo, re- plying to Sir D. Wolff, said that although it was desirable it was not always possible to have the first Lord of the Admiralty in the House of Commons.— COMMERCIAL TREATIES WITH FRANCE.—On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. Rums rose to move that an humble address be presented to the Crown praying Her Majesty to withhold her consent to any com- mercial treaty with France, which proposed to substitute specific duties for ad valorem duties, to the disadvantage of any article of British manufacture, or in any way to raise the present rate of duties payable on such articles, and which did not leave Her Majesty's Government full liberty to deal with the question of bounties or which would bind Her Majesty's Government absJlutely to its prorisions for a longer period than 12 months. He said there was the greatest interest in this country regarding the new treaty, and it was felt that no treaty at all would be far better than one founded on-worse conditions than that which existed for many years. He pointed out that the British exports were diminishing immensely year by year, and insisted that some means ought to be taken to stop that downward progress, but he did not demand protection for- our manufactures as he did not think protection would benefit them as no increased duty could raise the price. What he did object to was our gradual exclusion from foreign markets. He then condemned the foreign bounty system. He wished that no commercial treaty ought to be entered into with France for more than 12 months.—Sir C. DILICE said the Government adhered to the de- claration that had already been made on the subject.

LATEST NEWS.
PUBLIC RECEPTION TO MINISTERS.

Arrangements for according a grand public reception to Mr. Gladstone and other members of the Government on the occasion of the Ministerial whitebait dinner at Greenwich, next Wednesday, have been completed. On arriving by the steamer, at a quarter to seven, the Ministers will be met by one hundred and twenty leading Liberals, who will conduct them to the Trafalgar, and there an illuminated address will be read, and, along with a handsome gok chair costing fifty guineas, prdsented to Mr. Gladstone, -the presentation indi- cating the determination of the Liberals of Greenwich al. ways to keep a "seat" for the right hon. gentleman. THE BLACKBURN RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

The Board of Trade inquiry was resumed at Bla-c.kbuin yesterday before Col. Yolland. James Livesey, district traffic inspector, said when a train was standing in the station the home signals should be at danger until an incoming train was almost brought to a stand, then lowered, and the train let in slow. John Graham, signalman, said he had taken off the home signal for the Manchester express when the train might have been a mile away.

div.head: IRELAND AND THE LAND BILL.
div.p: IRELAND AND THE LAND BILL.

The Dublin Freeman says :—Mr. Gladstone will pass the bill, the .whole bill, and nothing but the bill. One effect of the discussion in the House of Lords over the Land Bill must almost certainly be the final overthrow of Toryism in L Ireland.

The Dublin Exprcss says :—No disposition is shown to meet the most reasonable objections of the Lords, and not the smallest concession worth speaking of has been made. The Cork Corporation yesterday unanimously passed a resolution pronouncing the Land Bill the best effort to. wards restoring peace, prosperity, and contentment again amongst all classes in Ireland, and urging on the Prime Minister to parse :ere in his rejection of the Lords' amend- ments which would in any way mitigate against the general scope and efficiency of the measure. The resolution was ordered to be telegraphed at once to Mr. Gladstone, with a view to strengthen his hknds.

div.head: TWELFTH.
div.p: THE TWELFTH.

Eton s .—The morning broke most inauspiciously for grouse shooting, wind and rain keeping the older sports- men from the heather, while only a few of the more ardent expended powder and shot, and sport as yet may be con- sidered as a complete fiasco, in the Northern district scarcely a full bag being made. Good sport may, however, be ex- pected in a few days.
Fonuusr.—Weather has been wet to-day, but the good prospects have been realised, and goodbags have been made, the birds shot being in very fine condition.

In the event of a vacancy in the representation of Peter- boro' by the retirement of Mr. Whalley, Mr. D. McLiver, who has been already named as the Liberal candidate, will be opposed by Mr. Thomson Hankey, who represente I the borough for many years.
Miss Mabel Wilberforce was on Thursday committed for trial at the Old Bailey for perjury. She maintained her self-possession to the last, declaring herself to be the victim of a conspiracy.
The British- Medical Association yesterday decided to form a limited liability company to establish retreats for habitual drunkards.

The supplementary estimates were issued yesterday for £2,900, for new works and alterations in the House of Parlia- ment, and £400,000 on account of Transvaal items. Of the latter are £150,000 to repay in advance from the Standard Bank during the annexation period, £15,000 advances by Crown agents, £109,000 advances from the Treasury chest, including supplies to loyal colonists, and £135,000 contin- gencies, including the expenses of the Transvaal Commis- sion and compensation claims.

Five suspects, who are now lodged in Limerick county prison, lately adopted a memorial to the Lord-Lieutenant praying-for their release, but a reply has sbeen received refusing the request, and they are still detained.

The Central sews is enabled to state that the Lord Ad.. vocate has definitely accepted the vacant judgeship of the court of session. Mr. McLaren will issue his valedictory address to the electors of Edinburgh to-day. In it he will express his regret at parting with them. The vacant post of Lord Advocate has been offered to the SolicitorAireneral for Scotland, Mr. Balfour, M.P., and his post in turn will be filled by Mr. Asher, M.P., the recently elected member for Elkin Burghs. The names of several gentlemen are men— tioned as candidates for the vacancy which will be caused in the representation of Edinburgh. Mr. Duncan McLaren, who retired in favour of the Lord Advocate, has been meutioned, but it is understood he A ill not come for- ward. Mr. Trayner (advocate) and Mr. Jenkins are the most promising Liberals and Mr. Macdonald, Q.C., and Councillor Gowan the Liberals,

THE OLDHAM RAILWAY ACCIDEET.—Inquiry was opened at Oldham yesterday, concerning the death of the driver, John Butterworth, who was killed in the collision at Shaw. James Riley, driver of the second engine, stated that the guard told him to drive on as all was right. The train was running at twenty miles an hour when the collision took place. The inquiry was adjourned. An extraordinary demonstration took place at Rhode, King's County, last tight, to commemorate the release of Mr. Dillon. Thousands of persons marched to Leitrim Hill where a hogh bonfire was lighted, and the effigy of Mr. Goddard, of the Emergency Committee, was burnt.

At the Preston Police Court, yesterday, Thomas Powell (40) was charged with breaking and entering the shop of Richard Bannister, grocer, Friargate, on the sth inst., and stealing£l3. Prisoner was chased along the roofs of shops by Policeman Reid for 150 yards, and along several streetx, befoer he was captured. Stolen money to upwards of £l4 was found in his posse.sion, and it was ascertained that he had broken into six different shops in Friargate. He was com- mitted to the sessions for trial.

An Irish Industrial League is ptojected for the promotion of Irish manufactures, and it is said that the members of it will be pledged to use only Irish goods and to deal with houses which sell these goods alone.
The tenants on the Earl of Mayo's Kildare estates have- refused to nay rent unless an abatement of 25 per cent. is made.

The house of Michael Keegan, farmer, of Coone, county Leitrim, was visited last night by a party of Armed men, who first gave Keegan three stabs with a sword, and thus dragged him across a fire. 3hp eau.° of the outrage is the farmer baying cut a meadow Tyr an objectionable person. There have been two arrests.

COLONEL McCORQUODALE AND THE WARRING- TON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. Sir,—As one interated in the sanitary improvement of WarAington I protect against the action of the newly appbinted chairman of the Rural Sanitary Authority at their last meeting. What right has he to lecture the committee over which Mr. Alderman Burgess so ably presides for the benefit and protection of our fellow men. Contrast their business proceedings. Sanitary Committee, War- Rural Sanitary Committee, rington Town Council, pre- with Colonel MeCorguodale as aided over Alderman Burgess, Chairman. J.P,

--ifeets every Wednesday at Meets the 11.-st Friday in T o'clock p.m. every month at 1080 am. The Clerk speaks when his Ihe Clerk interposes at advice is sought. every tura, or whenever be pleases. Every recommendation of Any ad ice is usually talked their officers is fairly con- out, or referred to the Local sidered, and if practicable Government Board. osrrled out. The meetingis not concluded Business hurried over and until all business matters are neglected to please the Assess- carefully gone into. ment mittee, who meet On the same day at 11-30 and feed later on at the expense of the Ratepayers. Wo outsider is allowed to A member of the Assessment enter the room and interrupt Committee, notorious for his the business of the meeting, seniority, invariably inter- rupts every meeting, and is seldom if ever called to order by the Chairman. If Colonel McCorquodale will turn his horse's head in the what will he find there? A other direction, say Wigan, town governed by Toryism and polite Whigism with its badly paved streets, its open middens, numerous cesspools, and every other abomination. He has quite sufficient to do to persuade the electors of Wigan he is the Radical reformer they want. The work life Alderman Burgess has pre-eminently before the country as one of done places him the foremost sanitarians of the day, and before long the system he has so wisely introduced and successfully pioneered, will be adopted and sanctioned by the Local Government Board. If the Rural Sanitary Authority had their eyes open and read your valuable paper, they would have noticed that nearly all Her Majesty's Inspectors have visited Longford. The Urban Authority need have no fear of a visit from a disinterested sanitarian. He will, perhaps, not be able to say to Mr. Alderman Burgess "you have arrived at a finality in dealing with excreta and household refuse," but I prophecy that he will say "you possess the germs of success," and to that august body the Rural Sani- tary Authority, ho will ety "go thou and do likewise."—l am, yours, EXPERIENTIA DOCET. MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE EMPIRE. Sir,—A little while ago I came across two scraps which to my mind afford a strong argument in favour of the Eng- ish monarchical system, as opposed to the republicanism for which certain Radical demagogues, who seem to base their opinions upon the assumption that "whatever is is wrong," are so wildly clamouring. One contains the words of Lerothodi, Letsea, and Joel Molappi, chiefs of Basutoland and representatives of the Basutos ; and the other, a little of the eloquence of Hunia, a Mend tribal chief; and both alike express the loyalty which the dark races of the British Empire cherish towards the Queen. This loyalty, in an empire containing 250,000,000 inhabitants, the great majofity of whom have dark skins, is of the utmost impor- tance. A bond which unites dominions that extend into every quarter of the globe and embrace every degree of cli- mate and every variety of race, is surely too valuable to be cast heedlessly away; and a common loyalty to a common sovereign is an almost indissoluble bond. Substitute an English Republic for the present form of government and what becomes of this, perhaps the strongest of the ties of empire? Would the Basutos and the Maeries, and the countless other tribes, who are proud to be loyal to " our Queen and their Queen," offer the same spontaneous allegiance to an English republic ? I think not. They would rather reason, what have we to do with the English republic ? It is nothing to us ! We will not offer our homage to it ! And so the first step towards the disintegration of what John Bright calls "the greatest of the empires upon which the sun shines." would be coinci- dent with the abol:tion of the English monarchy, and the establishment of an English republic. This is a considera- tion which would urge upon the attention of "the speuters of stale sedition" of the year 1881; "the young men with long matted hair," as someone with perh ties more truth than delicacy, recently said of them, "who, when they have im- bibed a sufficient quantity of bad beer in Radical clubs, sing the Marseillaise in glory of dynamite and revolution," if they care to know that there are two sides to a question. Said Lerothodi, Letsed, and Joel Molappe : "Tell the Queen that we are her loyal and obedient subjects at all times, in the future as in the past, and will use our arms and stcrifice our lives in her interests." Said Hunia, and Sir C. W. Dilke, who describes the incident in his "Greater Britain," says that "the passage as Hunia spoke it, was of noble elo- quence and singular rhetoric art." "0 my guests, when ye return to our great Queen, tell her that we will fight for her again as we have fought before. She Is our Queen as well as your queen—Queen of Meories, and Queen of Palteha (white man). Should wars arise, we will take up our rifles, and march whithersoever she shall direct My cousin, Wiremu, went to England and saw our Queen. He returned . . . When you landed in this island, he was alredy dead . . . He died, fighting for our Queen." "As he died, we will die, if need be—l, and all me chiefs. This do you tell our Queen. I have said."—l am, cic., 11th August, 1881. ARTHUR BENNETT.

div.head: FRODSHAM BAZAAR CATASTROPHE..
div.p: THE FRODSHAM BAZAAR CATASTROPHE..

Dear Sir,—lt is but right and just to the public that this matter should be honestly explained, and as a Nonconformist of the Parish, also one having nothing whatever to do with the bazaar, or the Church Restoration Fund. I speak as a disinterested outsider, therefore, I am sure your readers will not charge me with interested motives. lam deeply grieved at witnessing such an account of bigotry, and intolerance in the Parish, and I could wish, together with many others, a different state of things existed, however, such as it is we ought to grapple with it, and do our best to get rid of it, it is hurting every good institution in the place. Directly after the sad accident, from the high wind blowing both tents down on Wednesday afternoon last, we heard on every side, so that T became astonished at the people's bigotry, and over- bearing manner. "Oh ! it just serves them right, nothing better could be expected. They were certain to be sufferers. God will be avenged. The Church will tumble down next. Anybody breaking the Sabbath, a retributive providence will follow. Sabbath-breakers are worse than thieves, for they rob God of His ewn. It was the Lord's avengine• wind to break down their idols." The above are but a few, specimens of the harsh and bitter words, heaped upon the vicar and working committee Of the bazaar. What for? Why, because the tent was erected on Sunday last, or the furniture was put up on that day; therefore these people look upon it as a judgment of the Most High for breaking the fourth Commandment. And according to my limited experience of such things, it is merely an excuse for the Nonconforming part of the parish to abstain from supporting the bazaar fund. It is not because they care for the Sabbath, for mcst of them travel by train, and do other things scarcely compatible with their professions on a Sunday. Now, let us look at the weather in a plain, common sense light. In the first place, pray what real harm has the vicar and churchwardens done? lam not goine. to stick up for any onemaking light of the fourth Command- ment, but they have not yet been proved guilty, hence we must infer they are innocent. The matter rests here—l be- lieve the vicar and his working committee ordered the tents to be ready for Tuesday morning, and with the order their onus rests, and no further. The men had plenty of time to be in reecliness without doing anything on the Sunday; even if the vicar had not interfered with the men working on the Sabbath. I fail to see how he can be honestly blamed; bat the real fact is, he did interfere, and do his utmost to prevent it. When I heard a respectable resident saying, "I shall never give a penny towards the old church, for it cannot prosper now they have broken God's Day," I replied, "My, friend, if the wind had not accidentally turned over the canvas tents, you would never have heard a word about the Sunday work of the men who put it up, and if you were wise you would never let it pa's year lips again, for you may depend the committee has about as much to do with it as you have." Mr. Editor, allow me to say one word in conclusion. The vicar (Mr. Blogg) has worked hard for the Restoration Fund, his efforts have been seconded nobly by his committee, and it is a great pity that they should now staffer loss from a cause over which they had not the slightest control. The loss and destruction caused by the falling tents, together with the heavy loss on sales, is quite enough; and ought to arouse the active sympathy of all kindly disposed towards the grand old Parish Church.— Your obedient servant, A LIBERAL. Brodebsin, 11th August, 1881.

TOW BLLMurcrinf BIIIIDINO SOCIETY CAS.—The ease of the Blackburn and Distrizt Benefit Building Society on Wednesday came before Vice-Chancellor Bristowe in the Lancashire Chancery Court, sitting at Liverpool, upon an application made by an investing member for an order directing the compulsory winding up of the society on the ground of its insolvency. It was admitted that the society was unable at the present time, owing to a depreciation in the value of house property, to realise its securities. It was on that 'acccunt that the plaintiff's demand for the with- drawal of a sum of £6BO invested with the society could not be met. The members, at a meeting attended by about 1,500 of the 2.000 on the society's books, had appointed a ComMittee of investigation: and counsel representing this Committee opposed the present application in the interest of tbe general body of members, pointing out that under the rules money could be withdrawn by an investing member only "providing the funds permit," and that a question whether the funds did permit was a matter referable to arbi- tration in the event of a contingency like the present arising. It WAS stated that the petitioner was the only member out of the whole body who moved for the winding up of the society. The Vice-Chancellor, who at the commencement had suggested that the matter should be aolflothwe arinedhetostgand over until the committee presented their report, made.an order that that shonld he done. He directed Oat two persons representing the petitioner should he Placed upon the committee; and furstthseteran further, that s o h t the ctomtmiettes ,se id society's be prepared with a full affairs to be presented to the Court at its next sitting in Manchester.

ST. HELENS CoUNTY COURT. WEDNEIDAT.—Before INIr. T. P. E. Thompson, judge. AN IMPECUNIOUS LAWYER.—Robert Goldsmith, Hard- shaw-street, St. Helene, sought to recover £4 on a judgment summons from a Mr. Parkinson, solicitor, formerly of St. Helens, but now of Wigan —Mr. Swift appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Riley for the defendant.—Mr. Swift said the defendant, he was sorry to say, was a solicitor, and this judgment had been obtained against him a very long time, but he had never paid anything. His friend Mr. Riley, he 'thought, had some offer to make.—Plaintiff said the claim was for money lent to defendant when be lived in St. Helens. Defendant now resided in Wigan, and practised in Wigan and Liverpool. Defendant might have paid the money three years ago.—Mr. Riley said it was true he nominally appeared for the defendant, and he simply did SO because he was in the same profession, and bad written appealing to him tb do what he could for him. The letter said, "My only desire is to get an adjournment for one month, in order that I may get some money owing to me. I told Mr. Swift I would pay last April, but the negotiations I was making fell through, and I was unable to carry out the promise." He then went on to say that he hoped to get some money in a month, and asked Mr. Riley to try and secure an adjournment, and concluded by saying, "When a man is thoroughly hard up what can be do r Mr. Riley did not know whether Mr. Goldsmith knew that defendant really had had the means to pay.—Mr. Geldsworth: Oh, yes; I met him in Wigan.—Mr. Riley: But he has no office, has he? just gets cases in court—Mr. Goldsmith: He has offices in Wigan, and had that case of the election commission.—Mr. Swift: The judgment has been in force for more than four and a half years, and the debt existed long before that--Plaintiff: The first order was las a month, but he would not pay that. He told me be would get £2O out of the election petition. There is no doubt that unless there is a committal he will not pay, but if that is granted he will pay it.—His Honour made an fader of com- mittal, Mr. Swift promising, on behalf of his client, not to enforce the order if the ntoney be paid within two months. IMPORTANT DECISION AS TO BILLS OF sean.—An inter- pleader summons was heard in which Mr. Swift appeared on behalf of the claimant, William Clason Rush, now of Den- ton's Green-lane, St. Helens, recently carrying on business in Liverpool-road, and Mr. Trelfall, of Southport, for the execution creditor, Mr. Higson. William Cary Ward was the judgment debtor.—Mr. Swift said the action upon which the execution took place was brought in the county court at Southport; and he believed that it was brought to recover a quarter's rent due from the judgment debtor Ward, on the let of March last, and the judgment was obtained on the 22nd March. A commitment summons was afterwards taken out, and was partly heard before His Honour at South- port, but was ultimately adjourned for evidence, before the arrival of the day to which the commitment summons was , adjourned, the execution creditor, Mr. Higson, abandoned his commitment summons and issued the execution which was levied at St. Helens, and which they interpleaded. Mr. Rush, the claimant, was a solicitor's clerk, at Northampton, where he had been employed in one situation for about 20 years. He married the sister of Ward. Previously to Sep- tember, 1879, Ward was a commercial traveller, and resided in Birmingham. His wife was a milliner, and in 1379 Ward's health failed him, and he determined to leave Bir- mingham and go and live at Southport, where he corn- meneed business as a draper in a house and shop belonging to Mr. Higson, the execution creditor. In order to Commence business he was obliged to borrow some money, and in the month of August, or September, 1879, he borrowed £4O from his father, who agreed to lend it on his son aud the claimant Rush joining together in a promissory note for the repayment of the money. The debtor also borrowed £5O from his brother-in-law about the same time, then further in January, 1830, he borrowed £29 se. sd. from a relative of his, an uncle. For that lean a Mr. Sperkes took a promisory note of the debtor along with a guarantee from the brother-in-law, Rush. These moneys were necessary for the debtor to com- mence and go on with his business which he was endeavouring to establish in Southport. Ward seemed to have gone on until the 15th July without any more loans; and at that time he was being sued by one of the dealers who supplied him with goods, which action obliged him to file a petition for liquidation. This was done in the court at Liverpool in July. The first meeting was held on the 3rd August and the second on the 13th. At those meetings resolutions were passed, confirmed, and afterwards registered, and all the creditors were of one mind, ard agreed to accept a composi- tion of lOs in the pound, payable by instalments at three, six, nine, and twelve months. The first instalment the creditors did not require to be secured, but the rest they did, and Mr. Rush agreed to join in the neceseiry promissory , note for securing the payment of the third and fourth , , instalments. At the same time Mr. Rush came to an agree- ment with the creditors that he would not take any security for the goods of the debtor himself so long as either of the first or second instalments remained unpaid. The first series of instalments became payable on the 19th February last year, and the debtor met those notes himself. The second instalment became due on the 19th February in the present year, and the debtor had previously to that, in December, borrowed from Mr. Rush £5; and in February, when the second instalment was due, seeing that the composition could not be made without assistance, he borrowed from Mr. Rush a further sum of £3O, which was advanced to him on the 10th February, and Mr Ward applied that money in payment of the second instalment. On the 19th February the position stood thus: Mr. Rush had lent to Mr. Ward £5O, £5, £3O, altogether £B5, actually lent by Mr. Rush to Mr. Ward, and he (Mr. Swift) might sly in passing, with regard to some of that money, Mr. Rush had had to berrovs it to lend it to Mr. Ward. And before that he had become security for £123. He did not see that anything could be plainer or more honest than those particulars appeared to him to be. His friend Mr. Trelfall had been very reticent and had not told him what his contentions were going to be, and consequently he had been more elaborate than he was accustomed to be.—Mr. Trelfall contended that the bill of sale was void : first, that it was for a past consideration, that the consideration was not truly stated in the bill of sale, and that thebill of sale was given to one creditorinpreference to other creditors' claims.—Mr. Swift submitted there was no fraud. Hie client had lent £B5, and he also became secu- rity for £l2B, altogether £213. And baying regard to the decisions of the judges in numerous cases, which he con- tended supported his argument, and which he referred to, there was nothing in that statement in the consideration to impeach the validity of the bill of sale. It might not be stated with literal accuracy, but a substantial statement was all that was necessary,—His Honour said he had to decide against the claimant Rush, because he thought the claimant failed by reason of the consideration not having been suffi- ciently set forth in accordance with the requirements of the Act. Any person reading the statement woulel understand that the bill of sale was given in consideration of £2lO already paid, whereas only £125 was paid; the rest was made up of a sum which became due, and might or might not have to be paid by the mortgagee. But really the words of the document would lead any person to believe that the whole of the sum of £2lB was paid.—Mr. Trelfall asked for costs, which were granted.—Mr. Swift gave notice of appeal against the decision of the judge. A QUARREL ABOUT GOODS AT PARR.—In this case Martha Grimes was the plaintiff, and Enoch Perry the de- fendant.—Mr. Swift, who appeared for the plaintiff, said the action was brought to obtain the return Of some house- hold furniture and other goods or their value, and damages for their detention or conversion. Grimes Nvas a woman who was living apart from her husband, and she held an order made by two of Her Majesty's justices of the peace for this county, and duly sealed with the seal of the County Court at Warrington, which stated the following facts : That she was married to James Grimes, on the 16th December, 1337, and that in the:year 1888 Grimes deserted her without reasonable cause, and that she was now maintaining herself by her own industry and property. Enoch Perry was in some way related to the plaintiff, being brother-in-law to plaintiff's son-in-law. (Laughter.) In May last, Perry, along with the plaintiff's son-in-law, Clubb, were brought before the magistrates on a charge, and rightly or wrongly they thought that Mrs. Grime's daughter had been instrumental in getting them brought up on that charge, and alter getting away from court they assaulted plaintiff and took away her goods. The plaintiff formerly lived in Burtonwood, in the Warrins,r- ton district, and while there Chubb and his wife lived with her, and the house was furnished with her furniture. She afterwards went to Golborne, taking with her the goods, and ultimately she removed to a house at Parr, also removing her goods. After the close of the court at St. Helens Town Hall, the defendant and Clubb, and five other Clubbs went to the house of the plaintiff and took away the goods that were in it. The goods were all re- moved from the plaintiff's house and taken to defendant's house. Defendant was asked about them from time to time, but his invariable answer was, "I got them,ancl I shall stick to them." If the goods were not there now he had pledged them or disposed of them in some way.—Plaintiff gave evidence as to defendant and the CI übbs taking away the goods, which she valued at £8 Rise:M.—Cross-examined by Mr. Catterall : Plaintiff said all the goods were taken. She sometimes lived at the house. She always kept two houses on. None of the furniture was taken to the other house. She had many a house of furniture besides those two,by buying and selling.— obeing shown some blankets Catherine because3l Makina sheki n gotd e p o her deposed flying which plaintiff had bought of James Clubb, the father of plaintiff's daughter's husband.—Plaintiff's two sons having deposed to seeing defendant help in taking away the goods, Mary Ellen Clubb, daughter of plaintiff and wife of Charles Clubb, said she was not living with her husband, who was continually leaving her and getting int. trouble. Since the 14th of May he had been in gaol three timee—a month for poaching, seven days for an assault upon her mother, and another term fer stealing hens. The goods belonged to her mother and not to her husband.—Ellen Francis said plaintiff bought the bedsteads, chairs, and mattresses from her in August last.—Mr. Catterall said he was instructed to state and call Clubb, to prove that those goods were bought by him, but after the evidence, he thought he should be exercising a wise-discretion in not calling him. The only question would now be as to the amount and value of the goods. Some of the goods, he was instructed, had been sold to James Clubb.—James Clubb, a middle-aged man, said ho sold a pair of blankets to his son, in the presence of plain- tiff, and he received the money from hia son.—His Honour gave judgment in favour of the plaintiff for £8 14s. fide to be reduced by the value of any goods according to the list being returned within a week

LITERATURE.

WORTHIES OE THE WORLD (London: Ward, Lock and Co.)—Part 10 of this excellent work contains biograpbies of Alexander the Great, Confucius, Oliver Cromwell, and Allied the Cheat. They are well written, most enjoyable, and full of vivacity and interest, not being overloaded with uninteresting details which have a tendency to weary the reader. These sketches are also written in an impartial manner, rendering them acceptable to readers of all shades of political and religious thought. _

DR. ADAM CLARKE'S COMMENTARY ON TIIE BIBLE (London : Ward, Lock and Co.)—This is a new edition containing the author's latest corrections, with ad- ditional prefatory and supplementary notes, together with a life of the author bringing the work up to the present standard of Biblical knowledge by the Rey. Thornley Smith. It is issued in monthly parts, and the fourth part now before us—nicely executed engravings of Shechem, Egyptian representation of the ark, &c.—is well printed on good paper.

THE QUIVER (London: Cassell, Fetter, and Galpin).— This popular magazine, which is acknowledged to be admir- ably conducted, contains for August, as usual, a mass of in- teresting, instructive, and amusing information. The several stories are well written, full of interest, and useful lessons are conveyed to the minds of the reader in a pleasing and ac- ceptable manner. The following extract is taken from the affecting history of Charley Brown Eyes :—" When the doctor had paid his visit, and Charley had swallowed a warm drink and a dose of nasty medicine, he fell fast asleep, and when he woke it was getting dark, and the fire was throwing a cheerful flickering glow over the ceiling. In the cot next I his there was a little girl, who was looking at him as if she meant to speak. She was very small, and had a bright, sharp face. She eyed her new neighbour steidily for a few minutes, till he felt rather uncomfortable, and then she said in a quick, sharp voice—"l say, little boy, what's the mat- ter with you ?" "I don't know."—" Well, I never! I know what's the matter with me. It's hip disease. I'm lame. If you were to see me on the floor I should fall down. You've got a cough, ain't you ?" Yes, and a pain across my chest." —" Oh, then, I s'pose it's 'sumption. There's a girt on the other side's got 'sumption, and she's not near so big as you neither. I wish I'd 'sumption," with bitter emphasis.—"Do you? Why?"—" Oh, you get goodies for your cough, some- times, and don't never have bad pain.' "Oh, my !don't yar, though! I've got awful bad pain," said Charley, his mild spirit roused to indignation.—" Oh, I don't call that real pain. Why, it's not bad enough to holler. You should see me. Nurse has to held me when I get bad. Sometimes she has to say 'Gentle Jesus' to help me to bear it." "Does that make it better ?" inquired Charley much interested.— " Well, she says it oughter, I s'pose it does. Don't you ?" "I don't know nothing about that," Charley replied. There was a pate to the conversation, but it was presently re- sumed.—" Little boy, would you like this doll? I don't care for dolls. When I get out of the Hospital father's gob' to bay me a big book with readin' in it. You haven't got anything to play with on, your shelf, and I've got some blue beads and three pictures, so you may have the doll if you want to very much." "No, thank you, miss, if you don't mind," said Charley, timidly.—" Never mind, little boy; I ain't offendcd. Will your father come and see you on Sun- day ? Mine does." "I ain't got no father."—" Oh, poor little boy! I'll ask my father to speak to you, and that'll be as good, won't it? I say, nurse," she cried, as nurse Amy came up to give the children their supper, this new little boy's got no father." "Yes, he has, Polly, you know," said nurse, gently, "though we can't see Him."

div.head: BOWLING COMPETITIONS AT HIJYTON,
div.p: BOWLING COMPETITIONS AT HIJYTON,

HUYTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB: THE PRESIDENT'S PRIZE. The challenge cup presented to the club by the president (Mr. Alexander Eccles, of Roby,) was competed for by the members for the third time on Saturday last. The weather fortunately, was all that could be expected, but the attend- ance of spectators was rather meagre, which may be accounted for by the fact that at this time of the year a large number of the residents are away from home. Amongst the ladies present were Mrs. Crook, Mrs. Mourland, the Misses Ellison, Mrs. Fish wick, Miss Fraser' Mrs. and the Misses Dobell. The number of players was also very small, in fact, the smallest, with one exception, on record; but, nevertheless, the bowling was up to the usual standard. The green was in splendid condition. Play commenced shortly after four o'clock, and in the first round the winner of Sir A. B. Walker's cup this year and the president's cup last year was defeated by four points by Mr. Fishwick. In the second Mr. Aldrich, a veteran player, was disposed of by Mr. T. Graham, with, however, only one point to spare. In the third round Mr. Graham boa led with such accuracy of aim that his opponent (Mr. Crook) did not succeed in scoring a single point, and Mr. Leyland managed to win his game by four points. Mr. Leyland and Mr. Graham were therefore left to play off for the cup (the second time they have played off for prizes this year), and both gentlemen being accomplished bowlers speculation was rife as to which would succeed in carrying away the prize. After playing a short time Mr. Graham got ahead by some three or four points, and the chances seemed to be in his favour, but as the game proceeded his opponent gradually pulled up, and at last overhauled him. When the game was 10 all, much excite- ment prevailed, and as the bowls were again set in motion opinions were freely expressed as to which would be the lucky one. Eventually Mr. Leyland got one about six inches nearer the " jack " than his opponent, and, amid the applause of those present, was declared the winner of the cup. Mr. Leyland, therefore, will have the honour of holding the prize till next year, when, should he be again successful, it will become his own property. Mr. Leyland has been connected with the club for about 10 years and has, during that period, won three cups outright, although he has not been so successful for the last two or three years.
