div.head: BLUE BELL VERSUS HUNT'S CROSS.
div.p: BLUE BELL VERSUS HUNT'S CROSS.

It will be remembered that the first match this year be- tween the representatives of these clubs was played at Hunt's Cross, on Saturday, July 2nd, and resulted in a win for the visitors. In the single game the teams tied, but in the double game the Blue Bell players succeeded in carrying off the palm with five points to spare. The return match took place on Saturday last, at Huyton, and again terminated in a victory for the home team, this time on both single and double games. The green, thanks to the groundman, seas in capital order, the woods running splendidly, and the weather being propitious, the game was much enjoyed by all present —players and spectators alike. Play commenced about four o'clock, there being twelve competitors aside. In the single game the home team carried all before them, scoring 132 points against their opponents' 57, but nothing occurred calling for special remark. In the double game, however, the playing of Messrs. T. Brown and W. Webster and Messrs. J. Bustard and J. W. rember on behalf of their respective sides, was watched with keen interest, and when it was announced that the latter bowlers had won the greatest excitement and astonish- ment prevailed, as it was fully thought the two first-mentioned players would secure the premier posi- tion. Notwithstanding this, however, the game ended in favour of the home team—the scores being—Blue Bell, 86; Hunt's Cross, 41. .On both games the home team won by 120 points, the totals being—Blue Bell, 218; Hunt's Cros;, 98. The visitors, from the first, did not entertain any hope of being able to win, but they were hardly prepared to meet with so severe a defeat as they did. Mr. T. Birchall acted as captain of the home team, and Mr. J. Ockleshaw of the visiting team. The arrangements for the match were carried out by a committee of twelve members, of which Mr. T. HEALTH COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held on Wednesday, Dr. Twyford presiding. Therc were also pre- sent Councillors M'Kechnie and Foster, with Mr. Craik (deputy town clerk), Mr. Hart (borough engineer), and Dr. McNichol (medical officer).

div.head: VITAL STATISTICS.
div.p: VITAL STATISTICS.

The Medical Officer's return showed that during the four weeks ending August 6th there had been 181 births. There had been in the same period 3 deaths from fever, 20 from diarrhosa, measles 0, scarlet fever 0, diphtheria 0, other zymotics 0, total zymotics 23; from other causes there had been 65 deaths, making a total of 88 from all causes. Of these 40 were males and 48 females, 54 being children under five years of age. The rate of mortality per thousand was 1938, as compared with 24.72 in the corresponding period of last year.

div.head: SAMPLES OF WATER. .
div.p: SAMPLES OF WATER. .

The MEDICAL OFFICER reported as follows :—lnspector Williams has taken samples of Eccleston Brook at the following places: Spray's Bridge, Liverpool-road, by the timber yard, and Messrs. Lyon's bottle works. These con- tain no acid, but a sample from the Bridgewater works drain has a weak acid. The canal opposite Messrs. Doulton's works did not contain acid when the samples were taken. One sample taken from Garden - street sewer is rich in sulphur, and gives off sulphuretted hydrogen very freely, and one taken six days after from the same sewer has no sulphur, but is strongly acid. Samples of Hardshaw Brook had been taken by Inspector Houghton. A trace of acid is found in one taken from the Gas Works yards, caused by a weak acid flowing into the brook from I Messrs. Kurtz's works. Samples from drain of St. Helens Chemical Works show that the nuisance is greatly abated. Acid is flowing from the Atlas Foundry drain into the St. Helens Chemical Works drain. This does not come from the foundry itself, but through the foundry from a source beyond, that is not yet discevered. A slight acid is found in the drain of Messrs. Newton, Keates, and Co., as it emerges into Sutton Brook. Rainford Brook is free, with the excep- tion of a faint acid in overflow received from the canal near Merton Bank Bridge.—No action was taken. A CASE OF SMALLPDX.

The DOCTOR said : My attention was called on July 25th to a case of smallpox in a house off Sut- ton-road. Richard Leadbetter had loom to Neston and must have caught it there, or in travel- ling. Inspector Houghton and myself have watched the case, and have given instructions as to the isolation and disinfection. The man is convalescent, but is not per- mitted to leave the house. The premises have been disin- fected, and every precaution taken to prevent the disease spreading, which has so far been successful. THE STREETS ON SUNDAY MORNINGS. The CHAIRMAN said the streets on a Sunday morning were in a disgraceful state, all sorts of rubbish from the shops being left in the street.—Mr. HART said the shop- keepers brushed the rubbish out betore shutting up.—The CHAIRMAN said that great pieces of paper could be seen ;flyino• about, and flashing up at the horses heads, causing ' the 'horses to be greatly frightened. Mr. HART said it was a matter for the Paving C ommittee.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The usual fortnightly meeting of this board was held on Thursday, Mr. S. Marsh, presiding. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers and J. Barnacle, Messrs. Tyrer, Fidler, Hall, Paris, Leatherbarrow, Penketh, Ranson, Lowe, Harrison, Syder, Gilbody, Sadler, Gerrard, Scotson, Leigh, and Jackson; with Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). WORKHOUSE MASTER'S REPORT.

The MASTER reported that there were in the house 438 in- mates at the end of this week, as compared with 492 in the previous week, and 549 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 140 boys and girls at Kirkdale Schools. The number of vagrants relieved during the week was 156. The Master further reported that on the nights of the .9th and 10th of August, some bread, a coat, and several othpr trifling articles were stolen from the Workhouse premises. THE GUARDIANS AND THEIR LUNCHEON.

The CLERK read the following entry from the master's report book:—" The matron regrets very much her inability to provide the usual luncheon for the board, in consequence of having no person to assist her in the kitchen, the only person competent to assist her having been ordered out by the revising committee. The matron will be glad to recommence the luncheon as soon as she gets suitable help." —An amusing discussion ensued, in the course of which Mr. Fidler deprecated the Guardians being prevented from having their luncheon in consequence of one inmate being sent away from the workhouse, aud that the master should glow sue'll an amount of temper as to put it in his book that he would practically see the Guardians " blowed" if they sent the woman away. That they should not have their lunch he regarded as most outrageous, and an insult to the Board.—The Rev. J. BARNACLE considered it a great shame that those Guardians who came from a distance should be deprived of their luncheon by the caprice of one individual. —The CitainmArt pointed out that it was optional with the master whether or not he provided the luncheon. He thought luncheon should not be provided by officials or on the workhouse premises, even though it was paid for in- dividually by the members —Rev. Mr. CHAMBERS criticised the action of the relief committee, and expressed a hope that the Guardians would not quarrel about trifles with so good an officer as the master.—After further conversation, the matter was allowed to drop. THE GUARDIANS' DINNER: A DEBT OF HONOUR. The CLERK read the following letter from Messrs. Swift and Son, solicitors, St. Helens :—"Mr. Thomas Bennett, of Prescot, butcher, has instructed us to apply to you for pay- ment of a balance of .£6 13s. Mi., which has been for some time outstanding between the Guardians and him. In a letter, dated 23rd July, 1880, Mr. Hartley, your clerk, in- timated to Mr. Bennett that the balance in question would be paid shortly. Will you kindly give instructions for an early payment of the amount, or inform us upon what grounds it is withheld."—The CLERK explained that the amount referred to was for materials for dinners supplied to the Guardians in 1878, and stated that he wrote to Messrs. Swift and Son, informing them that the Guardians could not legally pay the amount as it was beyond the time fixed by law.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS and Mr. Tvuxu disclaimed being participants in tin? dinners referred to, and although the Guardians were not legally bound to discharge the debt, it was still a debt of honour, and suggested that the mem- bers should subscribe to pay off the debt. It was under- stood that this Course should he adopted. RESIGNATION OF A ST. HELENS RELIEVING OFFICER. The CLERK read a letter from Mr. S. F. Wensley, dated August 6th, stating that he had received the appointment of collector of rates under the Wallasey Local Board, and tendering his resignation as relieving officer for the St. Helens N 0.2 district. He thanked the Guardians for the great kindness they had shown to him durin3 the past two years.

MINISTERS AT THE MANSION HOUSE.

The annual banquet to Ministers was held on Saturday, at the Mansion House. Mr. Gladstone, Lord Spencer, Lord Kimberley, the Mafquis of Hartington, Mr. Bright, Mr. Childers, Lord Northbrook, and Mr. Forster were present. Mr. Childers, in responding for the army, said that at present the army of England was in a most efficient condi- dition, and full of valour and endurance. Lord Northbrook responded for the navy. Mr. Gladstone, who had an en- thusiastic reception, in responding for Her Majesty's Ministers, said tbey had now been fifteen months in charge of affairs. In consequence of the partial paralysis of the machinery of legislation the session now drawing to a con- clusion was disappointing in its results. It had, unfortunately, been necessary to restrict liberty in Ireland, but he trusted the Government would be enabled to add to the Statate-book a measure which would leave the history of the session not altogether un- honoured. Referring to foreign affairs, he observed that the country had been travelling on the way to peace and tranquility. A Convention destined to establish friendly and, he hoped, permanent relations between Great Britain and the European community of the Transvaal had just been signed. T.wo important territorial questions which upon Ministers taking office remained over from the •Berlin treaty had been settled.—the Montenegrin frontier and the Greek frontier questions—and that without bloodshed, thanks to the European concert and ultimately to the good sense of the Sultan of Turkey. Lord Hartington replying for the House of Commons, said when the history of the past session was written it would be found to be mainly a record. of the achievements of one man, a record of the energy and resolution, of the knowledge and the resource, with which one man had conducted a great measure through the House of Commons. Mr. Bright also addressed the assembly. The right hon. gentleman referred to the "defective state of the legislative machine," and remarked that it stood greatly in need of repair if the "tre- mendous amount of business of the Empire" was to be got through. There must be considerable changes, but "above all it seemed to him necessary that the House should be composed of men with a gentlemanly spirit." The Irish Land Bill Mr. Bright pronounced to be as great and noble a measure on that question as it would be possible for the English Parliament to pass. "If when it is passed the Irish people are not able to discover that it is a great measure of satisfaction and redemption for their country, they will be simply unable to understand a policy which has been in- tended directly for their benefit."

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: STATE OF IRELAND.

About 2,000 men with 50 horsea on Monday assembled on the property of Dr. Thompson, County Wicklow, and erected a substantial house for the tenant who was evicted last week. There was a large force of police preEent. A number of Emergency men have arrived near Boyle to save the harvest of a Boycotted tenant, under the protection of a large force of military. The Dublin Freeman says:—When the Land Bill went to the Upper House it would have been accepted by Ireland as a boon and a concession. It would in its present shape be regarded as an insult and a mockery. The Lords have be- haved with cowardly audacity. The Express says the Lords have been moderate, and it trusts they will now be firm.

The discharging of the Boycotted ship was resumed at an early hour on Tuesday at Cork. Owing to the de- meanour of the crowd, there were present 50 of the Rifle Brigade and 50 Dragoons.:Stone-throwing at the dischargers, car drivers, military, and police was resumed. As the laden carts passed through the streets stones were thrown from the backs of houses, and one man has been seriously injured. Gillabbey-s'reet was ripped up in two places to prevent the passage of the carts containing the Boycotted timber from the ship to the schools on College-road. THE LAND LEAGUE AND ITS FUNDS.-011 Tuesday, shortly before the close of the Land League meeting, a scene occurred.—The Rev. Fr. Russell, of Charleville, county Cork, addressing the chairman, said that the branch of the League which he represented had applied to the central body for assistance, and the response they got was that unless they let their farms be sold by the Emergency men there would be no expenses paid from the league. Hp wished to know whether this response was correct. If so, he, as president of the Branch League, would no longer be re- sponsible for it. Ile had had an interview with Mr. Dillon. —Mr. Rylett rose to order, and objected to the introduction of Mr. Dillon's name.—The Rev. Fr. McCree confirmed the statement of Fr. Russell.—The.Chairman said the matter was one for the Executive of the Land League.—Father Russsell again rising to address the meeting the Chairman peremptorily ruled him out of order.—Father Russell, speaking in a loud voice, aid the whole matter should be explained. Large sums were coming in to the Central League, and no one knew where they went to. The whole matter should be investigated. They would not let themselves be turned out on the roadside in order to let the Emergency men buy their farms.—lt is stated, that the cor- respondent adds, that the design of the League has been to allow the Emergency Committee to purchase farms where rent disputes arise, which then become a useless burden to the committee and hamper their action.

div.head: CRICKET AT IHJYTON. myt, E. JACKSON'S HUTTON ELEVEN v. HASLINGDEN.
div.p: CRICKET AT IHJYTON. myt, E. JACKSON'S HUTTON ELEVEN v. HAS- LINGDEN.

One of the best matches played on the Huyton cricket ground took place on Wednesday. when a team from Has- lingden, including Nash (one of the county bowlers) and a team selected from the Hnyton and Sefton clubs, but chiefly from the farmer, by Mr. E. Jackson, were opposed to each other. Mr. W. H. Crook, a lover of manly English games, had been mainly instrumental in getting up the match, and he must have been fully satisfied with the result of his exertions. The match was timed to commence at eleven o'clock, but owing to the rain a start was not effected till about two o'clock, when the sky cleared and the rest of the day was fin.. although there was a strong wind blowing from the wesl, which materially interfered with the progress of the game. The visitors were the first to handle the , bat, with V. Shelton and G. Whittle being their first repre- sentatives, against the bowling of Messrs. F. Jones and H. Rigby. Two overs having been given an adjournment was made for luncheon. On resumption of play, Jones in his next over displaced the stumps of Whittle, and the latter's place was filled by H. Eastwood. Stallon succumbed to the bowling of Rigby immediately afterwards, and the next corner, W. H. Lord, after scoring a single, was disposed of by the same bowler. Harwood, who followed, p!ayed the ball on to his wicket without scoring., Pinder now joined Eastwood who, in the meantime, hadteen playing good cricket and had made several good hits off both bowlers. At 52 Raper took the place of Rigby at the wickets and tried his "lobs," and at his third ball Pinder gave a chance to square leg, but it was not taken. In the next over, however, of Jones, Pinder was dismissed, and directly afterwards the same bowler managed to find his way to the wicket of Eastwood after a careful and well-hit innings of 40, which included two 4's, five 3's, four 2's, and singles. Nash and J. Brown then became partners, but a separation was soon effected, the latter batsman beim, bowled by Roper after making a couple. His successor, L, Rawston, received his discharge from Roper the first ball, and soon afterwards he was fol- lowed by Nash who bad also succumbed to the." slows." At 87 the last man went in, and at 94 H. Eccles relieved Roper at the wicket, and another single having been added, the tenth man, T. Speed, was bowled by a bailer from Eccles the innings closing for 95. .

At 40, however, Roper returned the ball to the bowler (Nash) after adding a score of runs, including three 3's, three 2's, and singles. H. Eccles, who follow, was run out at 49, and he was sac- needed by Marriott. At 63, Rigby stepped out to Nash, and, missing the ball, was aharpty stumped, after a freely-hit inn- I logs of 23, including three 3's, three 2's, and singles. The next man, W. Jack- son, who, having scored nine, was caught and bowled by Nash, and he was succeeded by F. Jones. Soon after, Marriott was "bulleted " by Nash, and his place was filled by F. Jowett. The score now stood at 87 for the loss of nine wickets. A trio having been put on) Jones was caught behind the wicket. When the last man (C. Aldrich) went in, the telegraph board. showed 90, and the chances of winning the games seemed to be rather critical, but Aldrich, with one or two well-directed hits secured the victory amidst exceeding loud applause. tolerably well-conducted man.—The Bench sentenced him to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. A BUTCHER FINED M.—Elizabeth Darlington, butcher, of Bridge-street, St. Helens, was• summoned by Superinten- dent Johnston for having in her possession for use in trade 17 weights which were unjust, and 4 unetamped. On the 29th July, the Superintendent found the following weights in defendant's shop :—One 561bs. weight a ounces light; one 561bs. i ounces light; one 561bs. 1 ounce- light; one 281bs. 1 ounce light; one 71b5.4 drachms light; one 41b5. 4 drachms light; one 4lbs. 3 drachms light; one 41bs. 2 drachms light; one 21bs. 1 drachm light; one 2lbs. 1 drachm light; one 21b. 10drachms light; one 11b. 1 drachm light; one 11b. 1 drachm light; one *lb. * drachm light; one lelb. 2 drachms light; one *lb. f drachm light. There were also four weights undamped. The Superintendent said this was the worst case he had ever seen or read. of.— Colonel Gamble said there was no doubt the public had been defrauded by defendant giving light weight, and she would be fined £.3 on the first charge, and £1 on the other. —Alphonais Delimit, grocer, Bridge-street, who did it appear for having in his possession for use in trade a 21b. weight a drachm light, and 11b. weight a drachm ligld.— He was fined 30s. and 12s. costs. SurmlNG Dams TO DRUNKEN MAN.—Ellen Silcock, New Church tavern, Weatfield-street, was fined 10s. and costs for supplying drink to drunken men, and with per- mitting drunkenness on the premises. TAN MAINTENANCE OF INCOB.RIGIBLE Boys.—Thomas Kelly was summoned to show cause why he should not be ordered to contribute to the support of his son, who is now in a reformatory at Liverpool.--P.C. Peebles said he had made inquiry, and he had ascertained that defendant was a chemical labourer at Gamble's works, Gerard's Bridge, and earned 16s. per week.—Colonel Gamble said that although defendant got low wages, it was not to be supposed that other people should keep his children.—Ordered to pay is. a week.--Lawrence Garvin was summoned in respect to his son.—Defendant in this case was in reedit of 245. a week, and was employed at Mr. Crosfield's works.-2s. a week ordered.--Anthony Ban- nister, one of the men who was robbed and assaulted in Chain-lane, Parr, on Bank Holiday, and who described him- self as a fruit hawker, was ordered to pay is. a week to- wards the maintenance of his son.
WEDNESDAY.—Before His Worship the Mayor (Alderman
Harrison.

A &MANGE OLD Wcaukte..-1--Ania, Padden. an old woman, was charged with sleeping in' the open air and not giving a good account of herself.—P.C. Young said the prisoner was sleeping•in an entry off Phythian-street, Eccleston, where she had been for the last seven nights. She had some old furniture there, but it was not worth anything. The re- lieving officer had taken a cab to her to take her to the workhouse, but she would not go. Several had offered to take her in,lut she declined their offers. She had been warned several times of the consequences of her sleeping there.—The magistrate: You have been warned, and you would not go to the workhouse when you had the chance. You will have go to prison for seven days, and see if that will do you any good. A. DESERTER.—Wm. Fright was charged on his own con- fesssion with being a deserter from the • 96th Regiment of Foot, the Brigade Depot, which is now at Ashton-under- Lyne.—lnspector Wood said that a telegram had been re- ceived from the commanding officer corroborating the pri- soner's statement.—He was committed to gaol to await an escort. CHAreme or STEALER° Co.—Joseph Topping, a married man, was charged with having stolen a quantity of coal from a wagon the property of the London and North- Western Railway ,Company, that morning.—A detective officer in the service of the company said he was Watching the coal wagons at half-past seven at the Havailah Colliery, when he saw the prisoner get on the top of a wagon, and take away a lump of coal, which he carried about ten yards, when he put it down as a platelayer was about to pass him. He then apprehended him.—Remanded. TUESDAY.—Before His. Worship the Mayor (Alderman
Harrison.

A DAUGHTER ROBBING HER MOTHER.—Mary Walsh, a young married woman, was charged with stealing a shawl, a pillow slip, and a sheet, value 2s. ed., the property of Mary McEgan, wife of John McEgan, Rimmer-street, Parr—Pri- soner took the articles while the complainant was absent from the house and pawned them at Mr. Alonon's shop.— Complainant said his daughter was very good and very kind when she was out of drink and bad company.—Prisoner, who said " some "of the articles belonged to her, was re- manded until Friday. A Pawner/in YOUNG Womix. —hmily Hunter, a young woman, was charged with being-drunk on the licensed pre- mises of David Kenny, in Liverpool-road, on the previous night.—Mr. Kenny said at a quarter to eleven, on the pre- vions night, the prisoner, who was drunk, entered his house. He told her to go away, when she got hold of a bottle and threw it at him, but fortunately it missed him. He then gave I her into the custody of the police.—Sergeant Jackson said I prisoner was drunk when he booked her.—Prisoner, who has served a month for assaulting the police, a month for drunken conduct, and who has been fined for drunkenness, was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment. —Pri- soner, who had appealed for a lenient sentence, was ap- parently pleased with the decision of the magistrates, whom slat rewarded with a polite " Thank you." A WANDERING LUNATIC. James Swallow, a rough haired man about 50, with shaking limbs and vacant looking eyes stood in the box, and nis described by the superinten- dent as a wandering lunatic, whom P. C. Smith had found early that morning measuring the road.—Magistrate r What have you to say, Swallow. What are you doing here ? Nothing. What were you doing yesterday? I was at my house.—ln the house? Yes.—What house? Where I live, in Ilague-street.—Where do you come from? Gorton.— What have you been doing for a living? Well, nothing, always working,—Are you going back again? What are you going to do? Stop where I am.—What, in prison? Swallow (smiling): No, I don't know about that.—He was then taken below to be given into the charge of a relieving officer. BREAKING A MAN'S LEG.—Luke Mullen, a middle-ageff man, who has been several times remanded, was charged with having, on the 4th June, inflicted grievous bodily harm upon Thomas Taggart. Superintendent Johnston said that two men were in the Norton Arms public-house in East-street. Prisoner drank some beer belonging to the complainant. Some words arose between them, and ultimately blows were struck. The landlord turned them both out into the street, and there the prisoner kicked complainant violently on the leg.—Coraplainant said he was a labourer, . and at present resided at the Whiston Workhouse liospital. At the time of the affray he lived in Market-street. ' While the disturb- ance was going on the landlord turned them both out, and prisoner' who had hold of him, threatened to knock his head ' off, and he would do the same to anyone who took his part.

On getting Outside prisoner kicked him violently on the left leg causing him to fall, and whilst down on the ground be kicked him again on the same leg. He was unable to get up, and•was taken inside the public-house, then carried to his lodgings, and subsequently taken to the Workhouse.— Dr. Hall, visiting surgeon, said he found the complainant suf- fering from a wound on the lower part of the left leg, with fracture of both bones. Although plaintiff could now wl,- pretty well, he was not very strong., and would not be able to commence his work for a forttliknt.—ln answer to Super- intendent Johnston, whims,' said that one kick would be sufficient to inflict the injury.—Prisoner: Could that wound be done with a fall as well as a kick ?—Dr. Hall: The two combined would do it; but the fall itself would not produce the wound.—Prisoner; If that man's leg came in contact with the edge of a kerbstone could not that wound have been cans, and with me falling at the top of him ?—This question was not answered.—After Mr. Leigh, the landlord, had given evidence, prisoner was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool sessions.

div.head: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.

131" A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. [SP EC I A L] NO. XI. JAFFA OR JOPPA. At eight o'clock on Wednesday morning, March 9, we found ourselves standing out on the verandah of the Jerusalem Hotel, Jaffa. I say in my note book, "Here we are, landed on the shores of Palestine, after a pleasant run of twelve hours from Port Said. Looking from the verandah southward, we have the town of Jaffa rising on the face of the hill, with its pyramid of houses overlooking the Mediterranean on the right, and sloping down to the well cultivated plain on the left. In the immediate fore- ground are orange groves of considerable extent, the land- scape being dotted with palms and enlivened with neat residences, mostly erected by the American and German colonies established here some few years ago. The air is breathing around us as fresh and balmy as on one or our sweetest May mornings in England. The dew drops glistening on herb and flower remind us that we are no longer in the dry sultry clime of Egypt, and we almost wonder how in so short a space of time, we have made such an exchange. Were we not last evening on Egyptian soil, within a few miles of the burning deserts of Ghizeh and Sakkara, with their weeping pyramids and desolating sands? Yes; but it is equally certain that this morning, as we came on deck of the crowded steamer, the glorious sun was rising over these Judean I hills, fringing their beautiful outline with his brighter beams, and flooding the landscape with the softer glow of his more diffused light. These Judean hills! Where is the heart over which Christianity has thrown its Divine spell, that throbs not to look, for the first time, upon these Judean hills ? But to have them bursting upon your vision bathed in sunlight such as this, with the orb of day coming forth from his chambers behind "the seeet singer's' own hills; while his lofty minstrelsy, in celebration thereof, is rolling in well remembered strains through the soul; why, it was a surpassing joy, an earthly day-dawn rsore to be remembered in one's life history than any other. But oh, the landing on Judea's shores! Tell it not in Gath ; publish it not in Askelon, lest, even now, the Philistines should rejoice! Such a jabbering, fighting, pushing, haul- ing, screaming! I wonder how we ever got into our boats without being thrown into the water. The turbaned Arabs, with their loose calico tunics half covering their brown legs, were skipping in swarms around us like so many chattering monkeys, making the passage down the companion ladder to the stern of the boat a struggle for very life. We all managed it somehow, and got safely away from the side of the ship. But how are we to reach the shore with these breakers running in, and all these rocks standing out of the water? Between these immense sea-washed blocks, rising three or four feet above the surface, and spreading right and left, there is but one entrance, about twelve feet wide. Well, through it we go by the quick, vigorous use of the oars, and consummate knowledge of the situation. But, now, where shall we land? We see no harbour, no pier, no quay! The little landing place jutting out of the ramparts is crowded with boats, contending more fiercely for priority than they did alongsde the ship. Our boatman decides to land us through an embrazure in the sea-wall, and runs in among the rough, slippery stones, over which we have to make our way, picking our steps over their jagged points, and having to stoop pretty low to get through the wall. After thus landing, we find ourselves in a filthy lane, which runs inside the sea-wall, and leads to the northern outskirts of the town. Along this lane we have a dull, heavy wall hiding cut the view of the sea on the left; under foot an unpaved and unsewered street, covered with a sickening accumulation of filth, offensive both to sight and smell; and on the right a succession of dark, unhealthy looking alleys and open stores. Such are the surroundings for I about half a mile; then we come to the open country, on our way to the hotel, with the thick cactus hedges and orange groves on the right hand and left. The Jaffe oranges, let me say, are unsurpassed for size and juiciness, nor is the flavour inferior to any we gat in England. The i richest flavoured oranges grown n Eastern climes would not bear transporting to our shores, but we had them very plenti- fully supplied on our journey. Before we reached our I quarters we heard a wail on the road side, and looking round sew three lepers holding out their twisted fingers, and grin- ning horribly through their blotched and distorted features. We wondered how m iny of these poor, diseased ones we were to see in this old land of miracle-working without the gracious Redeemer's power to heal and bless. All we could do was to throw the " backsheesh " and pass on. But now breakfast is ready, and we must leave the verandah and isetake ourselves to the table. After an enjoyable repast, we sally forth to ply our respects to Simon, the tanner's house by the sea-side. I fear the house is as little to be men as Simon himself. No town on the face of the earth has passed through rougher and bloodier scenes than Jaffa. Bombardment after bombardment from the days of Solomon down to the present day, have reduced the town to ruins again and again; yet here it stands, restored from its ashes, and covering its ancient cone with a compact munition of houses, just as it must have done when Jonah sailed between these olhi rounded reeks to find a living grave, and to roll about in his cradle of blubber over the very sea that stretches before us. As to Simon's house, the one they show for it is doubtless of great antiquity, and it is, also, well out of the way. Lying almost the furthest house to the south, it is just possible that, while all the central ram- parts might be levelled to the ground, this little nook might have escaped. We partly took it for granted, as we stood upon the roof on which Peter is supposed to have had his vision, and gave audible thanks to God for having permitted us through many dangers to stand there, and, wile looking over the Mediterranean in the direction of Greece and Rome, to remember the wonderful means He took, on this very shore, to send His redemption to Gentile lands. Our vener- able friend and companion, Mr. Richard Allen, of Dublin, read the 10 of Acts, and we felt it Reed to be there. In the yard, as we came down the time-worn steps from the roof, we saw two men drawing water, with a skin bucket, out of a very ancient well. I hope they had no sinister desire of giving us a christening; but certain it is I got sprinkled , from head to foot as they emptied the bucket into a jar. I Passing again through the bare, white-washed house, with t immensely thick walls and arched ceilings, me were shown the place where Peter's meal was a-preparing when be fell ' into the trance, and were then very politely conducted to the door by a sister of charity, who evidently (personifica- tion of the highest Christian virtue though she was) felt the blessedness of receiving quite as much as we did that of , giving. Our steps were next directed to the English school 1 for Arab girls, under the care of Miss Arnot, whose zeal and ability in the work she has undertaken are deserving of all praise. Being a lady of good family and possessed of considerable means, she has evidently entered upon her arduous mission, and is prosecuting it, I with all the passion and energy of a pure and loving soul. Her desire to improve and elevate the condition of the ' people in this ancient doorway into Palestine, she allows no ' opposition or difficulties to quell or overcome. All honour to such women! We feel humanity exalted and ennobled in their presence! Here is a lady, as delicate and shrinking in nature and disposition as one of her sex can be, cutting herself off from country and friends, in order to devote her- ' self, her means, her every energy to a work, which she deems of paramount importance in contemplating the future of this sacred land! In the face of an organised and , persevering opposition, she yet secures a large plot of ground, selects from it a site for her schools, and then sells the remainder for as much as she paid for the whole plot. Then, lest the enemies of her mission should triumph by the work hanging too long in the wind, the noble woman t commences to build with her own means, strong in faith that, when the work is fairly in hand, friends in England . will come forward to her help. We were glad to hear that her appeal had been responded to, £BOO having been contri- buted the year before last, and £7OO last year. The building is large and substantial, and its internal arrangements admirably adapted to the climate. Mrs Allen,.of our com- pany, addressed a few nice words to the girls, founded upon her own mission experience in the east of London, and then sang, "Safe in the arms of Jesus," "Shall we meet beyond the river," and, in Arabic, "Sweet by and by," which sounded very sweetly. Seventeen Arab girls are boarded, and from 50 to 70 day scholars are taught in these schools. JAFFA TO JERUSALEM. The choosing of our ponies for the journey to Jerusalem was the next serious business. I had mounted mine, and was waiting for the rest on the road leading down to the town, when I saw two of our company coming tearing down the hill. "Stop the horse, it has run away !" screamed one of the riders in evident terror, while his companion, who was nearly blind, held on like grim death. My pony was eager to join in the race, true the instinct or habit which, makes all Arab ponies as prone to follow. as they are averse to lead. The two John Gilpin's managed to pull up at the bottom of the hill, and, in a fee/ minutes, the whole caval- cade, numbering, with attendants, about 22 persons, was on its way to Ramlah en route to Jerusalem. The north-eastern Outskirts of Jaffa through which we had to pass, are as truly Oriental in aspect as anything we saw in our travels. Before we reach the Jerusalem gate, which leads to the plains of Sharon, the market place or bazaar presents a ecene of varied interest. It motley groups make up a picture, in some sort a picture of Cairo, only a little more brightly tinted. Camels woe lying lazily chewing in the • gun; asses were standing about' or driven through the lanes of fruit piled up on the ground. In the midst of his mer- chandise sat the turbaned trader e sa bearded and bare-legged, while the purchasers,chiefly f b men and veiled women, in their many "ert colouredii c t eb , own costumes,r passed to and fro, bargaining over the various commodities spread out before them. These consisted f maize, coffee, sugar-cane, dates, ties, grapes tomatoes, and the large oval shaped oranges, whose splendid colour built up in higher mounds gave additional brightness to the scene. A more truly Oriental picture can scarcely be conceived, one's feel- ing was to linger until it was more vividly imprinted upon the mind's eye, but there was no waiting, on we must go, or we shall be left behind. Leaving Jaffa, we travel along a road on which the pen of history, from the earliest times to the present, has written more eventful records, in deeper and more thrilling lines than perhaps are to be found on any other pathway in the world. Over these sandy tractsthe feet of God's chosen people for ages trod. Along then the stranderiu Gentile worshippers from earth's remotest bounds went up to see the glory of the Lord, and to pay adoring homage in His temple. Since then, and during all these long dark Centuries of Israel's shame and banishment, the hoof of the war horse and the tramp cf armed men have

rushed into bloody conflict and spread devastation and carnage through the land. Roman, Saracen, Cru- sader, Turk, Egyptian, Frank, have all sent legions hither to see them scattered in heaps on these sandy roads, and pour out their life-blood on the too thirsty soil. One hour's ride brought us to the fine old well, near to the Arabian village of lamer. Here the road branches off to Lydda to the left, and, five of our party hav- ing resolved to see the place of Peter's early labours, and the place from which he was summonet when he raised Tabitha to life, an Arab guide was appointed to accompany us. Leaving the main party to pursue their way to Ranaleh, we rode forward through ploughed fields and sandy roads, flanked with thick cactus hedges, until we came near to Lydda, when our nearest path was through widely spread- ing olive groves, the shade of whose beautiful trees was exceedingly pleasant. Every step of the way we felt to be holy ground. Along this very way the Apostle Paul must have gone. I wondered whether, if we had met him travell- ingcicted step,the rapt x eye - et e towards Joppa on that memorable day, his aspect and bearingpres sn woof uhhils saintly y farrestedice, the collected calm attention—would gleamingl4 ts to withtb celestiallonely w fire—haveayf airer drawnp rProbably a boluyr t h oug not! tderTitge quick, discerning, spiritual eye Cometh only by prayer, and p yer, and by such communion with heaven as men like Peter enjoyed.
(To be continued next week.)

The following extracts from letters written by Dr. Verco one of the gentlemen who accompanied the writer of the above "Travels in the East" may prove interesting to our readers, more especially as some members of the party are well known in this district. Dr. Verco writing from Cairo says :—We went to see the howling dervishes, and a more ludicrously abominable sight it would be difficult to conceive. Standing in a ring around a priest they bowed and howled to the music of drums, while one of them spun round for a quarter of an hour. Then we visited the bazaars and had the good fortune to witness the return-of a good pilgrim from Mecca. A very rich man. He had all the dervishes or priests he could get in procession with banners, and bands, and singers, and incense, and scent, and readers from the Koran. He is sure to go to heaven be- cause he has been to Mecca. In the evening we went out to see the street dogs, and saw them, and more, a torch light procession, and the people sleeping in the streets on wicker- work bedsteads; so light that they could easily take up their bed and walk; in fact we saw very many so walking with the whole apparatus on their heads. To-day we have been as far as Boulak, to the museum of Egyptian antiquities, where we saw a great many mummy cases, and models of the chief of the old gods Osiris, Apis, and Isis. Since I left London, so much has crowded in upon me, so many new scenes, that I appear to have lived a year or two. Travelling teaches one a great lesson, to appreciate home a little more. I shall love England and the English more when I get home, than ever I have done before. It will require a good deal of soap and water and a new house, before I will consent to marry the Sheiklis daughter. On Sunday morn- ing we went out intending to go to the Presby- terian meeting, but when out found the service was in the afternoon. So we went to the Coptic Chapel. Here the service was concluded, for it appeared that it began about six o'clock. However, we managed to lay hold of a deacon, and learned from him a good deal about church gov- ernment and doctrine. How that the babies are baptised, twice up to the chin and the third time right over their head. We secured a little loaf of bread too with a square in the middle for the Saviour, and twelve little squares and tri- angles all round for the twelve apostles, which little loaf of bread has to be bought and eaten by those who do not attend to the Lord's Supper. We saw three funerals, and some of the party went to the Church of England Chapel for a bit. On Monday we went by coach to the great Pyramids at Gizeh—day beautiful. Very good road; quite pleased. Went up the pyramids; Mr. , Mr. Nimno, and the old clergyman preferred the base to the summit. It was not nearly so bad as I anticipated. Then we went into the pyramids. This was very odd. The passage so long and so low, one had to crawl on hands and feet; so up and down that one Arab was required to pull up and another to push up, and so dark that another had to carry a candle. I was surprised, astonished, and pleased with pyramids sphinx tombs; but of all the abominable pesterers for "back sheesh " ttle Arabs beat all. All the hours we were there these fellows were so close to us as we could walk in front, behind, and on both sides, a franc or half a franc, a piastre, a rupee, half, quarter, anything for lighting a candle, for carrying a water bottle, for catching hold of your arm when youtold them to leave you alone, a cigar, a penknife, anythirg in your pocket; buy this a mummey. a string of beads, a fossil, a handful of coins, and what they would ask a Napoleon for, that is, 16s. 8d they would sell eventually for a shilling. Backsheesh, at the pyramids, I never forget. On the road home I bir- gained with a little Arab, who was running by the carriage, for both sets of earrings she had on. She sold them for 10d., and then made money by them, which shows the poverty of the squalid wretches, and yet their love of finery. To-day we have been to the Island of Rhoda. It is in the Nile, not quite in the middle. It is all built upon. It is said to have been the summer palace of the Pharoabs, and the place where the infant Moses was found by the King's daughter. There are no bulrushes to be seen near the Place. Here, too, is the Nilometer, a!post down at hole, which communicates with the river. Asthe river rises se the water rises in this hole or room, and from marks on this post the height of the • river can be told, and from this can be roughly prophesied whether there will be famine from too little rise, plenty from just the proper rise, or destruction from floods to too high a rise. We didn't see Pharoah's daughter, nor the ark of bulrushes. In the afternoon we went to see the palace of ' the Khedive, a magnificent place. In the garden he has a menagerie, with full half a dozens lions, as well as a hyena, L ; a panther, jackals, elephants; in fact a small zoological col- lection. When one sees a good road, one knows it leads to a house belonging to the Khedive or one of his relations, and when one see i good house, he knows it s sure to belong to one of these. All our party are pretty well. I was a , little queer on the top of Cheops ; but I was well again ' ; before I came down, and have been quite well since.

At the fortnightly meeting, held ,on Tuesday, at the Workhouse, Dutton, the Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were present, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, W. Handley, T. Norman, G. S. Hazlehurst, J. Knowles, W. J. Mclntyre, James Darbyshire. W. Pickering, W. Whittaker, W. Fisher, and H. Linaker (clerk). VIE PAUPERISM OF THE UNION. Mr. HearnugY referred to the report by Mr. Dansey on the pauperism of the county, and said the pauperism of the Union had largely decreased, being exactly 1 per cent. lower than in 1872, which was a larger per centage than any other Union under Mr. Dansey. He noticed that the decrease was to be accounted for largely by the better administration of relief. Relative to the indoor and outdoor pauperism, in 1872 their per centage of pauperism indoor and outdoor was 15 in 85 out, but now there was a decrease in the number of paupers outside, there being 21 indoor and 79 out. The better administration of relief, which the Board inaugurated seven or eight years ago, had had its natural effect in better- ing the condition of the paupers themselves, and of course the Union. In regard to the cost, they found it compared very favourably, and, while it cost £645 in 1872 to keep 168, it was only costing now £6lO to keep the same number, so that the house was extremely well managed. The same proportion occurred in regard to the outdoor relief, which in 1872 amounted to £2,147, and now £1,656, a difference of £491 on the half-year. In round numbers that was over £l,OOO a year, so that they were better off now than in 1872. (Hear, hear.) When they considered the amount of relief ‘, given was on a more liberal scale—as in that period they I had 2s. 6d. per week as an average, and now Sc. 61—and \they had effected this saving, he thought it was very satis- factory.

THE STATE OE THE HOI7SE. The MesvEn (Mr. It. Jones) reported that there were 166 inmates as against 155 in the corresponding week of last year. During the week 10 men, 3 women, and 2 children vagrants were relieved ; and 14 boys and 23 girls were receiving industrial training at the Workhouse. Out-door relief has been administered to 593 persons at a cost of £59 16s. 3d. (Runcorn £33 33. 3d., Frodsham £l4 17s. 6d., Budworth £ll 155.), as against 641 persons relieved at a cost of £6l 78.9 d. in the corresponding period of last year.

REPORT ON TOTE COUNTY ASYLUM. The deputation, consistinß of the Rev. 3. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. T. Norman, W. Hmdley, J. Challinor, and H. Linaker, which .paid the annual visit to the County Asylum, Upton, Chester, on the 20th July, reported that at the asylum they were courteously welcomed by Mr. Davidson, the medical superintendent, and were conducted to two spacious corridors in which had been previously assembled the whole of the inmates chargeable to the Runcorn Union, 31 in number-18 males and 13 females—and one of whom had been there since 1852. They remained with the inmates a considerable time, and were of the unanimous opinion that they were kindly treated, being well cared for in the import- ant matters of food and clothing, and were surrounded with every inducement and encouragement favourable to their irn to society.

BURNING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON. —Au inquest was held at the White Hart Inn, Sankey-street, on Satur- day, by Mr. Driffteld, on the body of the man named John Murphy. . It appeared that deceased worked at Messrs. Horton's foundry as labourer to a moulder named George Lloyd. On the 26th ultimo, Lloyd was engaged with de- ceased carrying a pot of molten iron for the purpose of cast- ing railway chairs. They were walking quickly along some iron plates when deceased, who wore clogs, slipped and fell. Deceased was going first and about a pint of the liquid iron from the pot fell upon his breast and shoulders. The molten metal set him on fire, and one of the men got a bucket of water and threw it upon deceased, who was then wrapped in a sheet and taken to the Infirmary. Here everything was done for him that could be done, but he died on Thursday ' morning, the 4th instant. He was sensible up to Wednes- day, and did not blame anyone for the accident. Some of the other labourers wore clogs, but. there were no printed rules as to what they should wear in the foundry. Mr. Horton said the men had no occasion to walk over the iron plates. They simply went over them as a nearer way to their moulds. There was no rule forbidding the we of clogs in i thel,. v! cddis, but he was quite willing in future that there . should dbe °fle. —The jury returned a veldi,t of "Accidental death," ad recommended that the t.:le of clegs should be ! prohibited in tits woks.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 13, 1881.

WIDNES LOCAL BOAITI. The monthly meeting took place on Tuesday. Mr. E. Eustace Carey presided, in the absence of Major Cross, and there were also present Messrs. Sadler, Shuttleworth, Ker- shaw, O'Keeffe, Knight, Brown, Heves, Handley, Forster, Allen (clerk), Roberts (engineer), iligginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector.)

MR. BEASLEY'S AFFAIRS. The CHAIRMAN read the following (copy) communicat ion: —"Great Western Railway, General Manager's Office, Pad- dington, London, July 25,1881. Dear Sir,—l enclose here- with a notice addressed to the Local Board, and to you as their clerk, requesting the Board to pay tome all moneys due to my brother, their late clerk, under the terms of an agree- ment dated the 24th of November last (of which the Board had notice on the same date) whereby all moneys then due or thereaf,.er to become due, for costs, salary, or disburse-' merits were assigned to me to secure payment of a loan of £4OO and interest, of which £3OO and interest still remains unpaid. I give this notice, first, because I understand that my brother's bill of costs to December last has been taxed and allowed at £1,789 145. 7d., and that it is proposed to pay the money to other parties; and next, beca use I am told that, notwithstanding the notice of the 24th of November last, the Local Board have made payments to my brother on account of salary. It is unnecessary to say that want nothing but what is right; but, on the other hand, I cannot afford to lose £3OO and see everybody else paid but myself, and I must therefore insist upon the notice of Nov- ember last 'being acted upon. I had notice of the Bank's prior charge, but of no other; and, as at present advised, I can recognise no other claims unless and until the parties prove their right. lam in a position to give the Board a complete discharge, and, if necessary, will send you by an early post my brother's order to pay the money to me, and accepting receipt therefor. Please acknowledge receipt of the notice.—Yours faithfully, A. BEASI,EY.—T. Allen, Esq." The CHAIRMAN (continuing): I suppose that we had better send this to the Finance Committee ? Mr. KNIGHT: Does this emanate from Mr. Armond , Beasley? Mr.-BROWN : We have never heard of him before. Mr. HEYES : Mr. Beasley, our late clerk, gave a number of cash orders on the Board, and until certain persons are paid he is not entitled to anything. The CLERK: I acknowledged this letter, and said that it would be placed before the Board. Mr. HEYES remarked that the Board were not compelled to pay anything but what they owed. Mr. BROWN asked how the Board would be situated if they had paid some one else the money spoken of in the lefter ? Mr. HEyES: But we don't Pay anybody. We pay nothing but what is due to Mr. Beasley. The simple fact is that there were certain accounts mentioned in Mr. Thos. Beasley's bill for law expenses. One of them was that of Mr. Beasley's London legal agent, and we found that our late clerk had not paid these accounts, which were left in the bill and charged to us, but were not paid. The taxing master left these metters in the bill on the Understanding that we paid the people to whom they were owing in full. It DOW ap- pears that Mr. Beasley, or his brother, objects to us paying these people, and until the matter is settled, we shall not pay anybody. Mr. HANDLEY: You have not paid any of these cheques over since the last meeting? The CLERK: No; none with the exception of first charges on Parr's Bank. , It was agreed, without any formal resolution, to leave the, A:PROPERTy .13 I matter its the hands of the Finance Committee. A VISIT FROMowTIINEERBs& A , SPsOYC 1 After the Chairman had stated that a communication had i TAE er,Ts'io been received from Mr. Darlington, the Local Government Board auditor, fixing the date of the coming audit, he re- marked that Mr. Allen had placed in his bands a letter ad- dressed to Major Cross from the Widnes Owners' and Ratepayers' Association, dated the Bth inst. It stated that it had been resolved that a deputation from the members of the Association should attend the monthly meeting of the Board for the purpose of discussing with them matters re- lating to the new rate; and requested the Major to arrange with the members of the Local Board to receive them.—Mr. HEYEs : That is the first I have heard of the matter ; but I may remark that the rate was passed two months ago. Under those circumstances, I think it would be a waste of time to receive the deputation for the purpose of discussing matters having relation to the rate. The CHAIRMAN: Would it not be respectful to let them know that it is too late to receive a deputation on the subject ? Dr. O'KEEFFE : I would tell them that the matter is not now open to discussion.—The CLERK: The ratepayers have so many days allowed in which they may inspect the rate book.—Mr. BROWN: What opportunity is there for them to raise any objection if they want to do so 7—The CLERK : I think they simply ask for the interview as a favour from the Board. It ey have had the proper legal time allowed in which to make an inspection of the rate book. A certain number of days' notice is given, and the fact is published all over the town that the new rate book can be seen at this office. I believe the notice given is seven days, during which the ratepayers are also allowed the opportunity of making any extract from the estimate which they may wish.—Mr. BROWN: Ido not think that this is the right time to receive a deputation on the reetter.—Mr. SADLER: Well, when is the time to make any objection 2—Mr. BROWN : Mr. Allen says that there are so many days allowed them in which to make any objection to therate.— I —Mr. SADLER : I don't think they wish to raise any ob- jection, but they simply desire to obtain some information as to certain of the items in the estimate.—Mr. HEYES : It is quite preposterons to think of discussing the matter now.— The CHAIRMAN: The Board ought to be glad to receive a deputation of ratepayers at any time.—Mr. BROWN was of opinion that when a gentleman came to the Board meetings the fact that he represented any particular section of the public should not be shown by any remarks he might make; that feeling should all be put upon one side. At the same time if any of the ratepayers wished to be provided with certain information, he should be one to move that it he given them.—Mr. HEYES : Of course it will be given them if they apply at the proper time.— Mr. SADLER: Surely it cannot be called a waste of time to see the deputation, if they want proper information.—The CHAIRMAN: I see no reason why, if a deputation from any body of ratepayers wish to see us upon any subject, we should not admit them, but still I think they have expressed themselves in a somewhat unfortunate manner by talking of discussing the matter with us.—Mr. REYES said it was quite open to the Board to admit the deputation. At the same time, any member who happened to have business at home coald retire,—Mr. SADLER: What are they to do if they wish to make any objection to the rate?—Mr. HEYES : They may object by refusing to pay the rate. If they wish to know anything: further they had better go to a solicitor, and take his advice upon it.—The CmAirtmA.N: I suppose, gentlemen, you have no objection to hear what the deputa- tion have to say.—Mr. HEVES: Yes, after the Board's proper business is over.—The CHAIRMA-N: For nay own part, I should receive anyone with the utmost courtesy.—lt was then agreed that the deputation should be received at the close of the ordinary business. At the termination of the proceedings, they were admitted to the Board-room. The following are the names of the gentlemen who attended from the Association: Messrs. T. Rimrner (chairman), G. A. Forster (secretary), D. Wright, John Hesketh, R. Balshaw, and R. Webster.—Mr. RIMMER asked what was the sum owing upon the old rate.—Mr. HF,YES said the total arrears were £676, and of this sum £367 was owing by people who had liquidated. The total amount uncollected, irrespective of the amounts owing by liquidating creditors, was £309 ss. 413. Mr. TIMMER next inquired if the new rate had been confirmed.— Mr. HEYES: Two months ago. Sir. RIMIER said it appeared useless to ask questions in re- lation to the new rate after it had been confirmed —The CHAIRMAN: I must remind the deputation that we cannot consent to discuss the matter, or to rescind any of our reso- lutions.—Mr. RIMIER remarked that the first item to which he had intended to draw attention in the estimate Wee one of £7OO for team labour. There was a second one of £250 for watering the streets, and another of £5O for a cart.—A MEMBER OF TICK DEPUTATION said he thought it must be rattier a smart sort of a cartto cost £so.—Mr. KERSHAW said the cart referred to seas not an ordinary one, but a watering cart. The deputation must not forget that though £5O Was put down as the estimated cost of it, it did net necessarily follow that the Board would give that sum for it.—A DR- PUTATIONIST wished to know what was the good of having an estimate to lay before the ratepayers if the amounts men- tioned were not adhered to in carrying out the expenditure. —The CHAIRMAN desired to draw the attention of the depu- tation to the fact that all the members of the Board were supposed to represenkthe ratepayers, hint there were two or three gentlemen belonging to it who were understood to dis- tinctly represent the Property Owners and Ratepayers Asso- ciation. Ile, therefore, was at a loss to understand why the questions which were then being pet by a depilation from that Association could not just as well have been asked by the members wino represented it. If the Board were ones to oegin discussing matters relating to their business with any gentlemen who choose to form themselves into a deputation. they would never have done. The ratepayers of the town had returned their representatives to the Board.—Mr. RUMMER (sarcastically): They do in some places—The CHAIRMAN: We cannot argue matters with you, but we are quite willing to explain anything in respect to which von , require an explanation.—ONE OF THE DEPUTATION : Will you tell us at what time you can argue questions with the ratepayers P—The CHAIRMAN:I do not think it is usual to argue questions with the ratepayers. Mr. Brut-Ann WenesvEß (energetically): Then it seems we have nothing to do with it but to pay the money. (Laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN: The ratepayers send their representatives to the Board.—Mr. RIMMER observed that he saw from the estimate that only £l5O were put down for public lighting, whereas last year the anmunt put down for it in the estimate Was After an an explanation had been given by the CHAIRMAN teen 05 apparent discrepancy in the charge for lighting in the est-Move, as compared with the previous year, Mr. liimMER said the sum put down for night-soil removal was £762 100. This seemed a largo amount.—The CHAIRMAN: It is not so very large is proportion to the popl,latlon as we have In el for several years past. It is less than that of most towns of the some population. If you look into the figures you will find that there is a strict proportion for the last three or four years.—Mr. RAMMER asked a question with reference to the intereet paid by the Board, which he understood to be shown in the tetimate as about seven per c-nt —Mr. FOSTER, nor of the deputatien, went up to the Chairman on the matter, 1 and the CLERK immediately explained that the Beard were not paying more than 4 per cent, for borrowed capital.—

The Cuairtivor said that the question just put evidently arose entirely from a misapprehension. There was no such percentage as 7 or 7:1- per cent, paid by the Board, and if the gentlemen composing the deputation had only called at the offices, any explanation they required would have been given them—Mr. RUMMER said there were two other items to which he desired to refer, one being to £205 for stationery and £5OO for legal expenses.—The CHAIRMAN said he did not see that the Board could do with any less quantity of stationery.

u mg MILK FOR PUSSY. Mr. SADLER said that in the Health Committee's estimate there was an extraordinary item, the total of a certain line including "milk for the cat." (Laughter.)—The CHAIR- MAN did not know whether the speaker intended his remark for a joke or not. However, he (the speaker) was perfectly aware that a cat was kept at the hospital, and that they had to pay for the milk which it used. The committee, no doubt, considered it necessary to have a cat in the building to keep out rats; but really such questions as these were absurd. He must tell the deputation he was very sorry they had taken up the valuable time of the Board with such puerile questions, answers to which could easily have been obtained from the accountant.—Mr. WEBSTER said that when members of the association went to the offices of the Board for the purpose of seeing the estimate, the book was certainly placed upon the counter for them, but they were not even invited inside.—The CHAIRMAN: I am sure you will always find the accountant very courteous.—Another Deputationist : Then there is another item.—The CHant- MAN : I cannot really answer any more financial questions. You can appeal to the auditor on any suck matter. That will be the proper time. Upon this remark being made some of the mem* bers of the deputation appeared considerably dissatisfied.— The CHAIRMAN: I must remind you that you have really no leoul right to come to the Board meeting and ask questions. —Mr. RIMMER : We think u e have.—The CHAIRMAN: W 3 are very glad to see you and answer you any legal questions you like.—A Deputationist : We have a right to come to the Board meeting as ratepayers. We can come here if we wish. —Another member of the Deputation: Haven't we a right to come to any Board meeting, even if we do not ask any questions P—The CHAIRMAN: No, you have not ; that is quite clear.—Mr.liEnsilkw said the deputation were perhaps not aware of the fact that the Board were not even obliged I to admit reporters to the meeting.—The CHAIRMAN said he believed this closed the Board's business; and the deputa- tion then withdrew with the members. GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. Mr. BROWN moved, and Mr. FORSTER seconded, the con- firmation of these minutes, from which it appeared that the engineer wished for instructions how to deal with requests which were frequently made to purchase soil or peat at Pax- hill.—Dr. O'KEEFFE moved and Mr. HAvEs seconded, an amendment to a proposition in the minutes recommending that the soil be sold at a certain amount per load.—The amendment was carried with two dissentient., and the original motion was then passed.

HIGHWAY MATTERS. The minutes of the Highway Committee were approved, on the motion of Mr. KEnsulw, seconded by Mr. SnurrLE- WORTH, and stated that prompt attention had been promised by the railway companies as to making their bridges "drop dry." Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., had been written to as to having encroached upon Gorsey-lane.

THE TWO SEWERAGE SCHEMES. At a joint meeting of the Highway and Health Commit tees, held on the 18th tilt., the committee having considered the sewerage scheme from Moor-lane to West Bank outlet, proposed by Surveyor, and estimate for same, prepared by Mr. Copland; also two routes and estimates suggested by Mr. Kersbrw and prepared by Mr. Copland--one from the Police Station to West Bank outlet, and the other from Police Station to Marsh Brook outlet—it was resolved that the Board be recommended to advertise for tenders to carry out the scheme proposed by Major Cross, from the outlet to Little Briton, Moor-lane' it being the shortest and cheapest route proposed. Instructions were given to Mr. Copland to revise the quantities and specifications, where requisite, and submit same to committee. The meeting was adjourned to the 22nd ult., when plans and estimates preparen by the surveyor for the sewerage of Moss Bank, Halton-view, Warrington-road, Albert and Deacon-roads were submitted. It was recom- mended that they be approved by the Board, and application made to the Local Government Board for borrowing powers to carry out the same.—Mr. KERSHAW proposed, and Mr. HANDLEY seconded, the adoption of the committee's recom- mendations.—Mr. IlEvEs: I should like to make a remark as to Mr. Copland. Is he the Board's surveyor, and, if not, who is ? Mr. BROWN said he could not be a party to sanctioning such a large scheme without re- ceiving a full explanation about it. Mr. KERSHAW observed that the reason why the joint committee referred the specifications to Mr. Copland was because the Board's surveyor had taken no interest in the scheme brought forward some time ago by Major Cross. In fact, Mr. Hig- ginson did not appear to have even made himself acquainted with the Chairman's scheme. The committee asked the surveyor's opinion, the other day, upon Major Cross's pro- posal, and he admitted that he was not acquainted with them ; and, under these circumstances, the committee could pursue no other course than they had. Mr. Brown must know very well that the Chairman's scheme had once been passed by that Board and also approved by the Local Government Board. The members were aware that he (Mr. Kershaw) introduced the surveyor's plans to the Board, and the jo:n1 committee agreed to undertake the work of ex- amining them, but the fuElbei tney proceeded with the in- vestigation the more they were convinced of their imprac- ticability. It was, therefore, made very clear to the minds of the members of the committee that they could not recom- mend the surveyor's plans for the adoption of the Board. The Major's scheme was found to be preferable to the one brought forward by Mr. Higginson, and it would only cost £14,000 as against the surveyor's £19,000. The Chairman's plan of sewerage would provide an admirable outlet for the whole town.— Mr. Buowl; expressed himself somewhat astonished at the remarks of the last speaker, as the ratepayers generally were under the impresion that the Major's scheme would cost £40,000 and Mr. Huigginson's only £12,000.— Mr. CHAIRMAN was aimed if he could throw a little light upon the matter, and he then said the joint committee had gone over the schemes very carefully. They found that there was a point common to both of them, viz., one near to Little Briton. From that place to the outfall Major Cross's scheme took one route and Mr. Higginson's another. The route proposed by the surveyor was a longer one; it had to go under a greater number of lines of railway, and it was more difficult from an engineering point of view. The Chairman's was the shortest route, and the least expensive. Mr. Brown had said something about Mr. Higginson's scheme costing only £12,000, but they all knew that this was entirely owing to the very cheap materials mentioned in the estimate for the work. If they were to carry out Major Cross's scheme with the same materials as Mr. Hig- ginson proposed to use, it would cost less than that of the surveyor's, which was a longer route, had more easements Ito pay for, and did not provide so good an outlet as the other. The joint committee considered the Chairman's scheme to be so clearly the best that they did not consider it necessary to call in another opinion upon the matter.— After some further discussion an amendment was moved by Mr. BROWN, And seconded by Mr. SHIITTLENVORTH, that a special meeting of the Board should be held on the follow- ing Tuesday afternoon, at three o'clock, in order to have the two schemes more fully explained.—The amendment was carried by a large majority.—The minutes of the committee were then passed, with the exception of that part relating to the outlet from Little Briton to the river. THE HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT. The Health Committee's minutes contained the Medical Officer's report, which showed that the births during the month had been 94, or 45.1 per 1,000; deaths (total) 36, or 172: including children antler 1 year 11, or 52; children between 1 and 5 years 11, or 52; zymotic diseases 4, or 1.9 accident cases I.—The market receipts for July had been; £25 13s. 5d., showing an increase of £3 9s. upon the same month in last vear.—The minutes were passed, on the pro- position of Dr:O'KEEFFE, seconded by Mr. HEYES. HOSPITAL COMMITTEE.

These minutes contained nothing of special interest. They were connrmed, on the motion of Mr. HANDLny, who said the Committee would esteem it a favour if the representa- tives of the press would publish the following list of presents received on behalf of the hospital from June, 1870, to the same month this year:— Flowers and plants: Mrs. Deacon, Mrs. James White, Mrs. Purvor, Mrs. Thompson, Mrs. Jones (Hale), Miss Mather, Miss Ellis, Mr. F. H. Gossage, Dr. McLennan, Mr. Kent, and Mr. Whitby. Vegetables and fruit : Mr. F. 11. Gossage and Mr. Liddell. Weekly papers : Widnes Weekly News, from Mr. Swale ; Illustrated London IVews and Graphic, from Mr. H. W. Deacon; Christian Herald, from Mr. Thos. Whitby. Books and monthly magazines: Mrs. Deacon, Mrs. Cooper, Miss Dean, Miss Mather, Mr. F. H. Gossaze, Mr. Brunner, Dr. McLennan, and a friend. Christmas cards for each patient: Mrs. Deacon and Mrs. G. J. J. Wells. Old linen : Mrs. J. L. Muspratt. Bath chairs: Mr. Simpson, Liverpool. Bed cradle: Mr. Barrow. Water bed : Mr. Knight. FINANCE: INCREASE OF MR. ALLEN'S SALARY. The tioance minutes stated that instructions had been given to the clerk to write Mr. Beasley asking Lim to hand ever all papers and property belonging to the Board in his hands, by the Bth instant. It was recommended that the clerk's salary be increased by £lOO per annum.—The , minutes were approved, on the motion of Mr. HEYES.

FOOT...AIM-MOUTH DISEASE. On Wednesday the Clerk of the Peace at Preston was informed that four more farms in the Blackburn Hundred were infected with foot- , and-mouth disease, as follow :—Ono animal affected out of 21 on the premises of Mr. Daniel Leed, Hayhurst Farm, Hutton ; three out of 23 on the premises of the Rev. James Pennington, Stonyhurst College, Aighton Bailey and Chaigbley ; six out of 23 on the premises of Mr. Thomas Hardiker, Water Side Farm, Aighton Bailey and Chaighley ; and five out of 16 on the premises of Mr. Henry Ward, the Oaks, Clayton-le-Dale. These bring the number of farms infected in the Blackburn Hundred up to 46.: ST. JO3.IN'S Crancen, HIGHER WAI.TON.—The annual Itea meeting in connection with St. John's Church, Higher waiton, took place on Tuesday, when about 300 school t' children and friends sat down to tea at Rosewood Farm (Sir GUkt Greenall's). Afterwards the Vicar 'gave an address, in whlch be stated he was gratified to find that such good feeling ,xisted between himself and the rarisbionms, end he hoped the echool might cc:loth-me to be successful. Rev. S. an,l Sir G. Green:lll afterwards gave addresses, !at he e mclusion of which an adjournment was made to Sir Gilbert's fields, where rices and games were indulged in.
