div.head: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

SAgunnAv.—Before Mr. John Brundrit. A NICE WELCOME ON LEAVING GAOL. William Mil, lington and Joseph Rowlands, who had been apprehended on corning out of Kuutsford gaol, where they had been serving four months' imprisonment for stealing fowls, were charged ' with having on the 17th February, stolen a cheese weighing 601b5., and one cheese box, value £1 18s., the property of Samuel Tomlinson, grocer and provision dealer, Albert-street off Lowlands-road. Prosecutor said the cheese produced belonged te him, and on the 17th February he had it safe in a cheese box at his shop door. He saw the cheese about seven o'clock at night, and missed it about nine, after which he gave information to the police. Some time before he missed it, he saw the prisoner Millington loitering about his shop door.—Mr. Bonkem, shoemaker, and father-in-law of the last witness, gave similar evidence.—Thontas Williams, provision dealer, Canal-street, said he was brother-in-law of the prisoner Rowlands. About three weeks before Edward Ball was apprehended on the charge of being conterne I in stealing the same cheese, the prisoner Millington and Ball came to his shop. Millington came inside and Ball stood in the doorway. Millington asked him if he would buy a cheese, and he replied that he did not sell much at his shop. The man then said that the cheese had been won at a raffle, and he would take 4d. per pound for it. He answered that he did not care about buying a whole cheese, as he could buy cheese at about 4d. a pound in Liverpool. Millington replied, "Well, if you will give me that for it you can have it.' He told Millington that he must see what quality the cheese was, and he then went away, but returned in about half-an-hour with the cheese produced. Ball came with Millington, and he (witness) heard Rowlands outside. He agreed to give Millington 15s. for the cheese, or at the rate of 4d. per pound. On the following night he gave Milling- ton 55., and he and Ball left the shop together. He had known the former prisoner seven or eight years.—Edward Ball, labourer, who had suffered one month's imprisonment for stealing the cheese, said that on the 17th February, he was passing the Delph Bridge. as he was going from his work, and met Millington, at whose request he went into Savage's fields to help him to carry a cheese. They found the prisoner Rowlands standing in the fields, and, on being asked where the cheese was, he said he did not know. They soon found it, and took it to Williams's shop in Canal-street, Rowlands walking part of the way with them.—Prisoners both denied their guilt, and were each committed to Knots- ford Quarter Sessions for trial, after pleading that they should he sentenced by the magistrate, as they would have several weeks to wait before the sessions were held. MONDAY.—Before Mr. S. B. Chadwick and Mr. C. W. Hazle- burst.

A DISTRESS WARRANT ISSUED AGAINST A RUNCORN SOLICITOR.—An application was made by Mr. Wm. Sutton, assistant overseer, for a distress warrant against Mr. Thos. Beasley, solicitor, of Overton, and formerly of Waterloo. road, Runcorn, and Widnes.—Mr. Sutton said that on the Bth March the Bench made an order upon Mr. Beasley to pay the sum of £3 19s. 9,14. owing for poor rate, in three days. The money had not been paid, though application had been made to the trustee in bankruptcy, who stated that he was not in a position to immediately discharge the debt. —The distress warrant was granted. PROSECUTIONS UNDER THE CANAL BOATS' ACT.—Joseph Jones, owner of the canal boat May Flower, was charged with tieing an unregistered boat as a dwelling, contrary to the Canal Boats' Act. Mr. Farrington, canal boat inspector to the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, said he saw the boat at Preston-o'-th'-Hill, on the 23rd ult., and on speakine to the captain about its being unregistered, he told him there was a dispute as to where the letters should be placed upon the vessel. The captein's master wished them to be put on the top of the cabin, and he (witness) wished them placed on the panel of the boat, so as to be in a conspicuous place, as required by the Act. Defendant admitted the truthful- ness of the inspector's evidence, and said that since the time referred to the boat had been registered. The magistrates ordered defendant to pay a nominal fine of is. and 10s. 6d. coets.—Hugh Barlow, boatman, was also summoned for con- travening the Act by using his boat as a dwelling for six people when it was only registered for three. Mr. Farring- ton stated he saw the boat in the township of Preston-o'-th% Hill, on the 23rd ult., and there were three adults and three children on board. The defendant said he had only taken the children for a trip, as they were on their holidays. Mr. Farrington said he found out that defendant's children attended school very regularly, and, under these circum- stances, he would only ask for a nominal penalty.—Defendant was fined 61. and 14s. 61. costs. THE WOMAN AND HER LOVER.—Henry Ornle, a tall powerful-looking fellow, was charged with assaulting a woman named Martha Taylor, with whom he formerly co- habited, on the 2nd int.—Complainant said she did not wish to proceed with the case, but the Bench said she must give her evidence. She then stated that defendant knocked her down and blackened one of her eyes.—The magistrates sold it was not the first time defendant had been before the eourt, and he would have to be taught that he could not treat a woman in such a manner with impunity. He would be fined 20e. and 9s. 61 costa, or, in default of payment, be imprisoned one month with hard labour. A RIGHTLY SERVED SLEEPY DRAYMAN.—Frederick San- key, draymin in the employ of Sir Gilbert Greenall, was charged with having been asleep on his dray on the high- road, on the 26th ult.—P.C.Biker proved seeing defendant asleep on his dray as it was being drawn on the highway at Helton.—The Chairman said this was not th fir.t tim defendant had been before them. Last year he was con- victed twice and once in 1876. The public ran a great risk through the conduct of men like defendant. It was the duty of the magistrates to inflict a heavy fine in such a case, and defendant would have 40s. and 14s. 6d. costs to pay, or, in default, be sent to gaol one month. THE LANDLORD AND HIS CUSTOMER.—A man named Thomas Watson was charged with assaulting John Harding, landlord of the beershop Lord Rodney.—Complainant said that about half-Cast ten on the previous Tuesday night, de- fendant came into the house and had two glasses of beer, after which witness had to go into the cellar. On returning he found defendant thrashing a man named Jones. He told him to desist, and as he would not, he ordered him out of the house. Defendant refused to go, and said he was master there. He then told him that he should bring him before the magistrates, on which he hit him at the side of the head and " threatened to kill him as dead as a worm." Com- plainant at first said he did not wish to give evidence in the case, as defendant had a wife and children, and had for some time been out of work.—The Chairman remarked that the Bench had insisted upon Harding giving evidence, as though his tenderness of feeling might cause him to be dis- inclined to do so, it was necessary for the public good that people like defendant should be taught they could not be allowed to conduct themselves in such a manner. He would have to pay 10s. and costs 9s. 61 THE BOATMAN AND THE DONKEY: A STRANGE CASE.— John Smithom (50), apparently a boatman, was charged with cruelly illtreating and torturing a donkey, by biting it on the nose.—The case excited much interest in the town, and there was a large attendance of the public. James Buckingham, a man who sells hot potatoes about the town, in a machine drawn by a donkey, said that on Saturday night, about twenty minutes to seven o'clock, he was in High-street when defendant came up and bought a penny- worth. Smithom commenced to tease the donkey by lifting up its legs. He asked him to let it alone, on white he said "All right." Witness then went to the back of the machine, and on doing so turnel his back. Immediately afterwards he beard defendant saying to the donkey "This is the last one; thou wilt have to give me a kiss for this. Smithom then seized the animal by the nose and bit it with his teeth. Defendant held to its nose until he got up to him. In fact he held it so long that the donkey had time to swing him round the shafts. The donkey's noes bled, and witness wiped it with his handkerchief. He afterwards took the animal to the farrier, who found that the animal's nose was bitten right through. He told defendant he was very much in- clined to have him locked up for what he had done, on which he answered "You can do your best." He believed the man was drunk at the time.—A lad named Robert Cooper gave corroborative evidence.—Superintendent Wil- tiamsen said he had brought the donkey to the outside of the court, so that if the magistrates desired to see it they could do so.—The Chairman (to defendant) : You have pleaded guilty to an action both disgusting and revolting— one which seems more like that of a brute beast than of a human being: and you will be sent to prison for one mortb with hard labour.—At the close of the court defendant made an earnest appeal to the Bench to let him off upon the payment of a fine. He stated that at one time he was an abstainer for seven years, and it was only through drink that he had done such a thing. In fact, be was so drunk at the time that he had not the slightest recollection of what took place.—Mr. Chadwick said the magistrates would not re- consider their decision, and they could only express a hope that the sentence passed upon defendant would have the effect of making him a better man in the future. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds.

STEALING A SEIRT.—EIIen Howard alias Emma Hol- land, was charged with stealing a shirt, value 4s. 6d., the property of Samuel Worrall, hatter, High-street.--Samuel Greaves, painter, at Mr. Tonks's shop, which is on the op- posite side of the street to that of the prosec,tor, said be was standing near bit master's place of business, when be saw the prisoner go into the doorway of Mr. Werrall's es- tablishmeni, and take the shirt from a hook on which it was hanging, nut it under her petticoat, and then go into Mr. Charles Houghton's greengrocer. The prisoner was re- manded, on the application of Superintendent Williamson, in order that enquiries might be made as to her character. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. James Reynolds (chairman) and Mr. John Brundrit.

A DEALER IN BAD FISH SENT TO GAOL. Thomas Crackle, fish dealer, of Northwich, was summoned by Mr. John Parry, inspector of nuisances to the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, for having, on the 13th of November, last year, exposed for sale, on a stall in Ellesmere-street, 19 ' pieces of hake and 21 pieces of ray fish, which were unfit for toed, and also with not appearing to a summons issued against him.—Mr. Parry gave evidence as to taking posSes- sion of the fish, which was bad, and having it destroyed by a justice of the peace. He issued a summons against the prisoner, but he did not apnear.—Crackle, in answer to the I Bench, said that he was away in Liverpool when he should have been at court. He bought the fish in the city market, where it had passed the inspector. He was sure , there would have been no seizure made of it if it had not tren for 2R ellyiOßS person informing against him.—Mr. Parry said the prisoner was selling the fish at about a penny per pound.—Mr. Brrpdrit: I should think it wa, a very good thing that the Inspector was told, widen vett were poisoning peopfe.—TM Chairman said the VreNl'alons -prisoncr would be fined £5 aril costs, 235. 10c1., OT in default _of payment, one month's imprisonment, wigs hard labour.— 1 Defendant, who according to the technigat a the
Act under which he was convicted had rendered him- self liable to a fine of 1.800, said he could not pay the money. _

AGGRAVATE) ASSAULT BY A SUTTON YOUNG MAN.—John Foyer, brickyard labourer, aged 19, was charged with com- mitting an aggravatectassanit on Mary Bermardine Walling- ton, aged four years, the daughter of Mr. Wallington, manager at Sutton Bcmeworks.—Superintendent Williamson said that on the previous Sunday afternoon, a little after two o'clock, Mr. Wallington directed his daughter to go to a field adjoining the premises of the bone manufactory, and in the occupation of Mr. Acton, to see if she could find a mush- room. She did so, and whilst there the prisoner went up to her, and, by telling her she could find a large number of mushrooms in another part of the field, took her into a less exposed portion of it, where he eotnmifeed the offence. The girl screamed, and ultimately got away. Prisoner was arrested on Wednesday night, and at first denied his guilt, but on the way to the lockups admitted it.—P.C. Egerton, of Sutton, proved taking the young man into custody.— Prisoner, who only looks about 16 years of age, in answer to the Bench, said ho lived with his mother, who was a widow with eight chiidirn. He admitted his guilt.--He was sent to gaol three months, with hard labour, ailed the Chairman said he hoped the sentence would be a warning to him in future.

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. Mr. J. Harrison (chairman) presided on Wednesday,. at the meeting of the Board, and there were present the Rev. G. T. Roberts, Major Cartwright, Messrs. Oven, Hall, Darbyshire, Mackie, Greenall, Fairhurst, Appleton, Hunt, Blaekhnrst, Cooper, Woolfall, Garnett, Heaton, and J. C., Sutton (clerk.) ETHR UNION FINANCES :—ImPoRTANT:sTATEmENT. Major CARTWRIGHT asked how the out-door relief com- pared with that of last year. The CLERK: It is rather over my estimate. Major CARTWRIGHT : I am rather sorry to hear that be- cause we have a larger number in the house. There is nearly 30 of an increase to what there was this time last year. The CHAIRMAN: You are of opinion that the out-door relief would in the same ratio have diminished? Major CARTWRIGHT : Yes. The CLERK said he wanted to call the Board's attention to the increase in the state of the finances. He might tell them, to begin with that the balance in the bank in the treasurer's hands was about £9OO, and that day they had cheques in round figures from £2OO to £3OO, so that the balance would be reduced to about £6OO. He had an order before him to pay on the 22nd inst. £2,428 18s. Od. to the county treasurer. The Board had no discretion or control over the expenditure of that money, but were simply required to provide it from the public rates. ' Mr. DARDYSHIRE: It's a shame. Major CARrwraoarr : Oh, no; it is paid out for the lunatics is it not? Mr. COOPER : Oh, no. The CHAIRMAN: It is the county rate, contribution to asylums, arc. The CLERK said in making the estimates for the ensuing half-year, one Of the difficulties they had to deal with was in relation to amounts over which they had no control, and as to which they could only take averages; and therefore he presumed he should be about right in his estimate if he averaged the county expenditure at something like what it was in the corresponding half, when it was £1,603 38. 56. The consequence was that this half-year the sum demanded was £9OO over the estimate. The two sums for last year, £1,607 13s. 10d. and £1,603 3s. 56., gave £3,210 17s. 3d. That was for Lancashire only. The sums for this year were for Lancashire £1,748 85. Id. and £2,428 18s. 96.; total, £4,177 6s. 101, as against £3,210 17s. 3d., or an increase of £966 9s. 76. Mr. APPLETON asked, supposing a county rate was levied, what the amount would be. The CLERK said he would try to answer the question. The county rate warrant for July, 1880, compared with that for this year was as follows: For a county rate proper £253 98 6d, this year £l9O 25 (that is a reduction) ; for lunatic asylums last year—this was in addition to the lunatic bills the Board paid quarterly-1190 2s id, this year £570 6s 46. Mr. APPLETON asked how much that was in the £. The CLERK said—for county lunatic asylums 3-16 parts of a penny in the Z. The county bridges last half-year cost nil, this year £3O 68 Pd; constabulary £842 15s, this half-year £1,007 4s ; prisons last half-year £63 7s 46, this £l9O 2s 16; main roads and West Derby Hundred bridges last half-year £253 98 6d, this £440 17s 6d. The contribu- tions for county rate purposes.were—Burtonwood last half- year £124 6s 2d, this half year £175 5s lid; Cuerdley £4O 3s 86, £69 us 46; Haydock £2ll 2s, £3ll ds 106 ; Houghton £2O 158 4d, £29 7s 2d; Newton £370 13s, £524 4s 26; Penketh £55 10s 6d, £7B 10s 6d ; Poulton £44 103, £62 18s 7d; Rixton £6O 184 56, £B6 3s id; Sankey £64 711, £9l Os 46; Croft £46 Os 6d, £65 28 Id ; Warring- ton £424 Is lid, £752 15s sd; Winwick £94 138 Bd, £129 17s 26; Woolston, £37 Is 3d„ £52 8s 21 To meet the expenditure generally of this ball year, he estimated sums amounting in three payments of £2,929 13s. 46. to £8,789. If they took from the contributions those of fhslll.fthiret trunnihipa Ihn ',flunky rake now- borer° tli Dvaul almost came to one of the three sums levied for all Union purposes. The Board had spent about £7OO in alterations and extensions not estimated; but he had no doubt that could be well saved out of the ordinary expenditure of the half year. He would be able, he believed, to get through with the present money subject to the Board having early calls made in the next half year. But he must call attention to the great neglect ob- served .in meeting these calls in some of the townships. The whole of the money ought now to be paid in as the first call was due on the 2nd May, the 2nd on the Bth June and the 3rd on, the 3rd August. Yet of those three sauna of £2,929 there was now in arrear £4,966. Burton- wood he could not complain of as the overseers had paid their, first and second calls; Cuerdley had paid the first and second; Grappenhall the first call only,. Haydock first call only, Houghton first only, Latchford first; Newton had not paid him a penny. Major Caserwinearr : That is very creditable to report of the overseers! Mr. Coorzn: It is a good job he is not here. The CHAIRMAN: Have the overseers of Newton been com- municated with? The CLERK: These warrants have been served upon them, as upon other townships. Major CAnrwarener : How is it you have allowed them to be in arrear so much. There is a little favouritism, is there not? The CLERK: Oh, no. I say distinctly these amounts are due upon the dates stated in the warrants served upon them without any other notice from me. Major CAR:mimes= : Have you personally had a Con- versation with Mr. Winstanley ? The CLERK replied that he had rot. It was, of_course, not fair that several townships should keep them going when other townships were holding back. Penketh had paid the first call, Poulton first, Rixton nothing, Sankey had paid all three, Southworth nothing, Thelwall first and second, Winwick first and second, Woolston all three, War- rington first and second. The whole of thesearneunts in arrear were past due, and he was now in the position that he had practically about £6OO left, when under any circum- stances he ought not to have less than £l,OOO in hand over immediate demands. Mr. BLACKIMIZST asked what the calls for the first two quarters realise supposing they made the overseers' pay up. The CLERK said it would be a difficult matter to dissect the calls and payments in that way. They were all due. Major CARrwmairr: But these calls that are behind hand in Newton and elsewhere, do you knowlwhether they are collected ? The CLERK: I have no doubt the money is in hand. Major CARrwraoarr : But what is their object in keeping it from you? The CHAIRMAN: "Nemo " fund. The CLERK: I think there may be something in that. Major CARTWRIGHT : I think We ought to insist upon the first and second calls due being paid at once. Mr. HALL asked if the overseers did cultivate a " Nemo " fund, what became of it? The CHAIRMAN: The Clerk is forbidden to tell the secrets' of his office. Mr. DARDTSHIRE asked whether any other union were in- creased in the same proportion as Warrington. If so, there must be an immense amount of money required for some purpose. The CLERK said all the unions in the West Derby Hundred were proportionately increased Replying to Major Cartwright, he said he would have had a very favourable balance but for this increased call. Mr. BLICKHURST moved that the Clerk be instructed to take proceedings to compel the payment of the calls. Mr. COOPER seconded the motion, as he thought it was a great injustice, some townships having paid two calls and others none at all. Mr. HALL supported it, and said be would almost go so far as to demand the payment of the third call. He did not see why the sverseers should keep the money at all. Raves , no encouragement to the ratepayers to pay the money if it was kept in hand. Major CARTWRIGHT hoped that before long the office of overseers would be swept away entirely her they were per- fectly useless. The CHAIRMAN thought it likely they would be swept sway. Mr. BLACKHURST said so far as the Warrington overseers, were concerned every shilling went into the bank as soon aa they got it. After a little further discussion the motion was passed. • RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. MO Builders, Property owners, and otherS. Deposit - of Plans. The Burro:am IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS draw attention to the „Building Byelaws, which provide that every person who shall intend to erect or alter any building shall give Notice to the Commissioners, fourteen days pre- vious to its ordinary monthly meeting, of such intention by writing, delivered at their office, and shall at the same time leave, or cause to be left at the said office, a detailed plan and section, drawn to a scale of not less than one inch to every eight feet, showing the position of the buildinisa and appur- tenances of the property immediately adjoining, which are within ten yards of the proposed buildings, the width and level of the street, the level of the lowest floor of the intended build- ing, and of the yard or ground belonging thereto, the position, form, and demensions of the several parts of such building, and of the water-closet, privy, cesspool. ashpit, well, and all other appurtenances and means of supply, together with the proposed line of house drainage, and the size, depth and inclination thereof; and NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that the Commidsioners will not entertain any plan with respect to which the above re- quirements are not complied with —By order. WILLIAM BROOKS, Secretary. Public offices, Runcorn, August 10th, 1881. -

LIVERPOOL TO YORK. The revival of the Stage Coach, with its bounding steeds ' and far sounding isugle, was a pleasant reminder of the good old days when railways were not, although there are few who would care to recall the times when "George the the Third was'King ; " yet the remembrance of bye-gone days, with slow means of transit, and difficulty in reaching distant towns; no penny post; no gas; no telegraph, has a charm for the lju4s-. ^^-;12.! of the latter half of the pint, teenth century. In those days the existence of large Arms like THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY would have been an impossibility. A Coat purchased at a very large outlay had to last a man's lifetime, and descend from father to son, as a valued acquisition. With the introduction of railways and machinery, commercial enterprise in the , manufacture of Clothing, as in other branches of trade, effected a complete revolution. "Our Boys" of the pregeht day are clothed in a manner our grandfathers would not. have dreamed of. Talented artists are engaged In designing, and thousands of specially trained workpeople In making up, dress for the Boys. A quarter of a century ago THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY com- menced their operations, starting with a thorough know- ledge of the trade, and large capital at command. They soon became known in the commercial world for the uni- form excellence of their Men's, Youths, and Boys' Clothing; and probably at the present time they are the largest lidanufacturers of Clothing in the World. They reject all but the most reliable material in their manufacture; and, by constant supervision in the minutest details, maintain the pre-eminence they have obtained as producers of Clothing for all Classes: THE GRAND CLOTHING HALL COMPANY, 28, 30, & 82, BBIDGE-STREET, WARRINGTON; ROCHDALE, PRESTON, SHEFFIELD, DEEBY.
